When medical student Emmanuel Oyebadejo went to watch his friend's American football game, he had no idea he would end up being scouted himself for a sport he had never even played.
He wasn't even interested in it. In fact, while still at school in Manchester he'd delivered a speech titled 'I have a dream' in which he outlined plans to do "very well in basketball, return from the NBA and be the prime minister of the United Kingdom".
But now, four years later, he is being tipped to become the first Briton to be a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.
It is a rapid rise for the 22-year-old, who had to learn the game from scratch and win over his parents who "begged" him not to play and instead focus on his medical studies.
His biggest challenge at the start, though, was finding a pair of boots big enough for his size 16 feet.
It was 6ft 6in Oyebadejo's physique that had caught the eye of the coaching staff at Exeter Demons when he was a spectator for his friend's university game that was taking place at the club's home ground, The Crumb.
"I was talking to one of the other coaches, Jack Mullins, and we sort of turned around [and thought] 'that guy's freaking huge! We should go talk to him'," Lydon Ward-Best, one of the Demons' coaches, tells BBC Sport.
Oyebadejo had been a talented basketball player, playing for Manchester Magic - one of England's top junior clubs - from the age of 11 to 18. But by the time he was at the University of Exeter he was no longer playing competitively.
Lydon Ward-Best persuaded him to give a new sport a go.
"He started coming to training and just had the most ridiculous intro to American football I think I've ever seen," the coach adds.
A straight-A pupil, who had also learned the piano, guitar and drums while studying medicine, Oyebadejo had always been a quick learner.
"I always say that American football is kind of like violent chess," says Mullins, the Demons' current head coach.
"[Emmanuel] got the violent bit pretty quickly. He was fine at that - 'I am much bigger than you, watch me go'.
"The chess bit took a little longer because there's all these things that you have to think about."
But as Ward-Best puts it, "he's not just a big sort of jock athlete, he's a smart guy. He is so dedicated and disciplined with everything."
Oyebadejo played for the Demons at the end of the 2022-23 season, before the team went unbeaten in his first full season, 2023-24. When back home he also played for the Manchester Titans and helped them win the Britbowl in September 2023.
By December 2023, he decided he wanted to take things further. Could he make it in the United States? Would college teams be interested if he sent them videos of his highlights?
Coach Ward-Best told Oyebadejo it would be "tough", adding: "You know the percentages are not on your side here, but you are 6ft 6in and 280 pounds (20 stone), so you've got a better chance than most.
"I wanted to be realistic with him," he adds. "But I said I'd do whatever I could to help get him out there."
Emmanuel's father Oladini says he thought it was a "joke" and that he did not support him playing this "dangerous" game, explaining: "He had never played this game before. He'd only done it for a few months, so why would anybody from America want him?"
But they did.
There was interest from several colleges and Oyebadejo ended up at Jacksonville State, where he would study biology and play under legendary college coach Rich Rodriguez, having managed to win his parents round thanks to the influence of an uncle who lived in Dallas and understood the sport.
His first season was hit by injury but, despite coming up against players who have played American football since they were young children, his second was a big success.
As a defensive end, Oyebadejo's job is to get past the offensive linemen trying to block him and tackle the ball carrier or claim a sack - when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
He recorded 4.5 sacks, forced two fumbles and had 41 total tackles during the 2025 season.
Now the big college teams were paying attention.
College football is America's most passionate sporting pastime. While the NFL plays on Sundays, the college game dominates Saturdays during the autumn months.
And Oyebadejo transferred to the University of Florida to play for one of college football's biggest teams in the most prestigious conference, the Southeastern (SEC).
The Florida Gators are three-time national champions, have about 50 former players currently in the NFL and get home crowds of 90,000 at 'The Swamp'.
Oyebadejo was undaunted as he burst on to the scene. He had 2.5 sacks in a win at rivals Auburn in September and followed that up by impressing in big wins over Mississippi and Texas, the latter in front of 103,989 people.
After barely being on the radar of NFL scouts at the start of the season, Oyebadejo's form has propelled him into contention to be an early-round draft pick in 2027.
NFL teams do not have youth systems or academies. Almost all players have come through the US college system and they are recruited via the NFL Draft when they graduate.
One of the biggest events in the American sporting calendar, the NFL Draft takes place over three days in April, with the 32 teams taking turns to select players across seven rounds.
First-round picks in April will be guaranteed a rookie contract of at least $19.1m (£14.4m) and they are often fast-tracked into starting roles. The contract values decrease in a sliding scale so, for example, a third-round pick (top 96) will be guaranteed $7.3m (£5.5m).
Among the latest prospects, ESPN's veteran draft analyst Mel Kiper has ranked Oyebadejo as the fifth-best edge rusher (defensive end). That is regarded as the sport's second-most important position behind quarterback - and therefore the second-best paid in the NFL.
The reason is that Oyebadejo has everything needed to be a starting defensive end in the NFL. Firstly, his height and weight are ideally suited for the grappling battle required in what is known as 'the trenches'.
He has very long arms (7ft wingspan), perfect for winning a wrestling match against the kind of enormous opponent he faces, and unusually for a man as big as him, he's extremely quick. That's the money-making trait.
Although he now weighs about 300lbs (more than 21 stone), it is believed he has a remarkable body-fat percentage of about 12%. All his measurables are seen as ideal for a defensive end, if not better.
There are simply very few people with Oyebadejo's physical talent, and given the fast-tracked nature of his rise in American football, he does not look as raw as you might expect.
"He's British and has only played the sport for three [full] seasons," says his mentor and former coach Ward-Best. "You'd therefore think he must be very green, but he doesn't look that way.
"The physical qualities are clearly there but he's worked a lot on mastering aspects of the position as well."
Menelik Watson, also from Manchester, holds the record for being the highest-drafted British player. He was the 42nd pick in 2013 and spent six years in the NFL, earning a total of $16.4m (£13.7m).
London-born Osi Umenyiora, the 56th pick in 2003, enjoyed an illustrious 12-year career - winning two Super Bowls with the New York Giants.
"I have spoken to Osi, he's a really cool guy," says Oyebadejo, who is also of Nigerian heritage.
"To be a first-round pick out of the UK, it would be amazing. It would do so much for the American football community back home."
Oyebadejo impressed again in an upset win at Kentucky on Saturday and has 4.5 sacks with two regular-season games left. Florida could then play in a 'bowl' game, an end-of-season exhibition.
After that, Oyebadejo is expected to participate in a physical-testing event called the 'scouting combine', where he will be assessed by representatives of all 32 teams in March.
The draft then begins in Washington DC on 27 April, and if Oyebadejo hears his name called, he will complete an unlikely journey and make his now fully supportive parents very proud.
"It's mad," says Ward-Best. "I've been doing this for 20 years and I've never seen anything like this. We almost have to pinch ourselves."
Oyebadejo has stayed in touch with his former coaches in Exeter. The Demons hold watch parties for Florida games and there is a real sense of pride over where his journey began.
"It was just complete chance that he wanted to wander up to The Crumb and watch a game, just being there for his mate," says coach Mullins.
"If those things didn't happen, we wouldn't be having this conversation. He would be four years into his medical degree."

The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks
Global climate negotiations fell apart as delegates tried to tackle AI’s growing carbon footprint.
Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this”
To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit.
Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice).
With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever.
To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside.
Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency.
“That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event.
In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found.
To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation.
Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall.
“Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”
“In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”
There was some progress. Around 80 nations signed onto a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy consumption to 35 percent over the next decade, according to COP31 president Murat Kurum. The list of countries that includes, however, hasn’t been published yet, Carbon Brief reports.
Another voluntary pledge to keep AI from derailing climate action by calling on data centers to run on less polluting energy also failed to garner much support. Douglas notes that by using the term “low-emission energy,” the pledge still leaves the door open for natural gas (which produces less carbon pollution than coal when burned but is a significant source of methane pollution) to keep powering data centers.
“The Antalya A.I. pledge is a step in the right direction to address an important piece of the impacts, but needs teeth in order to translate into stronger protections for people and the planet,” the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council said in a statement when the pledge was first announced. “The speed, scale and scope of this challenge is bigger than perhaps anything before it, and the guardrails must be commensurate.”

It seems India's fintech investors may have counted their chickens too early. The timeline for the much-anticipated merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions has been deferred further down the calendar. The proposed monetisation of India’s UPI ecosystem was expected to be a post-Diwali bonus for digital payment companies, with a promise of a much-needed revenue stream after years of operating in a largely zero-MDR environment. However, uncertainty around the rollout is now weighing on investor sentiment, with shares of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik enduring a sharp correction. Consequently, the optimism that once buoyed fintech stocks is fading. As of Friday (November 20), Paytm parent One 97 Communications had already fallen as much as 10.8% over the past week, while One MobiKwik Systems declined 6.6% and Pine Labs dropped 9.4% on the BSE. According to a Financial Express report, the implementation of MDR could be deferred until after the 2027 assembly elections in five states, amid concerns over potential pushback from merchants and trade associations. There has been no official confirmation of a revised implementation date. The proposed framework envisages a 0.4% MDR on eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000, subject to a cap of ₹300 per transaction. Certain categories, including railways, telecom, insurance and fuel, are proposed to attract a flat ₹5 charge, while P2P transactions and specified small merchants would remain outside the framework. For payment companies, MDR represents more than an incremental revenue stream. It offers a route to monetise transaction volumes that have expanded rapidly but historically generated limited direct revenue. Initially scheduled for October 15, the rollout was first deferred until after Diwali. Now, the prospect of a further delay has put the earnings assumptions behind recent brokerage upgrades under scrutiny. With the market jumping the gun on UPI monetisation, what does it mean for companies like PhonePe and Razorpay that are preparing for their public-market debuts? But before answering that, let’s understand how much MDR earnings upside was priced in for Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik. When The Market Jumped The MDR Gun The September MDR announcement had triggered a wave of bullish brokerage commentary on payment companies, with analysts betting that the proposed charges would improve the economics of UPI transactions and open up a new source of recurring revenue. For Paytm, the potential upside was particularly significant. Goldman Sachs estimated that the framework could generate incremental EBITDA of around ₹1,400 Cr for Paytm in FY28 under a high-end scenario. The estimate represented 43–70% of its existing FY28 EBITDA projections, highlighting the potential scale of the earnings opportunity. The brokerage maintained its buy rating on the stock. Jefferies and JM Financial raised their target price to ₹2,150. JM Financial estimated incremental revenue of ₹210 Cr in FY27 and ₹470 Cr in FY28, with incremental adjusted EBITDA reaching ₹440 Cr in FY28. Pine Labs was another expected beneficiary, given its large merchant-acquiring and payment acceptance business. Jefferies estimated an incremental revenue opportunity of ₹160 Cr by FY28, equivalent to approximately 20% of its FY28 EBIT and profit estimates, and raised its target price to ₹235 from ₹180. Emkay, meanwhile, projected ₹155 Cr in UPI MDR revenue for FY28, assuming a realised take rate of six basis points, and increased its target to ₹230 from ₹190. The opportunity was supported by Pine Labs' transaction mix. In its Q2 FY27 investor presentation, the company said more than 70% of its digital checkout point transactions were UPI-led, with monthly UPI gross transaction value (GTV) of approximately ₹20,000 Cr. More than 65% of this UPI GTV came from transactions above ₹2,000, potentially placing a significant portion of its merchant payment activity within the proposed framework. Pine Labs also said its monthly UPI GTV could reach ₹33,000–34,000 Cr by FY28. MobiKwik, too, outlined the potential benefit. During its November earnings call, cofounder Upasana Taku said MDR implementation could add at least ₹100 Cr to the company's payments revenue in FY28, although the charges would be shared among issuing banks and other payment ecosystem participants. Atul Thakkar, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, believes the recent sell-off in the fintech stocks is largely a reversal of the optimism surrounding the proposed framework. “This is MDR euphoria unwinding, not a change in the businesses,” he said. According to Thakkar, the trigger was the report of a further delay, with no new implementation date in sight. But the magnitude of the correction needs to be seen against the rally that preceded it. In the period around the September MDR announcement, Paytm rose approximately 11%, MobiKwik 12% and Pine Labs 21%. From their November highs, the stocks have fallen 8–11%, with Pine Labs returning to early-September levels. Paytm shares rose 7% to ₹1,903.05 on Thursday, hitting their highest level since listing in November 2021. “The market priced in more than a normal expectation, and that excess is what has come out,” said Thakkar of Anand Rathi. The MDR uncertainty also brings to the fore: how much of the optimism surrounding listed fintechs was fuelled by the promise of the proposed framework, and how much was grounded in the strength of their underlying businesses? Fintechs’ Other Revenue Engines All three fintech companies had reported profits in the latest quarter even without any MDR contribution. The proposed charges, therefore, were not what made their businesses viable. Instead, they offered an additional revenue stream that could improve the economics of payment processing and accelerate profitability. It is particularly relevant for Paytm. Its management has also sought to position MDR as an incremental opportunity rather than a prerequisite for growth. CFO Madhur Deora had said earlier that UPI MDR was an upside to the company's business model, not fundamental to it. The company's financial services revenue, which grew 49% YoY to ₹912 Cr in Q2 FY27, also points to the growing contribution of businesses beyond payment processing. For MobiKwik and Pine Labs, too, the case for growth extends beyond the proposed fee. MobiKwik is looking to build out its financial services business, while Pine Labs has revenue streams across affordability, issuing, online payments and international markets. The larger issue, Thakkar's assessment suggests, is not whether these companies can grow without MDR, but whether investors had begun treating the proposed framework as a more certain and immediate earnings driver than it actually was. Therefore, with the implementation date still unclear, companies may have to demonstrate that their core payment and financial services businesses can sustain growth and profitability without relying on the additional MDR contribution. MDR Overhang For Upcoming IPOs The uncertainty comes at a crucial time for India’s fintech sector, with several large private companies preparing to test the public markets. The correction in listed peers could influence valuation benchmarks of players like PhonePe. Sources told Inc42 that PhonePe is targeting an early 2027 listing (February or March) at a valuation of around $10 Bn. With approximately 45% of merchant payments, the company was expected to benefit from greater clarity on monetising its payments business. A further delay could now cloud those assumptions. Razorpay has also moved closer to its public-market debut. It is also targeting a January–March 2027 listing, with an issue size of ₹5,000-6,000 Cr and a valuation of around $5 Bn. Although Razorpay has diversified into business banking, payroll, lending and cross-border payments, payment acceptance remains central to its merchant ecosystem. Therefore, investors could scrutinise its payments margins and monetisation assumptions more closely if MDR implementation remains uncertain. All in all, the MDR delay may not derail upcoming fintech IPOs, but it could make investors more cautious. For now, companies will have to justify their valuations through profits, not just the promise of future earnings. Ben McKenzie promised his wife that he was through with being an activist; that he’d go back to the acting gigs that had made him famous. At the end of his documentary taking on the cryptocurrency industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money,” the former star of The O.C. and Gotham turned to his spouse and fellow actor Morena Baccarin and swore he was done.
Turns out, that scene might need an edit. McKenzie is launching a new nonprofit, The Public Trust and Transparency Project, that not only continues his battle with the crypto business but widens it to fight prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi.
McKenzie tells WIRED he’s worried about “the gamification of the economy and the notion that we're turning everything into gambling—both investments, in the form of cryptocurrencies, and “prediction markets,” which look an awful lot like online casinos.”
“The more gambling gets into our culture, the more people feel like it's somehow a good idea to view these things as legitimate investment strategies,” he says. The prediction markets reject the comparison (although 80 percent of Kalshi’s trades came from sports in September, according to Bloomberg). McKenzie rejects the rejection: “I mean, if your investment strategy is, ‘I'm going to gamble on the Spurs-Knicks,’ like, come on! So there's a real, real problem here.”
John Reed Stark, who spent 18 years in the Securities and Exchange Commission’s enforcement division, will serve as an adviser to the Project. American Kleptocracy author Casey Michel and Tonazin Carmona, who runs economic policy for the left-of-center Century Foundation, will sit on the board.
The group is coming together at a time when regulators and law enforcement officials at every level are looking to rein in prediction markets. Federal regulators have launched new probes into both major prediction markets. The GOP-led House Oversight Committee recently released its investigation into US troops and government insiders trading on insider knowledge on Polymarket and Kalshi. The Senate just passed a bill prohibiting prediction markets for military operations and assassinations. Executives at the markets know they’re in for a rough few months; Kalshi even launched an ad campaign, starring Martha Stewart, reminding its users not to trade on confidential information.
But insider trading is only one concern among many. There’s also the problem you find in old-school gambling houses too: The vast majority of people who use the markets lose their money. A recent Wall Street Journal report shows that .01 percent of accounts take in two-thirds of all of the profits on Polymarket. On Kalshi, unprofitable accounts outpace profitable ones by almost three to one.
Then there’s the corruption angle, which McKenzie says is going to be front-and-center for the Project, especially with it featuring as a top issue in the recent midterm elections. Donald Trump Jr. was, until recently, a paid adviser to Kalshi. Trump Jr.’s venture firm, 1789 Capital, made its latest and biggest in a series of investments in Polymarket over the summer; months earlier, the Trump Justice Department sued the state of Minnesota when it tried to ban the prediction markets in the state. (At a recent conference, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called Trump Jr.’s involvement “heavily overblown. We have all types of investors.”)
Prediction markets have been around for hundreds of years, as a forthcoming book on the subject notes. American academics have been turning to them as teaching tools since the late ’80s. Their advocates note that they can be an effective way to hedge against risk, and a form of trading on sports that’s far more consumer-friendly than the online gambling houses. “I accept that there may be some utility,” McKenzie notes. “I'm not saying these things should not exist. I'm just saying they need to be properly regulated.”
McKenzie’s plan will be to push Congress in that direction, sort of the inverse of how the former actor lobbied publicly and privately against the “Clarity Act,” which would’ve brought cryptocurrencies into the financial mainstream. (The bill was rejected in September.)
That pressure is only bound to increase when Democrats take control of Congress next year. “In the bold new world starting [on the] first Monday in January,” Representative Frank Lucas, an Oklahoma Republican, told Politico, “nobody’s untouchable anymore.”

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

The ongoing protests by members of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) against Meta's content moderation practices in India have again put the tech major's practices questions about political bias, algorithmic transparency and the extent of government influence over online speech. The demonstrations by IYC workers in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram come amid an allegedly sharp increase in the volume of content restricted by Meta in India under local laws. The company restricted access to more than 5.44 Mn items on Facebook and Instagram between January and June 2026, compared with around 41,400 in the preceding six months, as per Meta's latest transparency disclosures. The surge represents a roughly 131-fold increase over the preceding six-month period, placing India among Meta's largest markets for government-mandated content restrictions. The restrictions covered several categories, including content relating to online gaming, synthetically generated material depicting prominent figures, threats to India's sovereignty and integrity, gender-based harassment and the promotion of enmity between groups. The data has put the spotlight on India's evolving regulatory framework for social media platforms, particularly the tightening of timelines for content removal and the growing use of automated systems to enforce government directions. The Controversy Protesters have alleged that Meta is selectively enforcing its content moderation policies and removing posts and accounts critical of the central government. The primary accusation against the US-based company is its bias towards Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Case in point was the removal or restriction of Instagram accounts linked to opposition figures. Congress has demanded an explanation for these actions as well as restoration of affected accounts. The opposition has also questioned the role of Meta's recommendation and moderation algorithms and sought clarity on identification and flagging of said political content. As per Meta, its content moderation framework combines automated detection systems, human review and enforcement of local legal requirements. However, when restrictions are imposed following government requests, users may not always have sufficient information about the authority behind a takedown or the specific legal provision invoked. This creates a transparency challenge. Meta has declined to comment on the protests and Congress' allegations of politically motivated restrictions. The company has maintained that it restricts content in India to comply with applicable local laws. Nevertheless, the scale of restrictions has intensified concerns about the potential for overblocking, where legitimate content could also become inaccessible because of automated enforcement. India's Laws Governing Social Media Takedowns India's social media content moderation framework is primarily governed by the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, intermediaries are required to remove or disable access to unlawful information after receiving a valid court order or a reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer. The provisions cover content that threatens India's sovereignty and integrity, national security, public order, friendly relations with foreign countries, or relates to defamation, contempt of court, decency and morality, among other grounds. The framework allows the government to direct platforms to restrict specific posts, URLs or other online content. Platforms are required to comply with these directions to retain the legal protections available to intermediaries under Section 79 of the IT Act. However, the government has also introduced additional safeguards and compliance obligations over the past year. In October 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) notified amendments to Rule 3(1)(d), which came into effect on November 15, 2025. The amendments mandated that government takedown notices be issued by senior authorised officials and clearly specify the legal provision invoked, the nature of the alleged unlawful act and the exact URL or electronic identifier of the content to be restricted. They also introduced periodic reviews of government directions by senior officials to assess whether the restrictions remain necessary and proportionate. In February 2026, the government tightened the compliance timeline further. An amendment effective February 20 reduced the deadline for intermediaries to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content from 36 hours to just three hours after receiving a valid court order or reasoned government intimation. The shorter deadline has increased the pressure on platforms to maintain automated content detection and enforcement systems capable of responding to government directions within a narrow window.

'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?
- Published
"It's turning into our Super Bowl moment."
Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday night.
The NWSL showpiece was played out in front of a sellout crowd of more than 19,000 at Audi Field in Washington DC, with tickets retailing at more than $300 (£229).
Ultimately, the Current triumphed 2-1 to clinch their first title, condemning Spirit to an unwanted record of three lost finals in a row.
Just a few hours earlier on this side of the Atlantic, Alexia Putellas, who last month was crowned the best player in the world for the third time at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, was scoring twice for London City against Crystal Palace in front of 4,000 people in Bromley.
It is a totally unfair comparison. After all, a championship final is the type of jamboree the USA does particularly well.
Nevertheless, women's football is booming in America at the moment, with attendance figures at record highs, more franchises joining the league and club retail sales double those of 2025.
So what is behind the explosion in popularity?
And what can the Women's Super League learn from it?
A unique history of popularity
The US is the most successful nation in women's international football.
The four-time World Cup winners (1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019) and five-time Olympic gold medallists, the nation of Mia Hamm, Alex Morgan and Megan Rapinoe, has a history of winning - and the domestic game is key.
"If anything, soccer is more seen as a women's sport [in the USA]," says broadcaster Jacqui Oatley, who currently commentates on the NWSL for ESPN.
"Women have won World Cups and Olympic Games - and the men have been nowhere near as successful."
While teams in the United States became professional in 2001 - for WSL teams it was 2018 - the top flight has taken several different guises over the years.
The current NWSL kicked off in 2013 as an eight-team competition, and has since expanded to 16 franchises, with two more joining from 2028.
There is no relegation and Kansas City's victory on Saturday means the league has had eight different winners since its iteration.
As the below graph shows, the ownership picture for these sides is far more varied than in the UK, with American sides much less dependent on their male counterparts.
Indeed, Kansas City are blazing a trail. Established in December 2020, unaffiliated to a men's side and backed by ambitious owners that include Brittany Mahomes - the wife of NFL quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Winning the championship is the crowning achievement for an ambitious franchise and such success is something independent London City hope to emulate in the UK. They are four points from the WSL summit nearly halfway through the 2026-27 season.
Kansas City were also the first club to build a bespoke stadium solely for women's football and the demand for seats at their 11,500-seater CPKC Stadium is huge. Earlier this year, Brighton announced their own purpose-built venue, planned for 2030-31.
"I think our independence is a hallmark of the league," says the NWSL's Jones Simmer.
"It is something we are very proud of. It allows us to invest in our own growth, prioritise the women's game and ensure resources are flowing to it."
It is markedly different from the UK set-up, where all WSL teams bar London City are, at least, affiliated and more often financially reliant on the men's side.
But that presents just as much of an opportunity, according to Jones Simmer.
"I know Nikki [Doucet, chief executive of the WSL] and I admire what she is building," she says.
"There's a really unique opportunity to build on the legacy of these 100-year-old men's clubs that are household names, to build women's brands that embrace the legacy but also have their own identity."
- Bespoke women's football stadiums? Why US sides are making the move 
  - Published15 March
- Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built £80m women's stadium 
  - Published28 April
An on-pitch product that delivers
Fans of both the NWSL and the WSL are spoiled when it comes to talent.
Most of the US national team play their club football at home, with the likes of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Rose Lavelle household names.
International stars such as Malawi's Temwa Chawinga at Kansas City, who came 10th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings, and former Chelsea striker Sam Kerr further enhance the league's quality.
"Where it starts is the product on the pitch," says Jones Simmer. "The quality of football has to be incredible and we have the best players in the world.
"And they are incredibly engaging with our fans. For so many supporters, their entry point to the league is they care about a particular player."
Provided the standard of competition is present, Jones Simmer says fans will return - and her confidence is backed up by the numbers.
In 2026, the average gate for an NWSL match has been more than 11,000 - only Arsenal in the WSL consistently receive a higher attendance than that, albeit the US is almost five times more populous than the UK.
On Thursday, the final few tickets for the NWSL's showpiece were retailing at $300 on ticket site Viagogo, with Jones Simmer suggesting resale tickets could be purchased at six times market value in advance of the match.
As London City and Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang put it: "The answer could not be clearer that there is an audience for the women's game."
"It's our job to hook fans by making sure they have a great experience watching a game in a venue and that's about the quality of the product," Jones Simmer adds.
"Once folks have that experience, it's a really easy yes to tune in again."
- Families v loyal fans - women's football's attendance dilemma 
  - Published30 October
Not that quality is an issue in the WSL where high-class footballers abound. Take Putellas, goal machine Khadija Shaw and most of England's double European Championship-winning squad for example.
American stars such as Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma at Chelsea, and Manchester City's Sam Coffey, have also swapped the US for the WSL in the past two years.
Broadcaster Oatley, who has been covering women's football since the 2005 World Cup, is keen for such players to be more visible off the pitch.
"I would love to see WSL players on mainstream TV shows, podcasts, social media platforms, not just on women's football programmes where the audience already knows everything about them," she says.
"It would not be for everyone, but for those who are comfortable, who have the biggest personalities, I think we could use that much more to grow our audience."
A matchday experience that matters
Oatley has been covering NWSL games for the past four seasons and she believes US clubs have mastered putting on events.
"When you're trying to promote a product in sport, you can't guarantee the team is going to play well and win," she says.
"But you can ensure the people who come to the game have a great experience.
"I love the enthusiasm, the positivity, the vibe of 'let's make this big'. It's a brilliant experience."
It is a balance the WSL wrestles with. With attendances plateauing this season, questions have arisen around its target audience and whether to market matches such as the north London derby between Tottenham and Arsenal as a rivalry or a family-friendly event.
Oatley's perspective is that it ought to be both, while recognising the different challenges in this country.
"I didn't understand that criticism," she says, "because they weren't saying: 'Only come to this game if you're a family'. It was being promoted all round.
"I don't think it's one size fits all marketing wise - the main thing is awareness."
It is a challenge the NWSL has embraced, and seen attendances rise accordingly.
"We want to ensure that we provided a big enough tent where everyone can feel welcome and included, whether they're there for the rivalries and the competitive tactics, or they're experiencing it for the first time," says Jones Simmer.
"To grow the sport, all fans need to be able to come to an NWSL game and have a great experience."
This season, league finalists Current and Spirit played at a remarkable 17 different times between them, reflecting the four timezones and vast nature of the USA.
It is all part of the country's sporting landscape, but given the WSL's continued conundrum about fixture scheduling, it is interesting that NWSL supporters manage to find the matches regardless.
"I have a lot of sympathy with schedulers because men's football got there first," Oatley says.
"Maybe the solution is deciding certain time slots are for women's football and sticking with them."
It does not appear the growth in the NWSL will slow down any time soon.
The Women's World Cup in Brazil next summer will feature the USA as one of the favourites and women's soccer will feature at the Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028.
The US will also host the 2031 Women's World Cup.
"It is amazing how the NWSL is cracking into culture," Jones Simmer says.
"We get excited about these catalytic opportunities to expand the community engagement, awareness and relevance of the NWSL."

In November, a claim circulated that U.S. banks warned customers they could be liable for money lost to mistakes made by artificial intelligence agents acting on their behalf.
An AI agent is a tool that can act as a digital assistant and carry out tasks such as writing and sending emails or planning and booking travel. In October, Axios reported that major U.S. banks had found "unauthorized third-party AI agents" logging into banking services using details that belonged to real customers.
Some AI agents, such as X's Grok Bot and Meta's Muse, advertise their reported ability to manage a person's money. Bank executives who spoke to Axios reportedly feared the risks of giving such agents permission to move or manage real people's funds.
By November, social media users claimed banks had taken action to discourage customers from using AI agents to manage their finances. For example, one X user wrote (archived):
BREAKING:
🇺🇸 If an AI agent empties your account, your bank won't refund your money anymore
U.S. banks like Citi, PNC and Citizens changed their terms this week.
If you give your credentials to an external AI agent, everything it does counts as if you had done it yourself, even if it gets hacked or ignores your instructions.
Similar claims also circulated on Facebook and Reddit (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claims appeared to come from reporting by Tech Crunch and Business Insider that claimed major banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, Ally, PNC and Citizens (which included five of the Federal Reserve Board's 10 largest banks in the U.S.) had warned their customers they could be held liable for mistakes third-party AI agents made on their accounts if they gave them permission to use their log in details.
Based on Tech Crunch and Business Insider's reporting and our own verification, we find claims that major banks like the ones listed above warned customers they could be liable for money lost to mistakes made by AI agents acting on their behalf to be true.
Emails sent to customers and the various banks' own terms and conditions suggested that they either advised against or outright prohibited users from allowing third-party AI agents to access their accounts. If users did allow third-party agents to access their accounts, several of the banks listed above said they would treat any transactions that agent carried out as if it were approved by the customer themselves, meaning it might not always be possible to recover funds an AI agent had mistakenly spent on a customer's behalf.
What major US banks say about AI agents
JPMorgan Chase
Jamie Dimon, chief executive officer of JPMorgan Chase & Co., said on a company earnings call on Oct. 13 that the bank was "not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company," describing fears of "rogue" agents causing a threat to customers.
The bank was reportedly developing tools to find and defend against outside AI agents acting on behalf of its customers.
Business Insider reported that Chase bank warned customers in an email that, "authorized transactions may not be reversible if your information is misused," where AI agents were involved.
One Snopes reporter who is also a Chase customer received this email, which asked customers to "Keep your sign-in information private, including when using AI tools." The email continued (emphasis ours):
As AI tools evolve, it's important to understand how your financial information is being used. Always verify who you're sharing with, as authorized transactions may not be reversible if your information is misused.
The bank's "Digital Services Agreement," updated in October, outright prohibits sharing login credentials with third parties "including External AI, automated tools, or data aggregators" (Page 14).
Bank of America
At least three Snopes reporters recieved an email that also circulated online (archived) in October about Bank of America's stance on third-party AI agents. It read (emphasis ours):
Please remember that your username and password should never be shared with another person or provided to an outside service, including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf. If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access.
Citi
The bank updated its "Online User Agreement" in November to include a policy on third-party AI agents. It wrote:
You are cautioned against using any third-party AI Agent to access your accounts or use any digital services including, but not limited to, use of such agent to provide any information or instruction to Citi or perform any transaction through Citi Online or Citi Mobile.
It continued (emphasis ours):
If you disregard this caution and provide your Online Credentials to any third-party AI Agent or otherwise permit such agent access to your accounts or allow such agent to use any digital service and to perform any transactions on your behalf, Citi will consider any access and actions taken by the agent as authorized by You.
Wells Fargo
The bank updated its "Online Access Agreement," effective Nov. 24, to outline the customer's responsibilities if they allowed a third-party AI agent to access their account. It wrote (emphasis ours):
Unless otherwise provided by law or regulation, if you provide an AI Agent with access to the Service or any Eligible Account using your login credentials, or otherwise authorize an AI Agent to act on your behalf, you agree that:
- Any instructions, actions, or transactions initiated by the AI Agent are deemed to have been initiated and authorized directly by you, without further verification, and we have no obligation to investigate the validity or scope of such authority;
- We may rely on any such instructions, actions, or transactions as valid and binding and as evidence of your authorization; and
- We have no obligation to investigate, verify, or confirm the authority, authenticity, or validity of any instruction or action taken by an AI Agent.
Ally
Business Insider reported that Ally emailed its customers in November to warn against the dangers of using an AI agent for managing accounts. One Snopes reporter received this email, which read (emphasis ours):
When you use an Al service, you're responsible for any actions that the Al takes. Al can make mistakes, hallucinate, misunderstand your instructions, or follow them in ways you didn't intend, which could lead to significant loss.
PNC
The bank's "Digital Services Agreement," which becomes effective in December, included the following language on third-party AI agents (Page 9):
Unless PNC expressly permits otherwise for a particular Service, you may not authorize or permit a Third-Party AI Agent to initiate, request, submit, or complete a payment, transfer, or other transaction on your behalf.
It added:
To the extent permitted by applicable law, you are responsible for access and activities you authorize or permit in violation of these restrictions, including unintended activities or activities exceeding the authority you intended to provide.
Citizens
Tech Crunch reported that the Citizens bank sent an email to customers warning that they were "on the hook" for any actions a third-party AI agent might take on their behalf. Snopes contacted Citizens to verify the authenticity of this reported email and await a reply.
Industry group calls banks' precautions 'reasonable'
Though the major banks we investigated expressed in emails or policies that they did not approve of customers using AI agents, some banks were simultaneously developing their own alternatives.
Dimon's statement to investors that he would not allow "just any" AI agents access to the company suggested that some might still be allowed. CNBC reported in November that JPMorgan, which Dimon heads, was working on AI agents that could carry out foreign exchange transactions and aimed to test these in the first half of 2027.
Similarly, PNC said in its "Digital Services Agreement" (Page 9) that customers could "sometimes" be permitted to connect an AI agent to their account if the bank approved of the agent and its use.
Sucharita Kodali, a financial analyst whose specialisms include e-commerce and consumer behavior, reportedly told the technology publication Wired that banks were "fundamentally risk-averse," suggesting that any hesitation they had about AI agents at this early stage in their development might not remain forever.
The Bank Policy Institute, an industry trade group where Dimon sits on the board, predicted in November that "eventually, externally developed agents will be conducting financial transactions at banks and other financial institutions" but that, until the agents had shown they could safely manage people's money, banks that were disallowing their use were engaging in "reasonable risk management practices designed to protect their customers from fraud or mistaken transactions."
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated other rumors surrounding banks.

What happened at the Seattle airport? Outrage as ICE arrests man and daughter boarding flight
ICE says both had overstayed their visas
It's been described as "horrific," "chilling" and "distressing."
A chaotic scene unfolded at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning as a father and daughter were detained by masked immigration officers while boarding their flight at around 8 a.m. PST.
Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles recorded the struggle, which showed two men in unmarked jackets and khaki pants struggling with someone on the ground as onlookers screamed, cried and a woman shouted: "They're taking my dad."
The men "just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind," said passenger John Gaedeke, who filmed part of the confrontation.
The videos have since gone viral.
Lawmakers and other officials have decried the arrests, and protesters have been marching through the airport chanting "ICE out now."
A person argues with a police officer during a protest at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday. (David Ryder/Reuters)
So, what happened? Why did Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest the father and daughter? And what happens to them now? Here what to know:
Who was arrested?
ICE officers conducted an operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, the agency said in a statement posted on social media, and also arrested, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, later identified as Mendoza's daughter.
A lawyer for them both says they were travelling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and have been seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015. They have no criminal record, said Olia Catala.
- Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota released after federal court ruling
- U.S. ICE agents shoot and wound man during arrest in New York City, sparking protests
"They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said.
Mejia "went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit," she said. "So it’s just heartbreaking."
Catala told local media that Mendoza brought his daughter to the U.S. when she was 14, and that they entered legally on tourist visas. Mendoza later filed an asylum claim, the attorney told NBC-affiliate King5 News, and Meija married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status.
"The entire family is traumatized," she told King5 News.
People react as ICE officers detain passenger on the jetbridge for an Alaska Airlines flight from Seattle to Los Angeles in this screengrab from a video obtained from social media and verified by Reuters. (John Gaedeke/Reuters)
Mejia’s husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were arrested, Catala said, but was not detained.
"This is a family whose lives have been turned upside down," Catala said Sunday in a statement posted to social media.
Both are being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.
Why were they arrested?
The "targeted" operation was to arrest Mendoza, ICE said in a statement, describing him as "an illegal alien from Mexico" who had overstayed his visa.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said it no longer tolerates "aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country."
"This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport," DHS said in a statement to CBC News.
ICE said that, during the Saturday morning arrest, other travellers began to "obstruct and assault" the officers, and claims that one passenger "hurled hot coffee" at them. They identified her as Mejia, also calling her "an illegal alien from Mexico with visa overstay."
ICE said Meija "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."
Catala, their attorney, says Meija was holding a cup of coffee during the confrontation, but disputes that she threw it. Other passengers who witnessed the scene said it was knocked out of her hands.
"When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on."
People protest at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport Saturday. (David Ryder/Reuters)
What's the reaction?
In addition to the public backlash and protests, lawmakers and other officials have decried the arrests.
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called the videos "horrific" and "chilling," and Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said she was "outraged" by the sight of masked ICE agents "causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway."
"ICE is completely and totally out of control and today we are confronted with yet more evidence of this," Ferguson told a news conference on Saturday.
"These tactics are unacceptable and un-American," Wilson said in a statement posted on social media.

Washington Attorney-General Nick Brown also decried the arrests, writing on social media: "We are sick and tired of poorly trained masked federal agents vanishing people out of thin air.
"Washingtonians will never accept these stunts as legitimate or responsible law enforcement."
The Port of Seattle said in a statement it was "outraged" by the incident, adding that immigration enforcement at the airport are conducted without the port’s participation or knowledge.
"This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."
Alaska Airlines also said it wasn't provided advanced notice and that it was "concerned."
April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, called the ICE arrest a "smash-and-grab" action that injected fear and chaos during a delicate time for air travel.
The union includes local chapters representing flight attendants and ground crew at the airport.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
- Published
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there had been "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
'Recognition of our suffering'
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first nation to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest crime under international law.
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The verdict will have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, though, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A US State Department spokesperson said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention was of "paramount importance", as was "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court.
Noting that the US was the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response", they said they shared the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights" against Rohingyas and other minorities, adding: "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications."
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.
