The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.
The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.
His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.
Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.
The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.
After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.
The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.
Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.
A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters fired at the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.
Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.
In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.
He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations, and use and possession of a firearm in the US, and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast isolated heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and gusty winds across parts of South Peninsular India this week, driven by active easterly waves over the Bay of Bengal and off the Kerala-Karnataka coast.
In its latest bulletin, the weather agency also warned of dense morning fog across several northern, eastern, and northeastern states, alongside a gradual drop in minimum temperatures across Central, East, and Northwest India.
Under the influence of troughs in the easterlies, isolated heavy rainfall is very likely over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, and Karaikal from November 23 to 27, and over Kerala and Mahe between November 24 and 27.
Fairly widespread to widespread showers are expected across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry from November 24 to 26; Kerala and Mahe from November 24 to 27; and Lakshadweep from November 25 to 28.
The IMD has also issued warnings for thunderstorms, lightning, and squally weather across the southern peninsula:
While West and Central India are expected to witness largely dry weather during the week, night temperatures are set to decline across multiple regions.
Minimum temperatures will fall gradually by 3–5°C over Central India until November 26, by 3–4°C over East India until November 27, and by 2–3°C over Northwest India until November 28, the weather agency said.
According to IMD, dense fog conditions are very likely in isolated pockets of Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, and Tripura till November 25, and over Assam and Meghalaya on November 24 and 25.
East Uttar Pradesh is also expected to experience dense fog through November 24.

The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.
She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."
It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)
As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?
David and Nina's Four L's
When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:
Love. "You gotta love each other."
Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."
Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.
Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.
The Magic Six
I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.
Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?
The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.
Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.
Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.
Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.
Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.
Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.
Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.
State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.
Listen. Don't Fix.
Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.
"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.
Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."
It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.
Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.
Find Your Rhythm
Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?
Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.
As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."
So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."
For more, follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

This article is part of a new First Opinion series on the future of medical school.
By this time of year, the sky is black when I step outside. The day has carried me from lectures on gastrointestinal cancer disparities to TAing microbiology, from student government debates to helping free-clinic patients complete paperwork for expensive medications. With the cold nipping at my skin, I look back at the Stanford medical school building, its windows glowing. There is still so much to do, and even more to feel. I call my mother, my home base in human form. Three thousand miles away, she is preparing for bed. Circumstances beyond her control have kept her from taking a domestic flight for decades, let alone visit me in California. Her first question is always, “Did you remember to eat dinner?” Her second: “How were your classes today?”
I am a class-goer. Most of my classmates are, too, though preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic and the Step 1 exam’s transition to pass/fail. Given the flexibility of recordings and the time students devote to service, research, and other commitments, I understand why some choose to study independently and firmly believe in preserving students’ freedom to make that choice.
For me, though, attending lectures in person has become an important part of feeling at home. It is the most powerful way I take care of my mental health and the classmates I have come to see as my newfound family. I would like to make the case why it could for other medical students, too.
Part of that happiness comes from my daily calls with my immigrant mother. What I learn gives me something to share with the woman who gave up her dream of becoming a clinician so I could pursue mine: dissecting a cadaver for the first time, suturing, administering flu vaccines for undocumented folks, wrapping wound dressing around an unhoused man’s arm. Putting these experiences into words is an exercise of understanding the unmistakably human profession I am entering.
I once worried that telling her the good parts of my day would make the distance between us more painful. Her unconditional love for me throughout the years has taught me otherwise. There are many students like me who left the comfort of our communities to pursue higher education. We should not have to compromise on maintaining relationships with loved ones, which influences medical student well-being and belonging.
In graduate school, where life is more independent, class also gives us a place to come together. During lecture breaks, I learn about friends advocating against the medical bloodletting of horseshoe crabs, making spaces more accessible to people with disabilities, and bringing care to under-resourced youth through mobile vans. We ask to become involved in one another’s work. Other days, happiness is resting my head on a friend’s shoulder, sharing my next bucket-list read — Bryant Lin’s “Sunshine: An Exploration of Living When You Are Dying” — or suggesting that we try the new cafe with robot baristas. It is remembering I am not walking this road alone.
Just as importantly, being physically present gives me opportunities to check in with others. As smartphones and artificial intelligence mediate more of our lives, I worry how easily we can grow used to being alone. Hard workers are remarkable at hiding stress. Intelligent people are good at forgetting to be kind to themselves. Class gives us a place, an excuse, not only to struggle through challenging coursework in real time together, but be part of one another’s lives. In between lectures, I am giving a friend a relationship pep talk as we complain about dating in the Bay Area. The next moment, I am making plans to cheer on another friend at a marathon. After lab, I am curled up on the reading room couch beside a peer whose mother has just been diagnosed with cancer. Our parents are getting older and sicker. It is infuriating. You would think learning medicine would brace us for inevitable losses. False. But knowing there is an abundance of people here to catch you is a peace in its own form.
In the classroom, I have also come to see my education as one I help shape. Conversations with professors following lectures have allowed me to successfully advocate to integrate various topics in our curriculum: sex differences in aortic stenosis pathophysiology, the relationship between ALDH2*2 deficiency and esophageal cancer, overdose response training. Medicine is evolving by the day, and these exchanges make education a collaboration between learners and teachers, showing students that our voices matter.
I think often of watching Celine Song’s “Past Lives” with my mother in December 2024, when I was still in New York. The film introduces in-yun, the idea that an encounter between two people is the result of countless threads from their past lives intertwining. Today, I still wonder if this, too, is a past life, and we are already something else to each other in the next. Perhaps in the next, I am the uninsured one who needs translation, and she is the medical student sitting across from me at the free clinic. In this life, it is 2 a.m. Eastern, and she is calling to ask about my day. It is 11 p.m. in California, and I am at the beach with friends, squinting into the Pacific because someone yelled that they spotted a whale. I imagine the animal’s song, sung at a frequency so low it travels for thousands of miles underwater, enough to carry me home.
I crave a big future, expansive in experience and generosity. For others, that may mean studying independently to make room for research, paid work, service, or rest. Those choices deserve grace.
For me, it begins with being physically present during these four brief years. Honoring my mother means doing good when her familiar applause is far away and nurturing the classmates who will become tomorrow’s doctors. Here is my chance to find where I fit, then widen that space for the next person. I don’t plan to squander a second of it.
Brian Zhang is a second-year M.D. student at Stanford University School of Medicine, where he currently serves as student body president.
The First Opinion series on the future of medical school will run through the end of 2026. Have an idea for a big or small way to change medical school? Email us.

A video showing a white airbag emerging from the helmet of a biker who appears to crash is being widely shared on social media (here, here). The video claims that China has developed helmets equipped with airbags to prevent head injuries in the event of a motorcycle accident. The video has also been shared by several prominent media outlets (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the viral post.
Claim: A video shows a helmet equipped with airbags developed in China.
Fact: The viral video is AI-generated. While some companies are developing airbag helmets, the airbags shown in the video are exaggerated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, upon examining the viral video, we noticed that the bike and the biker are not visible in the phone recording of the fall for a few moments. After the airbags deploy, the biker suddenly disappears. Moreover, the way the bike loses control and the biker falls onto the road appears unnatural. Such visual inconsistencies are commonly seen in AI-generated videos.
Further, we verified the viral video using AI content detection tools Hive Moderation and Sightengine. Both tools indicated that the video was AI-generated, confirming that it is not a genuine video.
Moreover, a reverse image search of the viral video led us to the original video, which was uploaded on Facebook (archived) by a page named Zero Gravity Gang. We found that this page regularly uploads AI-generated videos depicting various vehicle-related experiments.
While it is true that a few companies are experimenting with airbag technology for helmets (here, here, here). However, these designs are not as large as the airbag shown in the viral video. They are designed to provide protection to the head and neck rather than inflate into a large structure around the rider.
To sum up, this viral video of the airbag helmet developed in China is AI-generated, not real.

- Deborah Ann Woll will reprise her role as Faye in the God of War live-action series.
- The actress previously portrayed Faye in God of War Ragnarok and will lead God of War Laufey, releasing in May 2027.
- Prime Video has ordered two seasons of the series, which will be filmed back-to-back.
God of War fans will get to see another familiar face when Kratos and Atreus make their live-action debut. Deborah Ann Woll, who portrayed Faye in God of War Ragnarok, is returning as the character in Prime Video’s upcoming God of War TV series. The actress is also set to lead the next video game in the franchise, God of War Laufey.
According to a new report from Variety published on November 23, 2026, Deborah Ann Woll has joined the cast of Amazon’s God of War live-action adaptation. The actress, also known for playing Karen Page in Marvel’s Daredevil, will reprise her role as Faye, the late wife of Kratos and mother of Atreus.
Woll will play the titular character in the upcoming God of War Laufey, which was delayed and is now scheduled to release in May 2027. She even performed motion capture for the role. With her latest casting, fans will get to see her portrayal of Faye beyond the video games.
However, Woll’s screen time in the TV series might be somewhat limited. Faye was already deceased at the beginning of God of War (2018), and it was her death that set Kratos and Atreus on their journey through the Norse realms, which also serves as the premise of the live-action series.
It remains to be seen how much of Faye’s backstory the live-action adaptation will explore. Woll isn’t the only actor reprising her role from the games, either. Alastair Duncan is also returning as Mimir. The God of War TV series cast includes Dave Bautista as Kratos, Callum Vinson as Atreus, Mandy Patinkin as Odin, and Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Thor.
Production on the God of War live-action series resumed in late October after Dave Bautista replaced Ryan Hurst, who suffered an injury on set earlier this year. Prime Video has already ordered two seasons of the show, which will be filmed back-to-back. However, an official premiere date has yet to be announced.

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

Srinagar- An online petition, seeking a halt to the construction activity near ecologically fragile Sheshnag lake on the Amarnath Yatra route in Jammu and Kashmir’s Anantnag district, is gaining momentum.
The petition on Change.org, named “Stop construction around Kashmir’s alpine lakes” and started by a person named Zarqua Banday, has garnered nearly 1,600 signatures on the site so far.
The petition also urges the authorities to engage with local environmental and community groups to develop a sustainable way forward.
It said that in the name of development and easy access, the government plans to construct roads that will cut through untouched havens in Kashmir.
However, the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) on Monday said post-Amarnath Yatra works are being carried out in compliance with all applicable safety norms and environmental safeguards.
The petition said, “This isn’t progress; it’s a threat to our environment.”
It added that the “excuse” of connectivity and increased tourism sounds appealing at first glance; but, if looked at more closely, the true cost of such advancements “becomes all too apparent”.
“Similar projects elsewhere have led to increased pollution, habitat destruction, and an influx of tourists who, often unintentionally, end up contributing to ecological imbalance. Recent studies and reports highlight that ecosystems as delicate as ours risk irreversible damage from such developments. We cannot let the same fate befall our cherished Alpine lakes,” the petitioner said.
The petition said that instead of constructing roads, “we urge our government to consider sustainable tourism initiatives that preserve our natural environment”.
“Solutions like guided trekking, limited access permits and eco-friendly accommodations could bring economic benefits without sacrificing our wilderness. Other regions facing similar challenges, like the Swiss Alps, have successfully implemented such strategies. We need to learn from them and prioritise long-term ecological health over short-term gains,” it said.
The people of Kashmir are not against development, but they advocate a form of it that respects their land and traditions, the petition added.
Asserting that once the natural state of the environment is compromised, the damage cannot be undone, the petition calls for working towards solutions that “enhance our lives without destroying the essence of who we are”.
PDP president Mehbooba Mufti expressed alarm over the reports of large-scale excavation, warning that deploying heavy bulldozers in the ecologically fragile zone threatens both the environment and the pilgrimage’s religious sanctity.
“The information we are receiving about what is happening there in Sheshnag is very terrifying that they have taken huge machines and bulldozers to Sheshnag, which is a few kilometres away from the Amarnath Ji cave, and excavation is taking place there,” she said.
Mehbooba, accompanied by party MLAs Waheed Para and Syed Muntazir Mehndi, set out on Tuesday morning towards Sheshnag along the Amarnath Yatra route in the south Kashmir district.
The PDP leaders tried to trek from Chandanwari towards Sheshnag, but were stopped by police.
The former chief minister asserted that forests, mountains and glaciers, including Sheshnag, play a huge role in the formation of the ‘Shivling’ — the naturally formed ice lingam — during the Amarnath Yatra.
“If you destroy Jammu and Kashmir’s environment, its glaciers, its mountains, and its forests like this, and take such huge machines up there, then how will this Shivling manifest? Then what will you come here for?” she questioned.
Jammu and Kashmir Pradesh Congress Committee (JKPCC) president Tariq Hameed Karra on Tuesday questioned the deployment of a JCB excavator near the high-altitude Sheshnag Lake along the Amarnath cave route, demanding that the government clarify the purpose of the work and disclose details of the permissions granted by various departments.
Kashmir’s chief cleric, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, who has also signed the petition, said, “We all have to collectively raise our voice to stop the mindless destruction of our ecology at its most fragile places.”
“Why is our Chief Minister @omarabdullah, mute? As people’s elected representative it is his duty to speak up and do the needful to ensure this plunder is stopped! I have signed this petition and urge all those who want to save Kashmiri’s fragile ecology do so,” the Mirwaiz said in a post on X.
Coming down heavily on attempts to politicise the Amarnath Yatra track widening issue, the Jammu and Kashmir BJP on Tuesday accused critics of practising selective environmental activism and applying double standards, asserting that it would firmly oppose any move to communalise development, undermine the annual pilgrimage or disturb peace in the valley.
A video showing an excavator deployed near the high-altitude Sheshnag Lake, a high-risk glacial lake, in the south Kashmir Anantnag district has sparked widespread outrage, with political parties, religious leaders, and environmentalists demanding an immediate halt to the activity along the Amarnath cave route.
“What is being projected as an environmental issue increasingly appears to be an attempt to manufacture controversy, disturb the peaceful atmosphere and exploit religious sentiments for narrow political gains,” J-K BJP spokesperson and former MLC Girdhari Lal Raina said in a statement.
Without naming any party or individual, Raina said attempts are being made by political parties and opportunistic leaders to revive the Amarnath land controversy and communalise the issue.

The British Independent Film Awards has unveiled the winners of its 10 film craft categories ahead of next month’s official BIFA ceremony.
Clio Barnard’s I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, which follows five lifelong friends struggling with life at the age of 30, won three awards including Shaheen Baig for Best Casting, who previously won the award for Blue Jean in 2022. Maya Maffoli took home the award for Best Editing while Connie Farr won for Best Music Supervision for the film.
Dark period comedy Savage House, in which status-obsessed nobles Richard E. Grant and Claire Foy romp through their crumbling 18th century estate, won two BIFAs. Jacquetta Levon, who was nominated in 2020 for Rose Glass’ debut Saint Muad, won Best Make-Up & Hair Design while Alex Bovaird took Best Costume Design.
André Turpin won Best Cinematography for his work on Andrew Haigh’s A Long Winter while Best Production Design was awarded by Gareth Pugh and Carson McColl for Ink, Danny Boyle’s energetic 1960s-set film about the birth of sensationalist tabloid journalism.

An incorrect or outdated spectacles prescription can leave a child’s vision inadequately corrected, affecting classroom activities and learning. Regular eye examinations are important because children’s eyesight can change as they grow, and wearing spectacles alone does not ensure that their vision is being corrected properly.
A study of 5,268 school-going children in north India found that only 23.03% of those prescribed spectacles were using the correct prescription. Inaccurate spectacle power was common, with younger age and longer duration of spectacle use among the associated factors.

After the leather-jacketed CEO, president, and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, his company initially announced an investigation. And then… Huang was back.
In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies. Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has warned consumers, particularly students and young people, against relying on protein supplements and nutraceutical products marketed with misleading claims about muscle growth and health benefits. Addressing reporters in Pune, Mundhe said several products, including whey protein supplements, were being promoted through questionable branding and marketing practices. He urged consumers to verify whether the benefits advertised by manufacturers were genuine and whether the products actually contained the ingredients and nutritional components mentioned on their labels. He also stressed that only businesses holding the necessary licences are legally permitted to sell such products. Munde said that those operating without the required authorisation cannot sell them. Mundhe cautioned young people who consume protein supplements to improve their fitness or build muscle, saying such products cannot, on their own, deliver the results manufacturers promise. He emphasised that muscle development requires regular exercise and adequate nutrition, including protein from natural food sources. "These health supplements, be it protein or the claimed nutraceutical items, are being presented in a very wrong way and are being used in a very wrong way. The branding, marketing or the kind of claims being made are wrong. It is important to check whether the claims are true or not," Mundhe said. He further warned that consumers may not always know whether the protein content advertised on a supplement's packaging accurately reflects the product's actual protein content. "To build muscle, you will have to exercise. You will have to eat the natural protein it contains. The protein that is being told to you, whether it contains the right protein or not, no one knows this," he added. The FDA chief said consumers should not automatically trust promotional claims made by supplement brands and sellers, particularly when products are advertised as providing specific health or muscle-building benefits. He reiterated that businesses must possess the appropriate licences to sell protein supplements and nutraceutical products. Selling these products without the necessary permissions is illegal. Mundhe also cautioned consumers against depending solely on recommendations from gyms and health clubs when choosing supplements, particularly where guidance may not come from qualified professionals. Mundhe advised consumers to read product labels carefully and check whether the ingredients and nutritional information match the claims made by manufacturers. He also recommended consulting a doctor before taking supplements, especially when consumers are uncertain about a product's suitability or potential health benefits. The commissioner highlighted that muscle development and overall fitness should be supported by a combination of regular physical activity, natural protein intake, adequate sleep and a healthy lifestyle, rather than relying on supplements marketed as quick solutions. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has sanctioned prosecution against packaged drinking water manufacturer Bisleri International after one of its water samples was declared "unsafe" in laboratory testing. The company, however, has disputed the findings, triggering a row over the presence of bromate and polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the sample. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), prolonged exposure to certain chemical contaminants in drinking water, including bromate and some PAHs, may pose health risks, including potential kidney damage and an increased risk of cancer. The two substances have different sources and potential health effects. Bromate is a chemical compound that can form during drinking-water disinfection, particularly when ozone reacts with naturally occurring bromide ions in water, according to the WHO. The WHO has set a provisional guideline value of 10 micrograms per litre (µg/l) for bromate in drinking water, primarily because of concerns about its potential carcinogenic effects. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified bromate as a Group 2B substance, meaning it is "possibly carcinogenic to humans". According to the WHO, while evidence of carcinogenicity in humans is inadequate, animal studies have shown sufficient evidence of cancer-causing potential. Bromate has also demonstrated mutagenic properties in laboratory studies, meaning it can cause changes in genetic material, or DNA. The WHO's assessment discusses oxidative DNA damage as one possible mechanism behind its carcinogenic effects. Animal studies have linked prolonged exposure to bromate with tumours in the kidneys and thyroid, among other tissues. These findings raise concerns about long-term exposure, although they do not mean that consuming water with a slightly elevated bromate concentration will immediately cause cancer. The potential health risk depends on the concentration consumed, the frequency of exposure and its duration. The WHO's guideline is intended to limit long-term exposure and reduce associated health risks. Polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, commonly called PAHs, are a group of organic chemical compounds containing two or more fused aromatic rings. According to the WHO, PAHs are formed primarily through the incomplete combustion of organic materials. They can enter the environment through industrial emissions, vehicle exhaust and other sources of atmospheric pollution. They may also contaminate drinking water through coal-tar coatings used in water distribution pipes. PAHs can enter the human body through food, air and drinking water. The WHO notes that these compounds may be present in food following exposure to airborne pollution and in fish from contaminated waters. They can also form during cooking methods such as grilling, roasting, frying and baking. Some PAHs are particularly concerning because of their carcinogenic potential. The WHO identifies benzo[a]pyrene as an important indicator of PAH contamination and has prescribed a guideline value of 0.7 micrograms per litre in drinking water. The WHO's assessment says evidence linking PAH mixtures to cancer in humans comes primarily from occupational studies involving inhalation and skin exposure. It also notes that human data on cancer risks from oral exposure are unavailable. The health effects vary depending on the specific PAH, the amount of exposure and its duration. Prolonged exposure to certain compounds, particularly benzo[a]pyrene, is a concern because of their cancer-causing potential. The dispute relates to a sample collected by FSSAI from Bisleri's Goa manufacturing facility on September 30, 2025. According to the company, the regulator collected six samples, of which five initially met the applicable standards. The sixth recorded bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre, it mentioned, as per PTI. Following Bisleri's appeal dated November 22, 2025, FSSAI sent the sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. The company said the laboratory found bromate within the prescribed limit but separately flagged the presence of PAHs. Bisleri subsequently arranged an independent test at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which also found bromate within the prescribed limit, it said. The company submitted the results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office through a formal letter dated February 2 this year. Bisleri said it received no further communication from FSSAI and understood the matter to be closed. It also maintained that it had not received any formal notice by email or in hard copy. However, FSSAI announced on Sunday, November 22, that it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after finding its packaged drinking water sample "unsafe". In its statement on Monday, Bisleri said it would cooperate with the regulator to address the issue and reiterated that its packaged drinking water was safe for consumption. "Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls of over 90 tests across our 10-step manufacturing process," the company said. Police authorities in Bengaluru’s Electronic City have reportedly registered an FIR against Karnataka Chalakara Okkuta’s president G Narayana Swamy, among others, for destroying recruitment posters of Green SM. Swamy and his group of unidentified cab drivers allegedly barged into a private hotel in Hosa Road and vandalised the property by tearing up banners, abusing company representatives, in a bid to impede the Vietnamese ride-hailing firm’s recruitment drive. As per a report by the Deccan Herald, the FIR was registered suo motu under five sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) relating to property damage, unlawful assembly, intentional insult, breach of peace and criminal intimidation. This comes about a week after the state government directed transport department officials to stop registering new Green SM taxis until further orders, even as around 100 vehicles operated by the company have already been registered to ply on Karnataka roads. The e-taxi operator, part of Vietnam’s Vingroup, which also operates electric car OEM Vinfast, received an aggregator licence from the Karnataka Transport Department earlier this month. The issuance of the same triggered protests across the state. Bengaluru-based private transport associations such as Karnataka Rajya Chalakara Parishath and Peace Auto Union demand protection citing interests of local taxi owners and drivers. Yet, the state government is yet to take a final call on whether Green SM will be allowed to continue its operations in Karnataka. My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
- Published
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Between the pages of a logbook recording Dakshina’s treatment are ₹100, ₹50, ₹20, and ₹10 notes. Dakshina’s mother, Minnal Rani, had filed them away for her daughter’s medical expenses. The child is gone, but the money remains untouched. “We will never spend it,” she says, fighting back tears.
Dakshina was five months old when doctors detected a hole in her heart. Born on June 13, 2025, she was taken to many hospitals, including one in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam’s capital. With surgery ruled out, she was eventually referred to a cooperative hospital at Perinthalmanna, in Malappuram district, a two-and-a-half-hour drive away from home. She died here, on April 13, 2026.
Rani and her husband Chandra Sekhar say the hospital refused to release their daughter’s body until they paid a bill of ₹10,000. They managed to raise the money with the help of a ward councillor.
“We buried her under that tree,” says Rani, pointing to a coconut tree near their house at Vechapathi hamlet in Sholayur panchayat of Attappadi, Palakkad district.
Dakshina’s death is among a series of 10 infant deaths reported this year from Attappadi, a predominantly tribal settlement. There have been four back-to-back deaths in October. Of the 10 infant deaths, six involved congenital anomalies, with heart defects among the commonly reported conditions. An expert committee of doctors and researchers is examining the deaths.

In October and November, several posts claimed advertisements in Times Square featuring Jesus Christ left New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani "furious."
A Facebook post shared a video of the advertisement, which reads "Jesus Is Coming." Another post said:
Jesus Christ is taking center stage in Times Square, New York City!
Images of Jesus appearing on massive digital billboards in the heart of Manhattan are drawing attention, with posts circulating online claiming that Zohran Mamdani is furious over the displays.
Regardless of the political controversy surrounding New York City, seeing the image of Christ displayed so prominently in one of the world's most recognizable locations is certainly making a statement.
Perhaps New York City isn't as far gone as some people believe!
(Facebook user "Robin Martyr")
There is no evidence Mamdani, who is Muslim, was "furious" over advertisements of Jesus on Times Square billboards. Mamdani has made no such public statement or criticized the promotion of images of Jesus. On the contrary, Mamdani has frequently spoken in favor of religious freedom and diversity. As such, we rate this claim as false.
We searched through Mamdani's recent statements and found no such expression of anger. In fact, in April, Mamdani posted a message for Easter Sunday (archived): "Happy Easter, New York! Today, millions of New Yorkers celebrate the resurrection of Jesus Christ and the victory of hope over despair and faith over fear."
A spokesperson for Mamdani told us over email, "There is no truth to this claim."
The footage of the advertisement of Jesus Christ in Times Square previously appeared online (archived) in December 2025 — before Mamdani took office — if not earlier.
The claim that Mamdani was furious spread via social media accounts that frequently share unverified information unsupported by reliable media coverage. One such Facebook page, Robyn Martyr, is devoted to pro-Christianity content.
Any company or organization can rent advertising space and time on a Times Square billboard. After Mamdani became mayor, we reported on how the Florida Chamber of Commerce paid for an advertisement in Times Square that appeared to mock him, calling him Florida's "Economic Developer of the Year."
Snopes has covered numerous false rumors about Mamdani.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Monday said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations, a net savings of 45% compared to what it would’ve paid last year had the negotiated prices been in effect.
This is the third time the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has negotiated drug prices following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, but it’s the first time those drugs have included treatments administered in doctors’ offices, which are covered by Part B. Only retail drugs covered by Part D were eligible during the first two years.
The estimated $9.2 billion in savings does not account for discounts the drugmakers pay to the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program. That program was created by the same law that created the price negotiation program. If those discounts were included, the estimated savings would be about $5.5 billion, or 33% in lower net aggregate spending.

Netflix has kicked off production on the second season of “Elite Force,” its hit French action thriller starring Tomer Sisley (“Largo Winch”).
Created by Julien Leclercq and Sylvain Caron and directed by Leclercq, the series spent four weeks in Netflix’s global Top 10 for non-English-language shows and cracked the streamer’s Top 10 in 91 countries.
The second season will see David and Max, after being dismissed from the GIGN – France’s elite counterterrorism and hostage rescue unit — find themselves at the center of an incident that raises suspicions within their unit and threatens its very existence.
“We’re starting filming on Season 2 of ‘Elite Force’ today. Audiences followed us throughout the first season, and it’s with great excitement that we’re embarking on a new storyline with everything dialed up: intrigue, emotion, action… Everything is in place to deliver!” said Leclercq.
Netflix has a track record with French action thrillers, notably “Under Paris,” directed by Xavier Gens, and “AKA,” starring Alban Lenoir and Eric Cantona.
“Elite Force” marks a return to familiar territory for Leclercq, who previously chronicled one of the GIGN’s most high-profile operations in his 2011 film “The Assault,” based on the 1994 hijacking of an Air France plane. He has since become a regular collaborator of Netflix, directing “The Wages of Fear,” a remake of Henri-Georges Clouzot’s 1953 classic, and co-creating “Ganglands,” a crime series inspired by his 2015 heist thriller “Braqueurs.” The latter ran for two seasons on the streamer.
	Sisley, meanwhile, is best known for starring in the franchise “Largo Winch,” adapted from the Belgian comic book series, as well as the French crime procedural “Balthazar” which ran for five seasons on TF1.

The Kallakurichi Collector handed over a formal complaint to the Superintendent of Police (SP) against Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) MLA C. Arul Vignesh, sources said on Monday (November 23, 2026) afternoon.
It is learnt that the Collector had accused the MLA of making inappropriate advances and sending unwarranted messages. The police are learnt to have registered the complaint against the MLA under the Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Harassment of Women Act. Senior police officers could not be reached for comment.
During the day, State Public Prosecutor R. John Sathyan told the Madras High Court that neither Chief Secretary M. Sai Kumar nor the police had received any representation/complaint from the IAS officer. He gave an emphatic “no” in response to questions from Justice V. Lakshminarayanan as to whether the police or the Chief Secretary had received any complaint.
Then, the judge asked the SPP to get instructions from the officer and report to the court by Tuesday (November 24).
The court was hearing a writ petition (criminal), filed by advocate R. Thrishuli, seeking a direction to the police to file a criminal case against the MLA on the petitioner’s complaint that he had trespassed into the officer’s bungalow in an inebriated state and threatened the officials there, besides sending the officer obscene messages.
When the judge wanted to know how the petitioner knew about the alleged obscene messages, her counsel S. Jeyakumar replied that the woman officer had complained to the Chief Secretary. On being asked to place the complaint before the court, the counsel said, “It is not available with me, I agree.” He, however, accused the official respondents of suppressing the facts of the case.
“Everything is available with them but they are suppressing all those things. They are sailing with the accused and not at all taking care of the law. All higher officers are protecting the accused. In these circumstances, what will the...[woman IAS officer] do MiLord?” the counsel said. Surprised at his answer, the judge asked, “You mean to say that an IAS officer does not know how to protect herself?”
The judge also referred to the 2021 sexual harassment complaint filed by a woman IPS officer against the then special DGP and said, “Last time when a similar incident happened, it was the woman officer who gave the complaint. Where is the complaint in the present instance? Are you and I going to do something that an IAS officer does not know...? She is the head of a district, I say.”
On being told by the petitioner’s counsel that the National Commission for Women (NCW) had taken suo motu cognisance of the issue on the basis of newspaper reports and called for a report from the DGP, the judge said, “They can act based on newspaper reports, I cannot. Give me some tangible material to show that the MLA had, indeed, sent obscene messages and I will issue a (writ of) mandamus.”
Stating that the petitioner appeared to be trying to fish in troubled waters, Justice Lakshminarayanan also said, “If the officer concerned has not made any complaint, where is the question of the police taking action? Do you want them [the police] to take action on the basis of newspaper reports? If there is no complaint by the woman, I will not interfere.”

In an intensive care unit, every second matters. A critically ill patient may be connected to several devices, including patient monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps, while laboratory systems and electronic health records continuously generate additional information. Together, these systems create a large and rapidly-changing picture of the patient’s condition. However, when the information remains fragmented across devices and platforms, clinicians may spend valuable time locating, verifying and reconciling data before they can act.
This makes interoperability a clinical priority in critical care, not simply an information technology requirement. Integration enables systems to exchange data, but true interoperability ensures that the information being exchanged is accurate, interpretable and clinically relevant. This can help care teams coordinate and prioritise interventions more effectively while reducing the need to move between multiple systems to assemble a clinical picture.

Thirty-four-year-old Sundar lives in Tappal village in Khair tehsil of Aligarh district, Uttar Pradesh. His name was absent from the state’s draft voter list published on January 6, 2026. However, in the final list published on April 10, his name appears four times, at serial numbers 730, 738, 739 and 757 in booth 19. Each entry carries a different Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC) number.
The official list of Form 6 applications, used for voter registration, records only two applications from Sundar, dated January 9 and 14. The office of the Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (CEO), however, said that he had filed four. The discrepancy aside, the CEO’s office’s response confirms a crucial point: Multiple applications by the same person resulted in the issuance of multiple voter IDs.
The Election Commission launched the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Uttar Pradesh in November 2025, with the removal of duplicate and incorrect entries among its stated objectives. Alt News compared the draft and final electoral rolls across 69 booths in 20 districts, covering 60,558 voters, and cross-checked newly added names against the corresponding Form 6 application lists. The analysis found 230 people whose names appeared at least twice in the final rolls, with some listed three or four times, each against a separate voter ID. Such duplicate entries were found in booths across the political spectrum.
On October 27, 2025, the Election Commission announced the second phase of the SIR across 12 states and Union Territories, including Uttar Pradesh. The exercise, covering approximately 51 crore voters, began on November 4.
The schedule for Uttar Pradesh was subsequently extended four times. The draft electoral roll was published on January 6, 2026. Those whose names were missing from the draft had to submit Form 6 to seek inclusion. Following the fourth extension, the deadline for filing claims and objections was March 6, while the final electoral roll was published on April 10.
At present a special summary revision (SSR) of electoral rolls is going on in the state. The draft roll was published on November 17.
The Methodology
For each of 69 booths in UP, Alt News read the draft list (January 6, 2026) and the final list (April 10, 2026) entry by entry, and matched the count with the totals on each list’s cover page. We treated two entries as the same person only if the name, father’s or husband’s name, age and house number all matched.
We checked every case against the scanned entry. We then looked up Form 6 applications in the Form 9 lists. The latter is a public list of every Form 6 application an election office received, with the applicant’s name, relative and address. The lists we examined cover 13 assembly constituencies. The 69 booths that we chose fall into the three following groups:
One Form, Several Voter IDs
Listed below are 11 voters (chosen randomly from the 230 to explain the nature of the anomalies) whose names did not appear on the January 6 draft list but were all added to the final list. In each of these cases, the entries share the same name, relative, age and house number, but carry different EPIC numbers. We use first names because they are private citizens.
Our findings revealed two patterns: For Ishlok, Najmeen, Himanshu, Pinki, Saurabh and Aakash, every form became a voter ID, and the entries sit next to each other on the list. Saurabh’s are serial numbers 1004 and 1005.
From Sundar to Sunita, the list has more entries than the published Form 6 list has forms. Married couple Vijay Lakshmi and Dharmendra have a cumulative total of five voter IDs. Vijay Lakshmi has three, while her husband has two.
Anushree Verma, whose husband is Akshay Verma, had filled Form 6 twice and received three voter IDs.
Sundar, mentioned at the beginning, had filled the form twice (According to Form 9) and in return got four voter IDs.
The biggest single cluster of duplicate voters is booth 449 in Chachoi, Sikandrabad (Bulandshahr), where the BJP won 94% of the votes in 2022. The final list adds 69 names to this booth.
Of these, 34 entries are for 17 people, each listed twice with a new EPIC. None of the 17 names are on the January 6 draft list. Fifteen of the 17 filed one Form 6 each on the published lists. For two, Hasmuddin and Heema Devi, we found none. Six of the 17 live at house 91. One of them, Vikas, is listed once as female and once as male.
Some duplicates were already there before the revision and were not removed. In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), two brothers appear twice each, at serials 108 and 109 and at 110 and 111 respectively, on both the draft and final lists.
In booth 1044 of Sahibabad, a father and son already on the list at house number 306 were added again with new IDs at house number 840. We found no Form 6 for either.
The published Form 9 lists for Khair village show one applicant, Bhuvnesh, son of Sanjeev Kumar of Simrauthi village, ten times between January 31 and March 6, 2026.
Across the Form 9 lists of the 13 constituencies, 3,369 people were found to have filed Form 6 between two to 10 times.
Missing Addresses, Renamed IDs, Suspicious Deletions
In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), 20 of the 64 new voters have no house number. The field holds a place name, Oramha, for unrelated families.
Across the 37 city booths, 62 new voters were added with house “0” or a blank. In booth 354 of Kairana (Shamli), 48 voters were already listed at “house 3” on the draft list, and eight more were added from at least seven different families.
In Khair constituency, house number 658, under which all four of Sundar’s entries are listed, is associated with 36 voters from approximately 19 families.
A shared or missing house number is not, in itself, evidence of electoral irregularity, as most villages do not have a system of house numbering. The concern, however, is how entries without a verifiable address could be physically checked during field visits.
Moreover, in booth 351 of Sidhauli (Sitapur), three women’s names appeared changed between the draft and final lists, while the EPIC number, husband’s name, house number and age stayed the same. Rekharani became Lakshmi Devi, Gayashri became Meena Devi and Shivrani became Neelam.
We found 15 such cases across 20 rural booths. These changes could be legitimate corrections. However, only the corresponding Form 8 applications, used to request corrections to electoral roll entries, can establish the basis for the changes.
The most striking example of renamed entries is in booth 327 of Gorakhpur Rural. Serial 799 was Bhathwa, male, 53, house 156, on the draft list. On the final list, the same EPIC belongs to Rusha Devi, female, 50, house 56. Rusha Devi, husband Parmeshwar, also appears at serial numbers 924 and 930 of the addition list under two new EPICs. We found no Form 6 for her among the 23,136 applications in the Gorakhpur Rural lists.
In booth 943 of Sahibabad, 298 entries from one part of the 2025 electoral roll were deleted, 280 of them marked as “absent”. The deletions occurred in consecutive chunks of 23, 17, 14 and 10 names (shown in the plot below). Since electoral rolls are arranged by house and lane, such clusters could simply indicate that an entire building or group of homes had been vacated. A door-to-door verification would establish this. Whether such visits were conducted is something the Election Commission can clarify.
It is worth noting how many voters in every 1,000 appear twice or more on the final roll. See the chart below:
Questions for the Poll Panel
The analysis above poses several significant questions for the election commission vis-a-vis the SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh. Some of them are the following:
- How did one Form 6 become two or three voter IDs – and how many times did this happen across UP?
- Why are repeat applications from the same person, at the same address, not merged before an ID is issued?
- How did officials verify new voters at house ‘0’, blank addresses and catch-all house numbers?
- How to explain the long runs of consecutive ‘Absent’ deletions – were these homes actually visited?
UP CEO’s Response
The Uttar Pradesh CEO initially denied findings by Alt News co-founder Mohammed Zubair, who flagged Sundar’s case of four different EPIC IDs on X. The office responded with the following post:
Mr Fact-checker please fact-check your own facts.
There is no such scheme as “Buy one Get one free” scheme by Election Commission.
As per your post, the voter had submitted only two applications and he got 4 EPIC cards.
This statement is false.
The voter had submitted 4 applications.
If you want to dispute our facts then you post the reference numbers of two applications that you claim he had submitted and we will post the reference number of the remaining two.
The problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long standing one. We do deduplication through ECINET periodically. We are on path to achieving the objective of catching multiple forms submitted by an individual at the submission stage only. We will achieve our objective very soon.
Please do not incite people by making patently false statements about ECI and thereby trying to create disaffection among the citizens towards a Constitutional Body.
You are advised to rectify your mistake by amending or deleting your post after completing your own due diligence now that you have been informed by us about your wrong information.
— CEO Uttar Pradesh (@ceoup) October 17, 2026
The CEO claimed that Sundar had submitted four Form 6 applications, resulting in four separate entries on the final electoral roll. This contradicted the official Form 6 application list, which recorded only two applications from Sundar. However, the CEO’s response also acknowledged that “the problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long-standing one”.
The discrepancy over whether Sundar submitted two or four applications does not alter the central issue: the Commission itself acknowledges that multiple applications by the same voter can result in the generation of multiple EPIC numbers. Its response also indicates that the system does not consistently prevent such duplication at the application stage, necessitating periodic deduplication through ECINET.
On October 19, the CEO directed election officials to expedite the removal of duplicate entries ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections and identify cases in which individual voters had submitted multiple applications during the SIR.
Readers should note that some of the errors documented in this article were rectified by the Election Commission in the intervening period between our initial identification of these anomalies and the publication of this report.

For more than two decades, artificial intelligence has played a growing role in the practice of radiology. Today, nearly every radiologist uses AI tools, whether that’s to triage the images they interpret, dictate their reports, or detect findings in the dozens of X-rays and CTs they read every day.
But last year, radiology experts and developers at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America began to foreground a new paradigm in AI. Business acquisitions and debates centered on technology, powered by vision-language models, that can do the core work of a radiologist: looking at an image, and drafting a report of the clinical findings within it.
“Last year’s RSNA was mainly focused on whether it’s actually possible that an AI model will write a draft for radiologists that would look like an actual radiology report, and that would be accurate enough to be even considered by a radiologist,” said Michael Braginsky, chief technology officer of Aidoc.
