NVIDIA has reinstated cofounder Jensen Huang as its president and chief executive officer (CEO). The reappointment comes 11 days after he resigned from the company amid reports of a foreign intelligence effort targeting him. In a statement today, the company informed that its board of directors unanimously approved the reinstatement, effective immediately, following a series of discussions and meetings with him. The board said it was satisfied with Huang's candour and ability to lead the company moving forward. Pertinent to mention that the company also took into account inputs from senior US government officials, based on which it felt confident that the reinstatement won’t pose any threat to the country’s security risk. The development reverses the leadership transition announced on November 12, when Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board with immediate effect. Huang’s exit came after the revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which involved a woman accused of spying for China. In a letter written to NVIDIA employees, Huang apologised for the issue. Before the allegations of the third affair came to light, the company’s board met on November 12, and voted to oust Jensen Huang. At the time, Nvidia appointed its executive vice president and chief financial officer (CFO) Colette Kress as interim CEO. "Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in a post on November 17. Post his return, Kress will transition back to the role of CFO, while Harvey Jones will remain chair of the board. Nvidia said its board had formed a committee comprising only independent directors to investigate the matter. The committee has retained independent legal counsel, and the investigation will continue to its conclusion. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the probe. The company has also constituted a separate National Security and Export Control Committee, comprising independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. Additionally, NVIDIA is beginning a search for a chief compliance officer (CCO), who will oversee compliance across the company and report to its Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. The company said it would continue cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

Just as GTA 6 has left fans around the world amazed by its expansive world and detailed storyline, the upcoming game has also impressed industry professionals. Developers are reportedly in awe of the scale and technological advancements showcased by Rockstar Games' latest offering.
Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzynski recently took to social media to share his apprehensions about releasing the next CD Projekt Red title in a world where GTA 6 has set such high expectations. Sarzynski jokingly announced that the game, currently codenamed Project Orion, had been cancelled.
Calling GTA 6 the 'single greatest artistic achievement', Sarzynski described its development as nothing short of a miracle. He also joked that the game's extraordinary scale had left developers such as himself struggling with 'depression'.
"GTA 6-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real. Probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history, I mean it. Scale, density, coherence, thoughtfulness of it all, just a technological and creative miracle," wrote Sarzynski in a post on BlueSky. He added: "Cyberpunk 2 is cancelled, imma go sweep autumn leaves in my backyard now."
Although Sarzynski used humour and exaggeration to express his admiration for GTA 6, he also acknowledged that the game's achievements could make other developers nervous about how their upcoming projects would be received.
However, he maintained that Cyberpunk 2 would offer something different rather than attempting to compete directly with Rockstar's latest title.
"Seriously though, I think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavour," he said. "GTA is impressive in a way all great art is: It expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed."
Sarzynski is not the only gaming industry professional to have expressed amazement at GTA 6. Michael Barclay, world design director at Naughty Dog, has also shared his thoughts on the technological advancements demonstrated by the upcoming title.
Barclay, who has previously worked on acclaimed titles such as Uncharted and The Last of Us Part 2, used an unusual comparison to convey how significant the game's technological leap appeared to him.
"I've made video games for 19 years, and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child," Barclay wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
GTA 6 has also generated remarkable commercial expectations. According to figures released by its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, the game recorded estimated worldwide retail sales of $3.79 billion (approximately ₹35,126 crore) within its first 24 hours of release.
The company said the estimate was based on worldwide sales and noted that 32.5 million units had been sold before launch, setting a new record across platforms.

Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
- Published
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.
The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."
If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh

Chapter 3: Tits Ass Drug Money introduces several new activities, vehicles, and collectibles in GTA 6. However, some of these become unavailable once you complete the final mission, The Cartel Heist. Here are all the missable items, activities, and rewards you should collect before the GTA 6 Chapter 3 point of no return appears.
Spoiler Warning:
This article includes spoilers for GTA 6 Chapter 3 missions, optional activities, and collectibles. Read ahead if you want to avoid missing any content during your first playthrough.
GTA 6 Chapter 3 Missables Quick Checklist
Before we dive deep into each missable in Chapter 3 that you can collect on the GTA 6 map, here is a quick checklist you can maintain:
| Item / Activity | Category | Location / Mission | Deadline | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Vanessa’s Growler and Free Garage | Vehicle / Property | Boobie’s Bayside Apartment and La Perle | Before Chapter 3 ends | 
| Monty’s 1992 Pistol | Unique Weapon | The Missing Link | Before leaving the photo room | 
| Gil’s Kalinga .50 | Unique Weapon | Safe Word | Before ending safecracking practice | 
| Race Against Yago | Side Mission | Vice City, Jason only | Time-sensitive | 
| Dubious Provenance Parts 2 and 3 | Side Mission / Vehicle | Evelyn Andrews Antiques, Capri | Before Chapter 3 ends | 
| Boobie’s Bricks ($3,500) | Mission Bonus | Bricked Up | Before leaving the first room | 
| Passion B.C. | Magazine | Bayside Apartment, Bathroom | Before Chapter 3 ends | 
| Two Pricks in the Bush | Magazine | Bayside Apartment, Living Room | Before Chapter 3 ends | 
| Y Hotel Driveway Cars | Free-Roam Loot | Y Hotel, Vice Beach | Before Chapter 4 begins | 
| Club Performance and VIP Conversation | Optional Interaction | Club, before meeting Dimez | Before meeting Dimez | 
| Bret Vogel’s Hunting Rifle | Unique Weapon / Activity | Lummox County | Complete during Chapter 3 if missed earlier | 
All GTA 6 Chapter 3 Missable Missions and Activities
Before completing ‘The Cartel Heist’ GTA 6 mission from Chapter 3 and moving to Chapter 4, finish the following activities to avoid missing optional content.
Vanessa’s Growler and Free Garage
Boobie’s Bayside apartment serves as your safehouse during Chapter 3. However, you will lose access to it after completing The Cartel Heist. Before leaving, solve the laptop puzzle inside the apartment to unlock a free garage in La Perle and claim Vanessa’s Growler in GTA 6.
First, find the three password clues inside the apartment:
- Check the memorial photo on the hallway side table to find the word Muffins.
- Inspect the notepad on the bedroom vanity to find the drawing of a Queen.
- Flip the notepad over to find the number 15.
Use Muffins, Queen, and 15 to unlock Vanessa’s laptop in the bedroom. Open her WhatUp messages and find the conversation with the Unknown contact. It mentions a gift near Auntie’s Place in La Perle and reveals the garage code 92665.
Head to Aline’s Thrift Store in La Perle and walk through the run-down motel parking lot next door. Continue past the closed Auntie’s Place until you find a garage with a bow drawn beside its door. Enter 92665 to unlock the Del Rio Boulevard Garage.
Inside, you will find Vanessa’s Growler, a pink Pfister worth around $22,660. Drive it out to register the vehicle for free. You will permanently lose access to the GTA 6 garage location and its vehicle if you finish Chapter 3 without claiming them.
Monty’s 1992 Pistol
During The Missing Link story mission, Lucia visits Sloppy Molly’s in Watson Bay to take photographs of the cartel. After knocking out Monty in a melee fight, you must shoot your way out of the location.
Before continuing through the mission, make sure you collect Monty’s unique 1992 Pistol.
- Defeat the first enemy during the shootout.
- Immediately turn around and return to the photo room.
- Look for Monty’s 1992 Pistol on the floor.
- Pick it up before moving forward.
Note: You will miss the weapon if you leave the photo room without collecting it. During the alligator pool interrogation as Jason, avoid lowering Monty all the way into the water while answering Raul’s questions. This earns the Professional bonus.
Gil’s Kalinga .50
Another missables you shouldn’t miss in Chapter 3 is Gil’s Kalinga .50, one of the best GTA 6 weapons. You will find it during the safecracking practice at Raul’s compound in the Safe Word mission. The unique weapon is inside the safe, along with $1,500 in cash.
After completing the main objectives, Lucia gets the chance to practice safecracking. Do not quit the session early. Instead, complete all three steps:
- Drill through the safe.
- Guide the cable through the mechanism.
- Hold the door open to finish cracking the safe.
Open the safe to collect Gil’s Kalinga .50 and the cash. Leaving the practice session before opening it means missing the unique weapon.
Race Against Yago
Race Against Yago is a time-sensitive side mission for Jason. It becomes available a few in-game days after completing Join a Street Race and Bumper to Bumper.
Once the mission appears, you will see an hourglass icon on the Vice City map. Head to the marker as Jason and complete the race against Yago.
Winning the race rewards you with $3,800 and unlocks his final mission, Brother to Brother. However, the Race Against Yago activity can disappear if you wait too long. Missing it can also prevent you from completing Yago’s questline for Strangers and Freaks progress.
Dubious Provenance Parts 2 and 3
Dubious Provenance starts at Evelyn Andrews Antiques in Capri. Your decision during the first part determines how you access the remaining missions.
- Accept Halifax’s offer: He gives you his watch as collateral. You can equip it through Accessories and Watches.
- Decline Halifax’s offer: You can make an optional phone call to Halifax later. You must make this call before Chapter 3 ends to unlock the remaining parts.
During Part 2, choose to trust Halifax at the motel. This unlocks Part 3, which takes you to a storage container with around $2,500 worth of cash and jewelry. You will also find a ’32 Hustler car in GTA 6 that you can keep or sell.
Make sure you complete the follow-up missions before finishing Chapter 3. Otherwise, Parts 2 and 3 become unavailable.
Boobie’s Bricks in Bricked Up
The Bricked Up story mission has an optional $3,500 reward that is an easy Chapter 3 missable in GTA 6. Before leaving the first room of the apartment, look for a red bag of drugs near the end of the table. Pick it up to collect Boobie’s Bricks.
Leaving the room without the bag forfeits the $3,500 payout and the Professional bonus. That will help you maintain your GTA 6 criminal profile.
Y Hotel Driveway Cars
The Y Hotel in Vice Beach becomes your new safehouse in Chapter 4. Once you move in, you will lose access to the cars parked in its driveway.
Before completing Chapter 3, visit the hotel and steal the high-end vehicles parked outside. Several of these cars can sell for more than $10,000, and some may also appear on Randy’s Wish List in GTA 6.
Club Performance and VIP Conversation
Before heading to the parking lot to meet Dimez, take some time to explore the club. There are two optional interactions you can easily miss.
- Turn up the bass dial on the dancefloor to trigger Dwnfly’s rap performance.
- Visit the ground-floor VIP booth to eavesdrop on the conversation between Boobie and the record producer.
Bret Vogel’s Hunting Rifle
If you have not already visited Bret Vogel in Lummox County as Jason, complete his short mission during Chapter 3.

Jio’s media arm, JioStar is reportedly looking to hand out the pink slip to about 150 employees. The job cuts will impact multiple departments, including marketing, production, studios, and other operational functions. Industry sources suggest that the final number could be significantly higher. The impacted personnel will be offered a “substantial” severance package comprising a minimum of six months’ salary alongside a pro-rata bonus for the current financial year. Confirming the development, a JioStar spokesperson told Inc42, “We are rebalancing our portfolio to focus our investments on the businesses where we see the strongest opportunity for long-term growth. This is a strategic decision aimed at strengthening our competitive position in a dynamic and rapidly evolving industry. We recognise that these decisions will have an impact on some of our employees and we are committed to treating every colleague with respect and providing them every possible support through the transition.” The development was first reported by exchange4media. This is the second round of major job cuts at JioStar since the entity was formed by the merger of Reliance Industries-backed Viacom18 and Disney’s Star India. The merged entity was valued at $8.5 Bn (₹70,352 Cr) with Reliance holding a controlling stake, while Disney retained a significant minority interest. Reliance had also announced an investment of $1.4 Bn to support JioStar’s growth. Following the November 2024 amalgamation, JioStar executed an extensive restructuring in March 2025 that resulted in over 1,000 employees exiting. However, those layoffs were focused primarily on eliminating redundancies rather than to protect margins. The layoffs come amid a mixed financial performance for JioStar, with revenue growing but profitability coming under pressure. For the September quarter (Q2 FY27), JioStar reported a 10% year-on-year (YoY) increase in operating revenue to ₹6,806 Cr. However, EBITDA from operations fell 11% to ₹1,372 Cr, while operating EBITDA margin contracted 600 basis points to 22.1% from 28.1% a year earlier. Profit before tax also declined 14% to ₹1,139 Cr. The company attributed the revenue growth to higher subscription income across digital and linear television, stronger digital entertainment advertising and increased sports advertising, supported by a higher number of cricketing events. Operationally, JioStar reported a 15% YoY increase in digital entertainment watch time during the quarter, driven by network general entertainment channels (GECs) and original content. It also said advertising revenue from digital entertainment grew on the back of higher connected TV (CTV) monetisation. On the sports front, the India-West Indies series recorded 12% higher digital viewership and 13% higher CTV viewership than the England-India series in 2026. Meanwhile, the ongoing Premier League 2026-27 season saw digital viewership rise 25% and CTV viewership increase 13% compared with the previous season, based on data up to October 25, 2026. JioStar also expanded JioHotstar into Singapore, the UK and Canada, reporting a 30% increase in its subscriber base following the international relaunch. The platform has additionally integrated food delivery services across its entertainment offering.

Genomic testing can answer a variety of pressing health questions a person (and their clinician) might face throughout their lifespan.
Unfortunately, these valuable tests have become fragmented and iterative for most patients. A patient may receive a carrier screening test before or during pregnancy; a cancer predisposition test to screen for inherited cancer-predisposition variants like BRCA, the breast cancer gene; and a pharmacogenomic test before starting a medication. Each test is a new blood draw or buccal swab, a new wet lab workflow, a new spot on a genome sequencer, a new analysis, and new costs borne by patients and insurance companies.
With the precipitous decline in the cost of whole genome sequencing, it’s time to consolidate testing by sequencing genomes once and reevaluating them when needed.
As research has shown, patients face many challenges to accessing genomic testing including financial barriers, limited access to providers, geographic limitations, and clinician biases. Since the genome can enable diagnoses and care for so many health conditions, a more streamlined and uniform approach to genomic testing would likely benefit many patients. I call it “test once, evaluate often.”
Is one test really enough?
A “test once, evaluate often” approach could start at any age. For some families, that might be at birth, as an optional add-on to the newborn screening their baby already gets. A single whole genome sequence could be stored, along with other medical records information, for future analysis. Any time a clinician orders a new genomic test, the lab would simply reevaluate the relevant genes and issue a report.
This approach would dramatically lower the cost and turnaround time needed to answer genomic questions by eliminating the sample handling and wet lab processing of patient samples, potentially improving access to genomic information for patients who would otherwise choose to forgo testing due to costs.
Such a paradigm would only apply to tests looking at germline DNA (the DNA we are born with). Clinical genomic tests seeking to understand the genetics of other biological characteristics, such as somatic DNA in a cancer tissue, circulating fetal DNA in a noninvasive prenatal test, or circulating tumor DNA in liquid biopsy panels would still be needed to look for genomic variants beyond germline DNA when patient circumstances dictate.
What about newborns?
Newborn screening is one of public health’s great successes. For more than 60 years, nearly every U.S. baby has had a heel-prick blood test for dozens of serious, treatable conditions, catching thousands of babies each year who look perfectly healthy.
For many, early diagnosis is the difference between life and death. Infants with severe combined immunodeficiency who receive a transplant by 3.5 months survive 94% of the time. Babies destined for the most severe form of spinal muscular atrophy who receive gene therapy before symptoms emerge go on to sit independently and breathe without permanent ventilation. Any interruption to newborn screening would cost children their lives.
Genome sequencing builds on that foundation. In the BabySeq Project, 9.4% of newborns had an unexpected genetic risk for childhood-onset disease. In New York’s GUARDIAN study, 72% of families opted in and 3.7% of babies screened positive, including for treatable conditions that standard screening misses. Because sequencing alone misses some cases that biochemical tests catch, it should add to the heel prick, not replace it.
In childhood, reporting can stay focused on conditions where knowing early changes care; the rest of the genome can wait until there’s a question to answer. And as with any public health program, clear consent and transparent data use must be built in from the start.
Regular evaluation of the genome is critical
The need for genomic information changes with patient circumstances and throughout their lifespan. This is why regular evaluation of the genome is needed in place of the piecemeal approach to ordering individual tests today.
Unfortunately, genomic science is not yet in a place where a single point of evaluation is practical. Evidence about emerging gene-disease relationships and new understandings of variants associated with hereditary cancer and other diseases continue to be adopted into clinical practice, meaning that an analysis conducted 20 years into the future would likely deliver more information than is currently possible.
The genomics community has honed a version of this practice, termed reanalysis, in the rare disease space. There, it is commonplace to reexamine a patient’s exome or genome based on emerging clinical evidence about gene-disease relationships.
Reevaluation is a bit different. Reanalysis is done for the same testing indication (i.e., finding the genetic cause of a rare disease) and reevaluation is studying the same genome for a new testing indication.
The National Human Genome Research Institute envisions a future where genomic data is systematically collected and used more regularly and efficiently for patient benefit. Getting there means moving clinical and laboratory medicine toward a system in which a genome sequenced once, whether at birth or later in life, helps a person’s clinicians manage their health throughout their life.
Making this vision a reality will require several changes to the way medicine is practiced and paid for today.
First, health systems, laboratories, and policymakers need to agree on how genomic data will be stored securely for decades and who can see it. Patients already trust online patient portals with their lab results and medical records, and genomic data can be held to the same standards of security and transparency.
These questions are already being actively worked on. Leading newborn sequencing programs, such as New York’s GUARDIAN study and England’s Generation Study, ask parents for opt-in consent, keep data under strict access controls, and are studying how long it should be kept. Leftover newborn screening blood spots have also been stored for years in many states, often without parents knowing, which is why consent and transparency have become central to this work. Any program that stores genomes, at birth or later, must start with fully informed consent: patients and parents should know what is kept, where, for how long and who may use it, and be free to say no.
Second, additional genetic counseling resources would need to support patients along their genomic health journeys, helping balance clinical needs, desires for information, and the familial implications of genomic insights. That support matters even more as care becomes increasingly patient-driven, with more people ordering tests themselves, reading their own results, and coming back with new questions.
Finally, and perhaps most important, insurers need a way to pay for evaluating a genome that has already been sequenced. Today, insurance can cover reanalysis, but there is no clear path to pay for reevaluation, the step that makes “test once, evaluate often” work. Paying for it would save insurers money, too, since it could replace repeat sequencing over a patient’s lifetime. Without reimbursement for prevention-oriented sequencing, genetic counseling, and genomic evaluation, we can’t improve equity in genomic testing.
Sharing data, finding answers
Something I’ve seen again and again in the rare disease setting is that parents of a child without a diagnosis are almost always eager to share their child’s genetic data. They know that a match with another family somewhere in the world may be what finally explains what’s happening, and many new gene discoveries start exactly that way.
If we protect genomic data well and show people what sharing makes possible, more of us may come to see it the way these parents do: not as a risk to minimize, but as a path to answers, prevention, and cures.
Kelly Hagman, M.S., is a genetic counselor and vice president of medical affairs and strategic integration at Ambry Genetics, a Tempus company. She led the launch of the industry’s first clinical exome and has authored more than 55 peer-reviewed publications.

Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.
“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.
Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.
“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.
A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.
“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.
Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”
Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.
The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.
“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

Western intelligence officials worry that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit before the end of the year, suggesting the country’s development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought, German media reported Monday.
The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia’s own spacecraft and Chinese satellites.
US lawmakers briefed on government intelligence first disclosed Russia’s ambition to deploy a space-based nuclear weapon in early 2024. At the time, US officials said Russia had launched a test satellite in 2022 to test the effects of radiation on space hardware and pave the way for a future nuclear-armed craft, but that Russia had not yet sent a nuclear weapon into orbit.
Reporting from three German news outlets—public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Munich-based newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung—indicates Russia’s launch of a nuclear-armed satellite could be imminent. The report says Western intelligence agencies, including the German Armed Forces and Federal Intelligence Service, believe Russia is preparing to deploy the weapon in space this year. Several NATO countries have exchanged their findings on the matter.
Ready and waiting
The nuclear-armed satellite, designated Sputnik-S, has been in storage in the greater Moscow area for years, the German news report said. German Space Command believes the satellite could be launched as early as December. Once in orbit, a nuclear weapon could loiter for months or years, ready for detonation on the command of Russian military forces.
The Kremlin dismissed the report. “Given the number of qualifiers like ‘allegedly’ and ‘possibly’—not to mention the fact that the claims are attributed to some unspecified source—they are hardly worth taking seriously,” said Dmitry Peskov, spokesperson for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

An 18-second-long video has been circulating on social media, which shows Sandeep Khirwar, Special Director General (SDG) of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), making a remark regarding the transportation of the bodies of two Special Police Officers (SPOs) in a dumper truck.
In the viral clip, Khirwar can be heard saying, “All military trucks and vehicles in the area were occupied. So we had no choice but to transport the bodies of our two martyred SPO personnel in a dumper truck. But the real issue is not whether they were transported in a dumper or a garbage truck. Their families received the bodies of their loved ones. What more could they possibly want?”
X user @cutegirlindia21 shared this video and wrote, “Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred Kishtwar Police officers had to be transported in a garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the Indian Army refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police.”
🛑 Heartbreaking 💔 😢
Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred @KishtwarPolice officers had to be transported in a #garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the #IndianArmy refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police. https://t.co/Jm9i7bScN0
— A N U S H I ❤️T I W A R I🇮🇳 (@cutegirlindia21) November 16, 2026
According to an NDTV report published on November 14, the bodies of SPOs Bobby Chand and Rashpal Kumar — who lost their lives in a recent terror attack in the Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir — were transported to their native village Kiyar in a dumper truck without coffins. This incident sparked significant outrage among locals, with many questioning the manner in which the bodies were transported.
Against this backdrop, the purported video of SDG Sandeep Khirwar began to circulate. Several other users on X, including @RedDeFactoIND, @NetaNamax, and @unknownnewss, also shared the video with similar claims.
The video is also circulating on Facebook with similar assertions.
Fact Check
To determine the authenticity of the viral clip, Alt News used relevant keywords to search for information regarding statements made by Khirwar. We did not find any credible news reports or official statements that substantiate the claims made in the viral clip.
We observed that the viral video bears an ANI logo. Performing a ‘reverse image search’ using keyframes from the clip, we found the original video, which was posted by ANI on its official X account on November 16, 2026. In the video, Sandeep Khirwar, SDG of the CRPF’s Jammu & Kashmir Zone, is seen speaking to the media in Srinagar regarding the deaths of two SPOs in Kishtwar.
#WATCH | Srinagar, J&K: On the mortal remains of two missing SPOs recovered in Kishtwar, SDG, CRPF J&K Zone, Sandeep Khirwar says, “Every loss of life to any jawan in the security forces is a huge loss to all of us… We stand with their families, and we will make sure that they get justice.”
— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
While the visuals of the video matches, the audio is different. In the original footage, Khirwar states: “All I can say is that, every loss of life to any Jawan, of any security forces are huge loss to all of us and we owe our utmost respect to all the fallen. And we stand with their family. We will make sure that they get justice, the families get justice.” He does not make any mention of the bodies being transported in a dumper truck, nor did he claim that the families were ‘grateful’ upon the recovery of the bodies.
Further, we found that the Khirwar’s voice and manner of speaking in the viral clip does not match the way he is heard speaking in the ANI footage, indicating that the original audio has been digitally altered or manipulated. We ran the viral clip through AI-detection Hive Moderation, which revealed that it is 98.9% likely to contain AI-generated speech.
On November 17, the official X handle of the CRPF’s Srinagar Sector addressed the viral claim. They stated that the video had been digitally tampered with and that false statements had been attributed to Sandeep Khirwar, clarifying that no such statements were made by him.
This claim is false and misleading. The video was digitally manipulated, with fabricated remarks attributed to CRPF Special DG Sh. Sandeep Khirwar, who is not the Kashmir Police Chief. The original footage contained no such statement. This is an attempt to spread misinformation and create an anti-India narrative.
— Srinagar Sector CRPF 🇮🇳 (@crpf_srinagar) November 17, 2026
Thus, the viral clip has been digitally manipulated using AI, falsely attributing statements about the transportation of SPOs’ bodies in a dumper truck to Sandeep Khirwar. The original footage by ANI does not carry any such comment.
Sajahan Ali is an intern at Alt News.

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.
Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.
Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.
The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.
“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.
Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.
Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.
“When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.
The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.
Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.
In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

Team science — or collaborative science across disciplines and institutions — is essential for scientific progress as modern problems are too complex for a single person, laboratory, or even field to solve alone. Some of the best work happens when scientists from different countries collaborate.
However, U.S. policies in place and in development increasingly curtail this vital foreign collaboration. There are foreign funding restrictions, visa and entry restrictions for researchers, mandatory institutional compliance and audits with respect to foreign collaborations, and tight export controls. These policies were implemented as biosecurity measures to protect from “countries of concern,” including China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.
Meanwhile, proprietary scientific research is easily accessible to anyone, including foreign actors, through a policy meant to protect Americans’ right to government information. In other words, we are locking the front door while the back window is still wide open.
How does this happen?
The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) is a U.S. federal law enacted in 1966 in response to concerns that the government was too broad and unaccountable. FOIA gives anyone the right to request access to records held by federal government agencies.
This means that through FOIA, anyone — U.S. citizens, noncitizens, and foreign nationals — can access U.S. government-funded science by completing a simple online form and paying a minimal fee. While FOIA is an incredibly important tool for citizens in a free society, it was never intended to allow anyone around the globe to access proprietary U.S. science.
People are readily climbing in through the open back window. As a scientist in the U.S., I personally experienced the impact of such a FOIA request. I was notified by a FOIA coordinator at an NIH institute that my scientific ideas, supported by a funded grant from the U.S. government, were being requested by a Chinese entity through a simple online request form. They only had to pay a $25 fee.
By law, I had to comply and release the grant to them. The requester was listed as a “Consultant” and identified by a generic email address and physical address in China that could not be verified.
I am not the only one to have this experience. The FOIA coordinator told me offhand that this specific individual had a track record of requesting numerous grants from different NIH institutes every year. More broadly, over a decade, the NIH received more than 13,300 requests for grant proposals through FOIA. (Meanwhile, journalists’ FOIA requests often face major delays and other hurdles.)
This loophole has significant negative ramifications on our society. Scientific grants contain unpublished scientific data and sensitive intellectual property. The release of this material could:
1) harm personal and institutional financial interests by divulging patentable ideas, product concepts, and precompetitive information;
2) mislead the public through exposure to unvetted and untested hypotheses and preliminary data;
3) ruin careers and livelihoods of U.S. scientists; and perhaps most importantly,
4) damage U.S. interests by allowing foreign nationals or foreign corporations to be the primary beneficiaries of work funded by the U.S. taxpayer.
Our policies are fundamentally not aligned to protect science. We say we are blocking competing foreign interests, yet through FOIA, anyone can access this science.
If the U.S. truly wants to protect science, Congress needs to close the open window that FOIA affords. Proprietary U.S. science should be exempt or excluded from FOIA. Failing that, those who can access our material must be scrutinized.
Almost exactly four years after receiving the FOIA request, a research team from China published findings that closely matched my team’s original hypothesis — one our own later experiments did not support. While I cannot say whether the FOIA request, my grant, and this recent publication are related, the timing has made me think more about how research, including my own, is ultimately used in these situations.
Francesca E. Duncan, Ph.D. is the Thomas J. Watkins memorial professor of reproductive science in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology in the Feinberg School of Medicine at Northwestern University. She is also an associate professor in residence at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging. The views presented here are her own.

At first preventive services panel meeting in more than a year, votes are cast in private
In its first meeting since March 2025, an influential panel of doctors that evaluates preventive medical care grappled with the ways Kennedy has upended science and medicine.
Last week, the 16-member panel voted on recommendations on screening for cervical cancer, perinatal depression, and unhealthy alcohol use by teens and adults. The recommendations have been awaiting completion for more than a year while Kennedy repeatedly canceled meetings and largely remade the panel’s membership.
The discussion was livestreamed to the public for the first time, though the votes were held in private. Throughout the session, longtime and new members debated a Trump administration policy requiring the removal of language on “diversity, equity, and inclusion,” after Roger Klein, director of the USPSTF’s parent organization, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, cut all sub-population data from recommendation language.
“I worry that having edits from political leadership on the topline may lead to the perception that the task force recommendations are no longer scientifically independent,” Alicia Fernandez, a member of the panel since 2025, said as members discussed cervical cancer screenings.
At another point, some members expressed concern about bias in the presentations from subject matter experts. Members also asked how they might accurately and transparently explain when and how artificial intelligence is used in their data and recommendations.
“Should our documentation say ‘supported by AI?’” new member Ronald Karlsberg asked. — Chelsea Cirruzzo
The American Diabetes Association is in chaos. Who are the real losers?
Over the last several months, the American Diabetes Association has been … a real mess. There have been recriminations, a raft of resignations, and a 1,221-member boycott. Who’s the loser in all this high drama?
Patients.
Experts say the impact of the ADA’s crisis won’t be felt immediately. But a dysfunctional professional organization could stymie advances in diabetes care for years to come. That’s because the ADA plays a key role in setting guidelines and sharing research in journals and at wide-ranging meetings that attract thousands.
“All of this has coalesced to make everyone anxious, uncertain about the future of diabetes research,” one expert told STAT. “And the ADA should at this point be standing up and being something that we can all rally behind. Instead it is being fractured by its own actions.” Read more.
MAHA think tank’s bank account isn’t looking so healthy
If you know the MAHA Institute, a think tank launched to support Kennedy’s agenda, it’s probably because of its roundtables.
Events, STAT’s Isa Cueto writes, are the organization’s “bread and butter.” They were also a money pit — one “Friends of MAHA” fundraiser cost $230,000 to put on and netted just $55,000 from three contributors.
That might help explain the group’s current financial troubles. As Isa reports, the Institute started 2025 with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, and ended the year with $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed last week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year. Read more, and also check out her companion piece on the MAHA PAC’s very odd spending habits.
After Chinese researcher is detained, international scholars wonder if travel in the U.S. is safe
When Eva Yi Xie moved to the U.S. from China in 2016, she spoke so little English she told her teachers she “probably won’t understand what you will talk about.”
But her biology teacher helped her bone up, giving her vocabulary lists and translated tests. By 2020, Xie was a Regeneron Science Talent Search finalist on her way to MIT. She has since become a rising star in science circles. As a graduate student at Princeton, Xie is combining neuroscience and AI to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions.
Xie was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last week while traveling home from a neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C. While her visa had expired, Xie’s lawyers said Xie has a pending asylum application and is in the U.S. legally.
The news has shaken academics across the country, who wonder if it’s safe for international scholars to travel to present their research. “We are very privileged as a country to have people like Eva continue to pursue academia at the highest level, and to share that with other people,” one said. “That’s literally the nature and reason why we go to conferences to present stuff. It is appalling to me that she cannot do that with reasonable certainty that she can’t be detained.” Read more.
Vaccine skeptics hijack federal autism committee meeting (again)
Halfway through Friday’s meeting of the federal autism coordinating committee, where members discussed the most important scientific papers about autism in the last two years, Ginger Taylor was “very angry.”
“Committee members have been robbed of their statutory duties in having limitations on what can be submitted,” said Taylor, a parent of an autistic child and the former director of the Maine Coalition for Vaccine Choice. She wanted to add more than 200 articles from her personal archives that investigate whether vaccines can cause autism. (There’s no evidence they do.)
As they had during the previous meeting of the committee, which coordinates federal agency efforts to address autism and advises RFK Jr., Taylor and several other Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee members intermittently hijacked the gathering. They suggested the group, handpicked by RFK Jr., should include research on “immunological triggers” in its annual survey of important autism research.
If you want to read the more than 500 papers submitted by the public and committee members, you can find them here. Befitting the wide spectrum of autism, the papers diverge in topic and tone. The group will vote on which papers to include in coming weeks. These votes and the group’s strategic plan will act as guides for Congress as it allocates federal autism research funding. — O. Nasscom seeks AI transformation scheme for IT firms in Budget 2027-28
The industry body said generative and agentic AI are changing what clients want, how technology work is delivered and how IT firms charge for it
The National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom) has asked the government to set up a dedicated scheme to help Indian IT services companies adapt to artificial intelligence (AI). This demand is part of its pre-budget recommendations for the Union Budget 2027-28.
The industry body said generative and agentic AI are changing what clients want, how technology work is delivered and how IT firms charge for it.
Building new AI products and retraining staff needs money upfront, it said, and companies have to spend it while still delivering for existing clients. Smaller companies are hit hardest as they struggle to fund development, hire specialists and free up staff to learn on live projects.
Nasscom wants the budget to commit to an “AI Services Transformation and Innovation Scheme” for an initial three years. Under the proposal, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the finance ministry would design the funding and implementation together with industry.
Also Read: Nasscom pushes back on US green card freeze: ‘Immigration, talent mobility distinct issues’
“A Budget 2027-28 commitment to develop the AI Services Transformation and Innovation Scheme for an initial three years, with MeitY and the Ministry of Finance designing funding and implementation with industry. This would support technology development and commercialisation, including offerings earning licence, subscription, usage-based or outcome-linked revenues, built and operated from India,” said Nasscom.
The scheme would back AI offerings that are built and run from India and earn money through licences, subscriptions, usage-based fees or outcome-linked pricing. It would also tie training to supervised work on real projects, so existing employees can move into new roles and freshers get hands-on experience. Smaller firms would get shared technical facilities, specialist support and joint projects.
Cybersecurity support for MSMEs
Cyber cover for MSMEs, tax clarity for Global capability centres (GCCs)
Nasscom has also asked for a contributory cybersecurity programme with a capped first-phase allocation. It would help manufacturing and services MSMEs put basic cyber protections in place and keep them running. Many of these small firms work inside the delivery chains of bigger IT companies that handle client data and run critical systems for enterprises worldwide, it said. Weak links there could hurt trust in Indian service delivery, the body said.
Also Read: Should the government own a piece of AI companies?
Tax clarity for global capability centres
Global capability centres (GCCs) are on the list too. These centres are taking on complex engineering, R&D and leadership work, and that brings more overseas specialists visiting, more secondments (overseas staff temporarily posted in India) and more India-based executives running global teams. Nasscom wants clear rules so none of this creates a taxable “permanent establishment” for the foreign parent.
Under Nasscom’s proposal, overseas staff could visit for up to 90 days in any 12-month period without creating a permanent establishment. A secondment wouldn’t create one either, as long as the Indian GCC directs the work and pays the salary, and reimbursing the actual salary cost wouldn’t be taxed as fees for technical services.

Mental health concerns among refugee communities are linked not only to past trauma, violence and forced displacement but also to legal uncertainty, limited work opportunities, poor living conditions and social isolation in host countries, finds a study of Sri Lankan Tamil and Rohingya communities in India, published in the International Journal of Migration, Health and Social Care.
Titled ‘Building mental health capacity in protracted refugee situations: Empirical pointers from Sri Lankan Tamil and Rohingya populations in India’, the study looks at common mental health concerns and barriers to accessing care. It calls for training community members and health workers to recognise psychological distress, provide basic support and facilitate access to professional mental health services.

A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.
Made by brain-computer interface company Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia. Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, says Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.
Today, Austin-based Paradromics announced a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.
That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.
“We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle says. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.
“We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he says.
Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.
Paradromics plans to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow users to interact with computers and other devices with low lag time. Brain-computer interfaces will need to work alongside other sensors, such as cameras and microphones, and Holoscan will help process these different data streams together so applications can respond to both neural signals and the context around them.
“Brain-computer interfaces must translate complex neural signals into meaningful actions in real time. Even small delays can make communication feel unnatural,” David Niewolny, Nvidia’s director of business development for health care and medical, tells WIRED via email. “Neural signals also change over time, requiring AI that can continuously adapt to the individual.” Nvidia’s technology processes neural signals and runs AI models in real time.
Reducing lag time is important for a brain-computer interface with a speech function so that users can have naturally flowing conversation without delays.
Through the partnership, Paradromics will also be able to integrate Nvidia’s foundation models into its brain-computer interface. Vikash Gilja, chief scientific officer at Paradromics, says AI models could help make synthesized voices more expressive and human-like. Also, if these models are running locally on Nvidia hardware, it means users won’t have to be connected to the internet in order to use their devices.
Niewolny says he sees “tremendous potential for AI to expand human capability.” Nvidia is working with other players in the brain-computer interface space, including Synchron. The chipmaker will not have access to brain data through these partnerships, he says.

AI unicorn Sarvam AI has defended its Token Factory business, saying the platform runs on privately procured GPUs rather than government-subsidised computing capacity, while reiterating that developing homegrown AI models remains its core focus. In a post on X, cofounder Pratyush Kumar addressed questions about the startup’s government support, its decision to host global open-weight models, and whether its expansion into inference infrastructure signals a shift away from building indigenous models. Notably, Token Factory’s launch had sparked online debates about Sarvam’s use of government subsidised compute capacity and its ability to anchor India’s indigenous AI ambitions. Kumar said the IndiaAI Mission gave around 20 startups access to GPUs at a 40% discount. Sarvam used this computing capacity to train its 105-billion-parameter foundation model from scratch, completing and releasing it in February 2026, he said. He added that the government did not make direct payments to Sarvam. Instead, the subsidy went to GPU cloud providers, which supplied discounted computing resources to participating startups. Sarvam’s access to the government-supported GPU allocation ended in March this year. The startup said Token Factory operates on GPUs it procured privately. Under the IndiaAI Mission, Sarvam received access to 4,096 Nvidia H100 GPUs to develop indigenous foundation models. The six-month computing allocation was valued at around ₹247 Cr, including a government subsidy of ₹98.68 Cr. The Inference Business Case The clarification follows the launch of Token Factory, which hosts Sarvam’s own models alongside global open-weight models, including Google’s Gemma and China’s DeepSeek and Kimi, on GPU infrastructure in India. The platform lets developers and enterprises access multiple models through a single API, without procuring GPUs or managing model deployment themselves. It charges customers for the tokens they use. Kumar said open-weight models offer enterprises cost advantages and greater control over their AI systems. However, Indian businesses requiring data to remain within the country and fast responses for interactive applications need access to locally hosted models, he argued. He claimed Sarvam has optimised its data centre-scale inference infrastructure to offer token prices comparable to or lower than global providers such as Fireworks AI, Baseten, and Together AI. Kumar said India consumes a few trillion tokens daily, with most of this demand served from overseas. Building domestic inference capacity could reduce that dependence while creating a commercial opportunity, he argued. He added that Sarvam would continue reducing costs and widening access to inference services in India. Sarvam Reiterates Focus On Homegrown Models Kumar said building inference infrastructure does not conflict with Sarvam’s core mission of training its own models. Over the past few months, the startup has optimised its training systems for NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs alongside building Token Factory and expanding its enterprise offerings, he said. Using this infrastructure, Sarvam trained Sarvam-105B-1711, an upgraded version of its 105-billion-parameter model, which it released yesterday. The company claimed improvements in reasoning, tool use, Indian languages, and work tasks involving multiple steps. Kumar described it as one of the strongest models in the Flash-Lite category, which targets high-volume applications such as customer support and voice agents. Kumar said the model can power its agentic AI product Indus. Alongside the model weights, Sarvam is releasing training and inference recipes to help developers build on the technology. The startup plans to release more models across vision, speech, and edge AI over the next two weeks. It is also working with partners to bring the latest training-grade computing infrastructure to India for its next generation of larger models. Kumar said Sarvam aims to pursue larger models while building a sustainable commercial business serving enterprises and population-scale applications.

Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).
DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.
The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.
On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.
