Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
The claim
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
The evidence
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
The bottom line
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend Molly Meldrum
- Published
King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".
Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".
King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.
"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."
Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

The photo of the ballroom with the White House is authentic, and therefore accurate. However …
… The other images greatly exaggerate the ballroom's size in comparison with the other structures.
The day after November's midterm elections, in which U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party was soundly defeated by the Democratic Party, Trump spoke to reporters about the ballroom under construction at the White House rather than on his party's losses.
With the spotlight back on the White House ballroom, which the Trump administration tore down the White House's East Wing to build, people have begun pointing out how large the shell of the new addition is compared with the rest of the building. For example, an image in one Facebook post (archived) compared the ballroom, which appears larger than the White House's main building, to the Taj Mahal, Colosseum and Sydney Opera House. In the image, it appears to rival the size of each.
Other users shared the same image on Threads (archived) as well as other (archived) places (archived) on Facebook.
The image, while leading with a real photo of the White House and the under-construction ballroom, inaccurately depicts the ballroom as rivaling the size of the other architectural landmarks, which are much larger than the White House and the ballroom. Therefore, we've rated this claim mostly false.
The photo of the White House and the ballroom was taken by MS NOW host Jonathan Capehart, who shared it to his Substack account and said he took the photo after takeoff from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.
The Trump administration has said the ballroom will be 90,000 square feet. Aside from that, there is no publicly released information on the ballroom's dimensions. 
However, there is a way to get rough estimates of the ballroom's dimensions. In February, the architecture firm working on the ballroom, Shalom Baranes Associates, submitted a proposal for the "East Wing Modernization" to the National Capital Planning Commission. This proposal included a floor plan of the planned ballroom and a scale on Page 19. Based on this, Snopes estimates that the new East Wing with the ballroom is about 340 feet long and 150 feet wide.
The image's other comparisons depict the ballroom to be much larger than the Taj Mahal's marble platform, comparable in size to the Colosseum and comparable in size to the Sydney Opera House.
The Indian government says the Taj Mahal's marble platform is a square that is about 313 feet long on each side. Considering that the ballroom would fall just short of being half as wide as the platform and only be a little longer than the platform, it's inaccurate for the image to depict the ballroom at nearly the width of the Taj Mahal's platform and much longer than it.
The Colosseum covers a yet larger space than the Taj Mahal does. It's about 620 feet long and 510 feet wide, according to local tourist agencies. So in reality, the Colosseum is nearly twice as long as the ballroom and over three times as wide. Once again, the depicted comparison in the social media image doesn't align with reality.
The company that created the facade of the Sydney Opera House says that the building is about 600 feet long, making it comparable in length to the Colosseum. At its widest point, the Sydney Opera House is about 390 feet wide. The ballroom looks too long and possibly too wide as compared to the famous Australian building. 
It's also worth noting that the buildings depicted differ vastly in height, not just in square footage. The White House is 70 feet tall at its tallest point. The ballroom appears roughly the same height or slightly taller than the main mansion of the White House in Capehart's photo, which is supported by Washington Post reporting from January that the ballroom was planned to be the same height as the main building of the White House.
The World Monument Fund says the Taj Mahal is more 200 feet tall. The Colosseum is nearly 160 feet tall. The Sydney Opera House is about 220 feet tall. While the images depict the ballroom as shorter than these buildings, it doesn't appear to be as short compared with them as it should be.
Finally, it appears all of the comparison images after the Capehart photo are AI-generated. The most obvious piece of evidence suggesting as much are the construction sites that inexplicably surround the ballroom in each comparison image. While each construction site looks largely the same, individual details about the site in each image, such as the location of the excavator, have small variations. AI image generators often struggle to keep small details like that consistent across a series of multiple images.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked other AI-generated images of the White House ballroom, including one claimed to be a render of the design plans that incorrectly placed the ballroom directly adjacent to the main building of the White House.

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.
The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).
Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.
Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.
Lead azide risk
Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

It was the most simple of questions. On Monday afternoon, during a NASA news conference about the International Space Station, Space News reporter Jeff Foust asked about an upcoming launch of a Russian spacecraft.
“It’s my understanding there’s another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress,” Foust said. “Can you confirm that, and give the date and time that will launch?”
This Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday. It is going to a space station co-operated by the US space agency. But no, NASA would not provide this basic information about the upcoming Progress launch.
“Regarding the Progress launch, I would ask you to please reach out to Roscosmos directly for any questions tied to that vehicle,” said the senior NASA official on the call, Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager for NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program.
Effectively, this is a “Go f- yourself” response from NASA. Roscosmos typically does not reply to Western media outlets, and everyone knows this.
So why is a bog-standard Progress launch suddenly a state secret? It seems to be a recent policy change, because, historically, NASA has televised every one of these cargo flights from Russia’s main spaceport in Baikonur, Kazakhstan. But there is no information about the upcoming launch on NASA’s television schedule for upcoming “live” events.
As recently as September, NASA provided live television coverage of Progress launches from Baikonur. It even issued a media advisory promising to update its broadcast schedule once Roscosmos provided launch details. Two months later, NASA officials apparently are unwilling to confirm that another Progress launch is taking place.
Who made this decision?
The question is whether this decision was made by NASA or was a request from Roscosmos, and, ultimately, whether any of this matters. We can make some educated guesses.
It is probably safe to surmise that the decision here was originally made by state-sponsored Russian space corporation Roscosmos. The company has not been advertising the preparation of the Progress spacecraft as it customarily does, some local sources say. Russian space reporter Anatoly Zak confirms that Roscosmos has “dramatically curtailed” its coverage of all launch campaigns in recent months. There is no mention of the launch on Roscosmos’ Telegram channel.

Canada's air force charts a potential future without the Gripen in 'Project Arrow'
Internal blueprint puts F-35s centre stage as Ottawa weighs alternatives
Canada's air force has developed a vision of a future fighter jet fleet — one that is built around the F-35 and includes autonomous drones as well as another kind of manned aircraft, but makes no mention of the Swedish-made Gripen.
The proposal is called "Project Arrow," according to a discussion paper obtained by CBC News that is circulating within the Department of National Defence and Canada's defence industry.
The department confirmed the document's authenticity and said it was developed within a branch of the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF), while emphasizing it is primarily intended to stimulate discussion and does not constitute a formal military policy or procurement project.
Despite that caveat, Project Arrow confirms a desire to place American F-35 fighters at the centre of Canada's air capability planning.
Defence analyst Justin Massie believes Project Arrow is further proof that the RCAF doesn't want the Gripen, as the federal government is still considering whether to proceed with its full purchase of F-35s.
The Royal Canadian Air Force has already officially taken delivery of and affixed its insignia to two F-35 aircraft manufactured by Lockheed Martin. (Cpl. Nicholas Brunshaw/Canadian Armed Forces)
"Canada makes its defence policies with little public debate," he said. "What are the needs of the Canadian Armed Forces? How do we defend Canada?"
The government of Prime Minister Mark Carney has had discussions with Saab about possibly buying the latest version of the Gripen fighter and assembling them in Canada.
For now, Canada is maintaining its plan to acquire at least 16 F-35s and has begun paying for 14 more of the American aircraft — while studying the potential acquisition of Gripens to create a mixed fleet.
Mapping out role of autonomous drones
Project Arrow also emphasizes the eventual development in Canada of collaborative drones, a new type of aircraft described as an essential component of future fleets.
Eventually, these autonomous aircraft could carry out missions alongside modern human-piloted fighter jets such as the F-35. The goal is to increase the combat power of fighter fleets at lower cost while protecting human crews.
According to a Defence Department spokesperson, Project Arrow was developed by the autonomous collaborative platform program within the air force and does not take sides in the debate surrounding the Gripen.
An example of a collaborative combat drone: the MQ-28 Ghost Bat, manufactured by Boeing in collaboration with the Australian Armed Forces. (Boeing)
"It is a capability development concept that does not advocate for any particular fighter fleet composition or procurement outcome," said departmental spokesperson Andrée-Anne Poulin.
However, the discussion paper notes that Project Arrow "empowers more than just final assembly in Canada," which appears to be a barely veiled criticism of Saab's intentions for the Gripen.
Project Arrow identifies the need to focus on three areas:
- Continuing the integration of F-35s into the Royal Canadian Air Force, a process already underway with the delivery of two aircraft this fall.
- Developing, in Canada and by Canadian companies, a fleet of collaborative drones that would fly in formation with F-35s and whose intellectual property would belong to Canada.
- Increasing Canada's participation in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP), led by the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan, to develop what is known as the "sixth-generation" of fighter aircraft.
Canada joined GCAP as an observer last summer. For now, that status establishes partnerships with the other countries and allows Canada to obtain intellectual property benefits.
Canadian interest in the program, however, has already shown some benefit with a memorandum signed between the U.K.-based BAE Systems Inc. and Montreal-based Bombardier at the end of October. The two companies intend to explore mission-system design and digital engineering for the future sixth-generation fighter.
The Project Arrow proposal suggests Canada could simultaneously learn from the F-35, an aircraft at the cutting edge of current technology, while participating in the development of collaborative drones and sixth-generation fighters under GCAP.
The project would draw in particular on expertise already established in Canada in software, sensors, communications tools, electronic warfare and weapons, while continuing co-operation with allies in the United States, Europe and Asia.
According to experts, the development of Canadian capabilities in collaborative drones could take place under the leadership of Bombardier or Dominion Dynamics, a newcomer based in Ottawa.
Dominion Dynamics is moving full-speed ahead on a roughly $500-million project to develop a Canadian collaborative drone nicknamed the Dominion Scout, which would be particularly well suited to missions in the Arctic.
The company recently announced an agreement with engine manufacturer Pratt & Whitney Canada, guaranteeing access to an advanced propulsion system.
Although the federal government has not yet committed to the project, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has praised the effort for "positioning Canada to lead in the next generation of aerospace manufacturing."
Eliot Pence is founder and CEO of Dominion Dynamics. Behind him to the left is a model of the Dominion Scout, an uncrewed aircraft the company is developing. (Matthew Kupfer/CBC)
The founder of the Ottawa startup, Eliot Pence, says the future Dominion Scout will operate alongside F-35s and other fighters, ships, ground-based sensors and the GlobalEye radar aircraft that Canada is in the process of purchasing.
According to Pence, the Scout will distinguish itself from its competitors by being able to receive orders from airborne, shipborne or ground-based command systems.
"Canada needs to focus on sixth-generation capabilities, that is where air dominance is going," Pence said in a recent interview.
'Economic return' part of Carney's decision
In an interview with the New York Times earlier this year, Carney said his government was still studying the option of purchasing the Swedish fighter jets.
"It is a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies and because of the economic return," he said.
Retired lieutenant-general Yvan Blondin believes the air force is trying to move past the Gripen issue.
"What's happening with Project Arrow is that the Royal Canadian Air Force is planning only [to continue using] the F-35," said Blondin.
The former air force commander says this illustrates the extent to which some military officials are prepared to ignore the risks of placing the F-35 at the heart of their long-term strategy.
Those risks include a future U.S. president being able to "control not only the use of our F-35s, but also the use of our combat drones," he said.
Massie said Project Arrow could fuel an important discussion about the future of Canada's aerospace defence program.
For now, he said he fears the debate surrounding the Gripen is focused on economic issues rather than Canada's long-term strategy for defending the Arctic against Chinese or Russian threats.
"We don't make defence policy to create jobs. Otherwise we'd have an economic policy," Massie said.

A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit
- Published
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.
It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.
But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.
"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.
Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.
"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.
In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.
"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.
Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.
Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.
Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.
"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.
Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.
Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.
While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

Bengal govt to amend land reforms law during Assembly winter session to ease acquisition
The BJP state government plans to introduce eight bills, including amendments to land reforms, MSMEs and ease of doing business.
The West Bengal government will introduce a bill in the Assembly during its winter session to amend the land reforms law to ease land acquisition for setting up industries in the state, official sources said on Monday.
With the winter session set to be held from December 4 to 14, the government plans to introduce eight bills, which include a proposed law on amendments to land reforms, as well as one related to MSMEs and another on ease of doing business to give a fillip to the state's dilapidated industry scene.
Though details of the proposed amendments to the land reforms law are not known yet, sources said the government was not planning to scrap the land ceiling, but would introduce provisions to make land acquisition easier.
The state government had been deliberating a lot since the BJP came to power in May to help industry get land without any political backfire.
When contacted, West Bengal Industry Minister Tapas Roy said he would be able to share details once the bill reaches him, and that it would not be proper to disclose them at this stage.
"Land pooling is a different matter, and the amendments may not include it," the minister said, but confirmed that the proposed amendments would try to ease land-related hurdles for industrial growth in the state.
Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has said the government would neither forcibly acquire land from farmers nor stay completely away from acquisition and ask industry to buy land on its own.
The government has already begun a drive to acquire land on its own, including in Singur. Adhikari expects to acquire 8,000 to 10,000 acres in the short term through various means via the West Bengal Industrial Development Corporation (WBIDC).
Adhikari has said the government has adopted the 2013 land acquisition law and will also use land pooling as a new mode of acquisition.
An industrialist, who did not wish to be named, said the government has come out with an investment policy and has assured industry that it would address land issues through a new land policy. "So we are hopeful of some better news on this front," he said.
The West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, caps maximum land holdings for a family or a trust at around 17.30 acres for agricultural land.

Many social media users have shared a 20-second video of a woman on a bus repeatedly moving closer to the man in front of her. According to the social media claims, the woman was trying to record a fake molestation video.
An X account, MenToo (@MenTooSave), shared the video claiming that the woman in the video was leaning on the man, trying to record a fake molestation video just for views. Noting that such false narrative can put an innocent man’s life and reputation at risk, the post asks, “When will society stop treating every man as guilty by default?”
She filmed herself deliberately pressing her breast against a man’s hand while he visibly tried to create distance and protect himself.
If true, this wasn’t an accident. It was a calculated attempt to manufacture a molestation clip — just for views.
One video. One false narrative. And an innocent man’s life, reputation, and freedom put at risk for content.
This is not empowerment. This is weaponizing accusations. When will society stop treating every man as guilty by default?
Innocent until proven guilty — even when the camera is rolling.
#FalseAccusations #DueProcess #MenToo #JusticeForAll
— MenToo (@MenTooSave) November 19, 2026
Men’s rights activist Barkha Trehan shared the same video on her Instagram account (@barkhatrehan16) on November 20. She also claimed the woman was trying to manufacture a molestation video for views, and the incident was from Patna, Bihar.
Social activist Deepika Narayan Bhardwaj (@DeepikaBhardwaj) also shared the video on X claiming the woman was deliberately sticking to the man so that she could “cry molestation”.
Fact Check
A close examination of the video shows that there is a release announcement poster of a film, ‘Janak’ at the end of the video. Below is a screenshot of the last frame of the viral video:
We then searched for the trailer of the movie, ‘Janak’, and found it on the YouTube channel of Marathi Cineyug, where it had been uploaded on October 14, 2026. The trailer contains the visual that is now viral. The same two people, the same background, clothing and movements can be seen at the 0:49-0:50-second mark in the trailer.
In the process, we also found behind-the-scene photos related to the movie shared on Instagram by Anushka Pimputkar, the woman in the viral clip. In one of the photos, she is seen with Avinash Narkar, the actor who is standing next to her in the viral video.
To sum up, the viral video does not show a real incident of a woman trying to record a fake molestation clip on a bus. It is a scene from the trailer of the Marathi film, ‘Janak’. Social media claims presenting the footage as real are false.

Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.
On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.
The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.
Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.
In a statement, the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.
The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."
Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.
Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.
The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."
The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.
More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.
But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.
The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.
Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.
However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.
Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.
The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.
“Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” says Greg Pollock, the director of research at security company UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”
The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.
Exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more important than ever to attackers.
The data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock says.
The China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He says the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.
Pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, says that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.
“Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he says. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”
The larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler says.
“After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how big it was.”
Among the vast trove were email addresses, usernames, passwords, cookies, session tokens, device information, and more. Fowler says it is the largest exposure of credentials he has found in an accessible database, with the file structure and other attributes appearing to be distinct from a collection of more than a billion passwords amassed last year. He adds that he broadly validated the data using sampling methods, but did not comprehensively check for duplicates.
Fowler says there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.
The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims. The details included usernames and logins along with cookies, application and browser data, operating system details, and other “important files” that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.
Fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting company, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.
The enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.

Misuse and overuse of antimicrobials could undermine decades of medical progress and make even common infections increasingly difficult to treat, a senior health ministry official said on Wednesday, calling for collective action to contain antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
Addressing the national observance of World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week 2026 virtually, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava described AMR as one of the most serious public health challenges and stressed the need for a coordinated "One Health" approach to tackle it.
This year's theme is "One Health, One Action: Prevent AMR Now".
She said medicines that have saved countless lives are gradually losing their effectiveness due to misuse and overuse.
Srivastava highlighted the interconnectedness of human and animal health, plant and food systems and the environment, noting that improper use of antimicrobials across these sectors contributes to the emergence and spread of resistance.
She said the government has accorded high priority to containing AMR, with the National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0 (NAP AMR 2.0), 2025-2029, providing a framework for surveillance, infection prevention, responsible antimicrobial use, research and coordinated action.
The health ministry's National Programme on AMR Containment, coordinated by the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), focuses on strengthening laboratory capacity for AMR surveillance, infection prevention and control, antimicrobial stewardship and awareness generation, she said.
Srivastava urged healthcare professionals to prescribe antibiotics only when clinically indicated and in accordance with treatment guidelines. She also asked pharmacists to ensure appropriate dispensing against valid prescriptions and counsel patients on their correct use.
She also advised people against self-medication, sharing antibiotics or using leftover medicines, stressing that antibiotics are not effective against viral infections such as the common cold and influenza.
More than half of antimicrobial sales in India take place without prescriptions, while nearly half of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions are inappropriate, participants at the event noted.
They called for scaling up public awareness campaigns, preventing self-prescription, ensuring proper disposal of antibiotics and expired medicines, and displaying legal warnings at drug shops against the sale of antimicrobials without prescriptions.
Participants also stressed the need to curb production of substandard and spurious medicines, promote appropriate antibiotic use in veterinary medicine, particularly for food-producing animals, and maintain quality standards in healthcare facilities to prevent infections.
The event was attended by senior officials from the National Health Systems Resource Centre, Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, Department of Animal Husbandry, Indian Medical Association and All India Association of Druggists and Chemists, besides officials from states and Union territories.
World AMR Awareness Week is observed from November 18 to 24 every year to improve awareness and understanding of antimicrobial resistance and promote best practices among the public, policymakers and One Health stakeholders.

Mumbai: Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Ltd (TMPV) has announced an average price increase of 0.5% across its entire passenger vehicle portfolio, effective December 1, 2026, as the automobile manufacturer grapples with persistently elevated input costs.
The latest price revision will cover cars and SUVs, including internal combustion engine (ICE) models and electric vehicles (EVs), making vehicle purchases costlier for customers from next month.
Rising Input Costs Drive Price Hike
Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles said the decision was aimed at partially offsetting the financial impact of rising input costs, which continue to put pressure on the company's operating expenses.
The automaker has been absorbing a significant portion of the additional costs to minimise the burden on customers. However, sustained cost pressures have prompted the company to pass on part of the increase to buyers. The actual price hike will vary depending on the vehicle model and variant.
Fourth Price Hike In FY27
The December price revision marks the fourth round of price increases announced by Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles during the current financial year. The company implemented a weighted average price increase of 0.5% across its ICE portfolio from April 1, 2026. This was followed by another price hike of up to 1.5% across conventional and electric vehicles, effective July 1.
In September, the automobile manufacturer raised prices by up to ₹25,000 across its passenger vehicle portfolio. The latest announcement highlights the persistent cost challenges facing the automaker despite multiple pricing adjustments throughout the financial year.
What It Means For Car Buyers
Prospective customers planning to purchase Tata cars, SUVs or electric vehicles could face higher acquisition costs from December. Since the announced increase represents an average across the portfolio, the financial impact will differ depending on the selected model and variant.
Customers considering a purchase before December 1 may benefit from checking existing prices and applicable dealership offers. Tata Motors said its pricing strategy remains focused on balancing rising operational costs with delivering meaningful value to customers across its passenger vehicle range.

Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.
Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.
The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.
The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.
Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.
"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.
"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."
The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.
The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).
Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.
Jude Bellingham
Age: 23 Country: England
Club: Real Madrid Position: Midfield
Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.
In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.
That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.
Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.
The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.
Harry Kane
Age: 33 Country: England
Club: Bayern Munich Position: Forward
In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.
His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.
Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.
Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.
Kylian Mbappe
Age: 27 Country: France
Club: Real Madrid Position: Forward
Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.
The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.
Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.
It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.
Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.
He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.
Rodri
Age: 30 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Midfield
Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.
By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.
His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.
Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.
His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.
Lamine Yamal
Age: 19 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.
Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.
For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.
At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.
He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

You can upscale low-resolution photos for free using offline AI tools. Use Upscayl on Mac and Windows, Upscal on iPhone, or Offline AI Image Upscaler on Android. These apps enhance image resolution up to 4x without uploading your photos to the cloud, keeping them private.
If there is one area where AI has truly revolutionized, apart from writing and coding, it is image upscaling. Whether it’s your old photo taken on a Sony Cyber-shot or one that’s completely distorted, you can give it to AI and you can get a clean, high-resolution version without changing its original form.
Not just your old photos, you can also upscale any standard photo taken on modern phones to the highest resolution possible.
However, one downside of using AI to upscale images, especially if you care about privacy, is that your images need to be uploaded to the cloud for any AI provider, processed there, and then sent back to your smartphone.
Although those images won’t be public, some companies use them to train their AI models. This is the reason why many users, even we, think twice before uploading sensitive photos to AI models for upscaling
Fortunately, tools like Upscayl let the AI model run locally on your device and upscale images to the highest possible resolution without your data leaving your device. Although it has specific hardware requirements, most modern PCs and smartphones support it, and it’s faster too.
It also supports batch processing, where you can upscale multiple images at once. The quality is pretty good too. In this guide, I will show you how to set up Upscayl, a local image upscaler on your Mac, Windows, Android, and iPhone.
Table of Contents
How to Upscale Low-Resolution Photos Locally for Free
Please note that the original Upscayl is only available on desktop platforms like Windows, Mac, and Linux; there are also free apps that use similar technology and work well. I will cover everything in this guide together and help you set up a free image upscaler locally on your device. This guide is designed for beginners, so every step is comprehensive and detailed.
You don’t need much setup to upscale images locally. Since everything comes in one package, the process is very straightforward. You can download the upscaler app; it installs the upscaler model locally and includes a beginner-friendly interface, making it even easier for first-time users.
Below are the steps for each device.
How to upscale photos on a Mac with Upscayl
Step 1: Open Safari or any browser, visit upscayl.org in the address bar, and press Return. On the page, click on the Download button at the top right
Step 2: Now, on the download page, you can see download options for various platforms, including macOS. However, do not click on the macOS button. It opens the Mac App Store, where Upscayl is a paid app. The same app is available for free from Upscayl’s own website.
Step 3: Tap on the alternative download option below and select the DMG version of the app
Step 4: Once downloaded, install the app on your Mac
Step 5: Open the app and complete the onboarding steps. They’re straightforward and easy to follow.
Step 6: Now using Upscayl is easy. In the sidebar, under Step 1, tap Select Image, or drag and drop the image into the right pane.

How to upscale photos on Windows with Upscayl
Next, let’s see how you can upscale images on Windows using Upscayl. The process is very similar to the Mac.

Step 8: Select the image you want to upscale and tap on Open

How to upscale photos on iPhone with Upscayl

Next, tap the settings bar just above Start upscaling. It shows the current model, scale, and format. You can tap the settings icon to customize the model, Upscaling methods, and more.

How to upscale photos on Android with Offline AI Image Upscaler

Give Your Old Photos a New Life With AI
This is how to set up an offline image AI upscaler on Windows, Mac, Android, and iPhone. This setup works completely offline, and many of these methods also support batch processing to upscale your images.
However, for local AI image models, Upscayl is currently the best option. However, it is not as good as any online model. Although it reduces pixelation, it adds softness; if the original image is too distorted and has fewer details, it can soften the image. In most cases with decent images, though, the upscaled version works well. But again, it all depends upon the quality of the original image.
Also remember that upscaling an image multiple times doesn’t improve its quality. Only the first output is the highest quality you can get. Commons reasons your Android phone's icons won't move and how to fix it
It’s most likely your home screen settings.
Android phones offer plenty of customization options to help you organize your apps. Some settings, unbeknownst to users, can reorganize your phone's icons or prevent you from moving them at all. A home screen that keeps changing can be frustrating, but the good news is you can fix it without much troubleshooting.
Many Android phones can auto-arrange icons in your app drawer, usually called automatic sorting. This causes your phone to organize icons in alphabetical order, by install date or by other listed criteria. App or OS updates can also change your home screen grid, so don't be alarmed if icons rearrange after a major software update.
If your icons aren't moving at all, check your home screen and launcher cache settings. A locked home screen is the main culprit on most phones. However, if you're using a Google Pixel or stock Android without a locked home screen setting, clearing your launcher cache is another option. Employing either solution is fairly straightforward.
Fixing a locked home screen
The most likely cause of locked icons is a locked home screen. Many Android manufacturers enable locked home screens by default, preventing you from moving icons. You can fix this by going into your phone's home screen settings and turning the setting off.
Most Samsung phones let you access this setting by going to Settings and searching for "Home Screen." From there, look for the option "Lock Home Screen Layout." Toggle it off to enable icon movement again. If you are using another type of Android device, you can usually find this setting under the "Home" tab of your device.
Once you've unlocked your home screen, you might notice that your icons will sometimes reorganize themselves without your input. This could be due to some auto-sort options in your phone settings. You can find these sorting options in your home screen settings—on Samsung phones, under "Settings," while on some Android phones, under "Home." If your home screen layout is still not to your liking, consider resetting your home screen and restart your phone.
Clearing a bloated launcher cache
On Android devices without a locked home screen layout, such as Google Pixel phones, you may want to clear your launcher cache instead. Your phone's launcher cache saves all temporary data related to your home screen. If this cache gets bloated, it can make your phone more prone to crashing and cause inconsistent home screen behavior, including frozen icons.
Clearing the launcher cache is similar across Android phones, though the launcher app varies by manufacturer. Head to your phone's settings menu and look through your apps. You're looking for your phone's launcher. Google Pixel uses the Pixel Launcher; Samsung phones use One UI. Select the app and head to its storage settings. You should see an option to clear its cache. After you clear it, you should notice your home screen is more responsive. We also suggest rebooting your phone once you've cleared the cache to ensure it actually gets cleared out. If your phone remains unresponsive, restart your phone in safe mode to see whether a third-party app is causing the problem.

Why a shortage of clinical psychologists in Keralam govt hospitals is leaving people with intellectual disabilities waiting for certificates
As per the last Kerala Disability Census in 2015, there are about 80,000 persons with various intellectual challenges. However, government hospitals and medical college hospitals in the State currently have only 22 clinical psychologists to conduct IQ assessment tests
Updated - November 21, 2026 01:40 pm IST - Kozhikode
As per the latest disability assessment guidelines issued by the Union government’s Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, differently-abled children must undergo assessment tests at least thrice before they turn 18 to obtain permanent disability certificates. (file image)
| Photo Credit: K. Ragesh
People with intellectual disabilities in Keralam are struggling to obtain and renew disability certificates due to a severe shortage of clinical psychologists in government hospitals to conduct Intelligence Quotient (IQ) assessment tests.
As per the latest disability assessment guidelines issued by the Union government’s Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, differently-abled children must undergo assessment tests at least thrice before they turn 18 to obtain permanent disability certificates. During all these assessment phases, an IQ test is a must. However, there are only 22 clinical psychologists under the Directorate of Health Services (DHS) and the Directorate of Medical Education (DME) put together – 17 under the DHS and the rest under the DME.

Prasanta Dihingia, the Head of the Department, withdrew the order hours after issuing it on Wednesday (November 18, 2026). The withdrawal followed a backlash from a doctors’ body.

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.
The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.
With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.
The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.
The food system could respond in unexpected ways
Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.
Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Suresh Mittal is 87. According to Uttar Pradesh’s latest draft electoral roll, his father, Vansh Mittal, is 23. Both are registered at house number 869 in booth 111 of the Dholana constituency in Hapur. The same roll lists Vansh as the son of Ajay, a 56-year-old in the same house.
Suresh is not an exception. Alt News found 1,10,875 voters in the Special Summary Revision (SSR) draft roll whose father or mother, registered in the same booth and the same house, is recorded as the same age as them or younger. The draft was published on November 17.
A Year of Revisions: First SIR, Now SSR
The draft comes at the end of a long year for UP’s voter list. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the rolls began on October 27, 2025 and ended with the final roll on April 10, 2026. In those 166 days the state’s electorate shrank from 15.44 crore to 13.39 crore.
As per the process of SIR, every voter was supposed to be issued an enumeration form, which was supposed to be collected by booth-level officers (BLOs). The Election Commission’s software then allegedly went through the data looking for what it called logical discrepancies. One of these was a parent less than 15 years older than the voter. About 2.22 crore voters in UP were sent notices for such discrepancies, and the Commission says hearings were completed on all of them.
On October 15, six months after the SIR’s final roll, the Election Commission ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) in 17 states and Union territories, including UP. The SSR draft roll, which merges the SIR roll with all supplementary lists, has 13.58 crore electors. Claims and objections can be filed till December 16, and the final roll is due on January 4, 2027.
What We Found and How
The SSR draft rolls are machine readable. We took every voter whose entry names a father or a mother, and looked in the same booth for a voter with that name living in the same house. If that ‘parent’ turned out to be the same age as the voter, or younger, we flagged the entry.
We found 1,10,875 such cases spread across all 75 districts and 403 constituencies.
In 35,523 of these cases, parent and child are the same age. In the other 75,352, the parent is younger, and in 6,860 of them by 20 years or more.
Some of the cases are shown below for representation:
What did SIR Actually Achieve?
The SIR was designed to weed out exactly this kind of error. It had enumeration forms, BLO visits, software flags and hearings. A parent who is younger than their own child is perhaps the most basic inconsistency a voter list can have. This raises a larger question: if a process this elaborate left the most basic errors untouched, what did the SIR actually achieve?
Moreover, spotting these anomalous entries is no rocket science. Each one is a contradiction between two lines of the same booth’s roll, often on the same page: An 87-year-old whose father is 23, a 123-year-old woman whose mother is 45, two women who are each other’s mother. A simple check on the roll itself would have thrown them up. Either no such check was run, or nobody acted on what it found.
As of now, all 1,10,875 are in the draft, and the window for corrections closes on December 16.
The district-wise and constituency-wise count of such cases is given below. Kushinagar district has the most cases (3,646), and Fazilnagar has the most for a single assembly constituency (711).
Skip to PDF content
In a related report published on November 21, Alt News showed several glaring anomalies that the final SIR list for Uttar Pradesh had, including at least 230 voters listed multiple times across 69 booths, missing addresses, unexplained name and gender changes, and suspicious deletions. The report can be read here.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children
