Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.
Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.
French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.
In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.
"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.
Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.
French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.
Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".
Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.
Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.
After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.
Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 on Friday, November 20, 2026, involving a child who tested positive for measles, the state health department said.
The department said the child was between 0 and 4 years old. It did not disclose additional details, including the child's vaccination status, citing the family's privacy.
Measles can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation, complications during pregnancy and death.
Virginia has reported 220 measles cases so far in 2026, including 40 among children aged 0 to 4 and 75 among those aged 5 to 12, state health department data showed as of November 19. Of those cases, 179 were in unvaccinated individuals, 39 were in people whose vaccination status was unknown and two were in vaccinated individuals.
Virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks in central region. Buckingham County has reported 127 cases, the highest in the state, while neighbouring Charlotte County has recorded 34 cases.
The death adds to a worsening national measles outbreak that this week cost the United States its measles elimination status after 26 years.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit U.S. state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of November 20. Wisconsin has also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death, involving a child.
The CDC has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.
A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after the CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.
The sharp increase in U.S. measles cases has coincided with declining immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under Kennedy, who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.

An experimental monoclonal antibody showed 70% to 90% protection against symptomatic Covid-19, Invivyd, a small biotech firm, said Monday.
The result, from a 2,359-volunteer clinical trial called DECLARATION, included three arms: a single 250-mg dose of the antibody, VYD2311; monthly doses of VYD2311; or a saline placebo. Results were released by press release. Invivyd said that it plans to file for accelerated approval for VYD2311 for preventing symptomatic Covid.
During the pandemic, monoclonal antibodies were employed both as treatments and preventatives for Covid. The technology, however, fell into disuse as the market shrank and people gained protection against the infection. Still, Covid causes tens of thousands of deaths in the U.S., and Invivyd executives argued that there is a need for a monoclonal antibody. Moreover, they say, for some patients the monoclonal could be more effective than existing Covid vaccines. Covid vaccines reduced symptomatic infection by about 30%.
“Clinically, I really do believe that most Americans who are interested in using a pharmacological agent to protect themselves from Covid would probably move over to a monoclonal if given the option,” said Michael Mina, the former Harvard University infectious disease expert who is Invivyd’s chief medical officer. “And I think we’re going to aim to have volumes that can accommodate that over the coming couple of years.”

Las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023, the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing.
The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very quickly, leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor.
And because it takes place at night, in the desert, in November, it’s cold—much, much colder than anywhere else the sport will visit all year. This coming weekend in the Middle East, track temperatures may well exceed 122° F (50° C ); on Saturday night in Nevada the track was a mere 59° F (15° C). Combined with the concrete streets, that spells low grip, but there is an added benefit—virtually no tire wear or overheating.
FP1 was completely rained out. A few drivers completed installation laps, but the risk of a crash was far too high.
Credit:
Bradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images
FP1 was completely rained out. A few drivers completed installation laps, but the risk of a crash was far too high.
Credit:
Bradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images
And finally, there’s the slipstream. This was far more powerful than in years past, thanks to the new aerodynamic regulations. We saw this play out in qualifying, which took place on Friday night, when Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli snatched pole position by being the last man on track and benefiting as the cars ahead cleared the air out of his way. Conversely, the Ferrari duo of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc had a torrid time by not working together—a preview for the following night, as we’ll see…
Antonelli’s pole was quickly forgotten, though, as the new World Champion would only start sixth due to a grid penalty for using an engine component outside his allowance.
These two hate each other
Because of the penalty, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen was on pole, with Mercedes’ George Russell next to him. To say there is little love lost between these two drivers would be to undersell the depths of animosity in that relationship. This was evident in FP3, when the pair clashed on track in what looked like a repeat of the Verstappen/Liam Lawson incident in Mexico. This time, no penalties were handed out.
Russell and Verstappen had a robust exchange of opinions on track during FP3.
Credit:
Stephanie Tacy/NurPhoto
Russell and Verstappen had a robust exchange of opinions on track during FP3.
Credit:
Stephanie Tacy/NurPhoto
“He does this week in, week out with many drivers, and everybody accepts it, and I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody’s got to stand up to that guy,” Russell said on Friday. That set up the prospect of a lap 1, turn 1 coming together, but instead the start of the race was remarkably clean. But not boring.
Within a lap, Russell had passed Verstappen for the lead on a straight, before the Red Bull reclaimed the position going into turn 17 on the last corner. This set the tone for things to come, with the Mercedes repeatedly getting past the Red Bull at turn 14, only for Verstappen to regain the lead through sheer commitment, taking back his lead in the corners.
Don’t be tempted to call this yo-yo racing; it was nothing like the races we saw early in the season, when everyone was still trying to understand their hybrid deployment and regeneration strategies. Like an oval race, knowing when to try to move up through the pack was vital; choosing it wrong meant losing multiple positions, not just one. But like an oval, it was also possible to work one’s way up through the pack.
The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar looked more competitive than at any other time this year, and, had the two teammates worked together, they might have been able to leapfrog each other to break free of the pack—a tactic we see used to good effect on oval races. Whether Verstappen’s temperament would allow him to let his teammate past even temporarily remains unknown (I have my doubts), but Red Bull never tried it, instead ordering Hadjar to hold position, leaving him vulnerable to attack from behind. His day was ruined when his front wing exploded on lap 25, dropping him from third to dead last.
The second Red Bull looked like it could stick with Verstappen. Hadjar was told by his team not to try to pass, but then his wing exploded.
Credit:
Bradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images)
The second Red Bull looked like it could stick with Verstappen. Hadjar was told by his team not to try to pass, but then his wing exploded.
Credit:
Bradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images)
His best yet?
So Verstappen never broke free of the chasing pack, with five or six cars covered by as little as 2.5 seconds for much of the time.
Again and again Russell took the lead briefly but lost it again to Verstappen, who worried over the radio that the Mercedes team had figured out his strategy and was going to be able to defeat it on the last lap.
“I think in the beginning we had the deployment immediately correct, but of course, people are learning and watching what you’re doing. At one point, I couldn’t get back into the lead before the start-finish line, so I just—that’s why I asked the question,” Verstappen said after the race. “But I think we had it set up well, and it was just a crazy amount of fighting. The slipstream was so big that you—it was just impossible to drive off, and it was just crazy how many people were just following you.”
But Mercedes fumbled. George Russell crashed into a barrier on lap 47—probably as he ran over a piece of Hadjar’s broken wing, preventing him from braking in time. And Antonelli blew his own chance when, instead of charging his battery for that last-lap, last-corner pass, he accidentally drained it entirely. The team that claimed the 2026 Constructors’ championship last time out in Mexico had to settle for another weekend off the podium.
George Russell went into 2026 as the clear title favorite. Instead, that went to his young teammate. He’s currently fourth in the standings, behind Verstappen and Hamilton.
Credit:
Kym Illman/Getty Images
George Russell went into 2026 as the clear title favorite. Instead, that went to his young teammate. He’s currently fourth in the standings, behind Verstappen and Hamilton.
Credit:
Kym Illman/Getty Images
Verstappen claimed his 75th win, one he said was more like Mario Kart than any of the previous 74. McLaren’s Lando Norris was just 0.64 seconds behind him, with the other McLaren of Oscar Piastri a similar gap behind his teammate. The orange pair worked well together and took home a big bounty of points in their fight with Ferrari for second place in the constructor’s championship as a result.
If you come at the King, you best not miss
Ferrari’s Friday was already being called a disaster, as the two red cars couldn’t make it into the third and final qualifying session. Had they worked together to tow each other, this might have been possible. But things are far from harmonious at Ferrari between their two very closely matched drivers, with plenty of fireworks recently in Mexico City.
During the race, things got worse. The cars stratified themselves according to performance, which meant teammates running together often. Early on, Hamilton and Leclerc kept it mostly clean, although Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty when he went off track to avoid Norris and Leclerc, dropping him to 14th at the time. With safety cars, strategy, and that strong tow, Hamilton clawed his way back up the running order and was again in front of Leclerc by lap 34.
Four laps later, Leclerc tried to pass Hamilton—despite being specifically told by his team five corners earlier to hold position. Leclerc misjudged it, like he did in Monza and Mexico, and the cars made contact, dropping Hamilton to 10th. The race stewards clearly apportioned blame to Leclerc, handing him a 10-second penalty. Hamilton eventually finished seventh, Leclerc 10th.
You just knew if any two cars were going to have a coming together, it would be the Ferrari duo.
Credit:
Tayfun CoÅkun/Anadolu via Getty Images
You just knew if any two cars were going to have a coming together, it would be the Ferrari duo.
Credit:
Tayfun CoÅkun/Anadolu via Getty Images
Leclerc appears desperate to show the team he’s better than the seven-time champion it hired to race alongside him, but time and again his efforts end badly, costing the team points instead. Team boss Fred Vasseur had evidently read Leclerc part one of the riot act before the media pen—the pallid, tear-stained face of the Monegasque driver was that of a man who looked like he knew he really screwed up this time. Having signed a massive multiyear contract, his position with the team is presumably safe. But were I Vasseur, one of Ferrari’s reserve drivers would be getting a call to get ready to replace him for the weekend in Qatar.
Like Leclerc and Hamilton, Russell has been writing checks about Verstappen that his racing hasn’t cashed, and in the post-race interview, Verstappen had simply epic levels of disrespect for the other driver.
“The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track, and honestly, you know, for me, it doesn’t really bother me because he’s so far below my level that it doesn’t really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that, you know? So it doesn’t bother me,” Verstappen said. “And today, karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening, so I was like, ‘Fantastic, my day is only getting better.’ And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”
Did you know Red Bull served hatorade?
Credit:
Mark Sutton/Getty Images
Did you know Red Bull served hatorade?
Credit:
Mark Sutton/Getty Images
Let’s move on from Canada 2010
So many unique circumstances went into making this particular Las Vegas Grand Prix as exciting as it was, and there’s little chance the next two rounds, which both take place in the Middle East, will see similar conditions. But F1 can take something away from this race to make future seasons better, and it’s to do with the tires.
It all goes back to the 2010 Canadian Grand Prix. Like this year in Vegas, Canada 2010 was chaotic. The weather was cold, the traction zones were covered in a low-grip surface to combat the tarmac disintegration seen in the years before, and the action was unpredictable as each team tried to figure out on the fly how best to adapt.
F1’s powers that be saw this, and when they awarded Pirelli a sole supplier contract for tires the following year, they instructed the company to make race tires that would cause the same effect. Of course, it hasn’t ever worked out like that. Canada 2010 was a one-off and caught the teams off guard. But running the same Pirelli tires race after race, everyone quickly figured out the optimal strategy, leaving little room for chaos.
I don’t think every race should be like Las Vegas, but I do think it’s earned its spot on the calendar.
Credit:
Clive Mason/Getty Images
I don’t think every race should be like Las Vegas, but I do think it’s earned its spot on the calendar.
Credit:
Clive Mason/Getty Images
And the Pirelli tires, while better than they once were, are still difficult to drive on. Pirelli mandates high minimum pressures out of fear of tire failures, and next week in Qatar has told teams they cannot run a set for more than 27 laps. As we frequently see in races, tires that stay within their temperature window while running in clean air can quickly overheat when following another car. In the wake of a car ahead, the following car has less downforce and slides more in the corners, which puts more heat into the tires, and the trailing car falls behind. Pirelli makes the tires that F1 asks for, but after this weekend’s race, it’s time for the sport to ask for something different.

The State Government’s ‘Pancha Guarantee’ (five guarantee) schemes are not merely ordinary programmes or projects, they are powerful initiatives capable of transforming society, Rizwan Arshad, Minister for Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affairs and minister in-charge of Udupi district, said on Tuesday.
He said that these schemes were implemented with the objective of empowering women, both economically and socially, within a male-dominated society, thereby enabling them to become self-reliant.

The number of unemployed youth is rising, with crores of young people facing hardships due to a lack of employment. The State government implemented the five schemes with the objective of providing financial assistance to the people, he said.
The ‘Gruha Jyothi’ scheme has provided relief to those struggling with rising electricity tariffs and the increasing costs of essential commodities. The ‘Gruha Lakshmi’ scheme empowers women to lead self-reliant lives, ensuring they do not have to depend on men for financial support. The ‘Shakti’ scheme enables women, who might otherwise be confined to their homes, to travel for work, visit religious sites, and explore tourist destinations. To ensure that the poor do not suffer from hunger, the ‘Anna Bhagya’ scheme provides 10 kg of rice per person. Additionally, the ‘Yuva Nidhi’ scheme has been introduced to provide financial support to unemployed youth while they seek employment, he said.
Speaking on the occasion, Deputy Chairperson of Legislative Council Umashree said that Opposition parties, which once criticised the State government’s guarantee schemes, have now gone on to implement similar models in other States.

In November, Robert Pattinson was announced as the seventh actor hired to play the titular British assassin and spy, James Bond. Pattinson, who is 40 years old, is older than some of the other actors who have played the role before.
A popular meme on Instagram captured all the previous Bond actors and the purported ages they were hired to play Bond:
Sean Connery: 31, cast in 1961 (Dr. No)
George Lazenby: 29, cast in 1968 (On Her Majesty's Secret Service)
Roger Moore: 44, cast in 1972 (Live and Let Die)
Timothy Dalton: 42, cast in 1986 (The Living Daylights)
Pierce Brosnan: 41, cast in 1994 (GoldenEye)
Daniel Craig: 37, cast in 2005 (Casino Royale)
Robert Pattinson: 40, cast in 2026 (Bond 26)
(Instagram user "thefilmthusiasts")
The meme is largely accurate, notwithstanding conflicting accounts about Dalton's exact age when he got the part. Below, we break down the ages of each actor cast to play Bond.
Sean Connery, according to "James Bond, Dr. No" a book about the making of the first Bond film, was cast in 1961 and the movie came out in 1962. Connery, who was born in 1930, was 31 years old at the time of his casting.
George Lazenby, an Australian actor, played Bond only once, in the 1969 film "On Her Majesty's Secret Service." Lazenby was born in 1939. In 1968, newspapers announced he was cast as the new Bond. He would have been 29 years old at the time, and 30 years old when the movie was released.
Roger Moore was born on Oct. 14, 1927. His first Bond film was the 1973 film "Live and Let Die." Moore was announced as the new Bond at the Dorchester Hotel in London on Aug. 2, 1972. He was 44 years old, just a few months shy of turning 45.
Timothy Dalton first played the role in 1987's "The Living Daylights" and was announced as the next Bond on Aug. 7, 1986, according to Reuters. If we go by the date of birth given on his IMDb page, March 21, 1946, Dalton was 40 years old when cast. If we go by the age stated in the Reuters announcement, he was 38 years old when cast and 39 when the film was released. In an interview on the official website for the Bond films, 007.com, Dalton said he was first approached for the role (which he turned down at that time) in 1968, when he was only "about 25 years old," which would make his year of birth 1943, while IMDb lists it as 1946. Dalton, who was much older when he gave the interview to 007.com, may have misremembered at what age he was first approached.
Pierce Brosnan was announced as Bond on June 8, 1994. He was born on May 16, 1953, making him 41 years old when he was cast.
Daniel Craig was announced as Bond in October 2005 and "Casino Royale" was released in November 2006. Craig was 37 years old when cast. He was born on March 2, 1968.
Robert Pattinson was born on May 13, 1986, making him 40 years old when cast.
In sum, while the meme is mostly accurate, there are conflicting accounts about Dalton's exact age when he was hired to play Bond.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous rumors about Bond and the actors who have played the character, including the true claim that Connery condoned slapping women and a fake Bond movie trailer.

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'
- Published
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc face yet another tense discussion over their ability to race together cleanly on track after colliding in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
Leclerc tipped Hamilton into a spin with 22 laps to go, costing both points in a race where at one stage they were racing with the McLarens, which finished on the podium.
Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, which meant he finished 10th, three places behind Hamilton, in a race won by Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
It was the second race-compromising incident within grands prix, and it came after the drivers had been brought together to clear the air at the last race in Brazil after their first-lap fighting in Mexico cost them a win.
Hamilton said such an incident "should never happen" but added that: "The question should be for Ferrari now."
Leclerc said: "We just need to fix whatever is not working."
Team principal Frederic Vasseur described the situation as "completely unacceptable".
- Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide 
  - Published3 hours ago
The Frenchman said: "It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsor, the same speech as after Mexico.
"We passed the message to Charles to not overtake because in this kind of race you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you're passed by others. It means you have to do your race and Charles clearly made a mistake.
"It's penalising the team a lot and it's completely unacceptable. Honestly we are more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico, we had a chat together in Brazil, today we passed the message to think about the team when racing together and the outcome is this one."
The battle between the two drivers has been tense all season, and in the second part of the year there have been a series of flashpoints, whether it be on-track racing, disputes about how best to work through strategy, and Hamilton ignoring two separate calls to pit in different races, both of which compromised his result, because he was looking at beating Leclerc.
Hamilton said: "It's not something I want to really get into."
The seven-time champion, who struggled against Leclerc last year but who has been revived in 2026, deflected questions about whether he should be given number-one status.
"I've never asked to be number one," he said. "I genuinely haven't ever asked.
"There was a point in the season where I was 40-odd points ahead, and at that point, the fight was with me and Kimi (Antonelli).
"I was the closest one to him. I was second for a long time in the year.
"At that point, we needed backing to make sure we beat Kimi. There were a few instances in the season where, with the support, I think we could have beaten Kimi.
"But no, that's not what I've asked for. We shouldn't have gotten together. That should just never happen. But I've said everything I can on it, and the question should be for Ferrari now."
Before the incident, the drivers expressed their differing views on team radio, Leclerc expressing his concern for the way Hamilton was defending, Hamilton saying they should be focused on catching the cars in front.
Leclerc said: "He needs to be careful with this squeezing because it's not going to end well."
Hamilton swore as he asked the team to tell Leclerc to "back off", adding: "I'm trying to catch these guys ahead."
This was similar to their different stances in Mexico, when Leclerc was attacking Hamilton on the first lap while the Briton felt they should be working together to defend their one-two positions.
Vasseur said he would talk to the drivers the day after the race, once the immediate heat of the situation had dissipated.
"You can't imagine the frustration for me, but more important for the guys at home," Vasseur said.
"I want to have a discussion tomorrow. Also, Charles to digest the situation. It's not the right place to discuss with them two minutes after the race."
Leclerc said: "I don't think it's going to be intense. None of our discussions were intense, but surely it cannot continue like that.
"I've taken a penalty, so I guess the blame is on me from the stewards and I guess from the majority, so as a result I guess it was deserved."

Prior to this in August, the VC firm also offloaded 2.94 Cr shares of the omnichannel eyewear giant in multiple block deals for ₹1,856.8 Cr. Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) also sold Lenskart shares worth ₹2,390.6 Cr in September, while SoftBank offloaded 4.5 Cr shares of the eyewear giant, worth ₹2,887.9 Cr, in August. An extended bull run for the stock has provided a fertile ground for investors to cash in. The company’s stock touched an all-time high of ₹767.40 on November 5, and has zoomed over 58.5% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. This surge has come on the back of robust financial performance. Lenskart saw its consolidated net profit zoom 124.7% to ₹232.5 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) compared to ₹103.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue also rose 35.7% to ₹2,845 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹2,096.1 Cr in Q2 FY26.

Car bomb tears through Colombian city wounding more than 20
- Published
A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.
The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.
No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details. Armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by De la Espriella.
Writing on social media, the president said that his government would "bluntly and forcefully" respond, external to "every drop of Colombian blood spilled".
"There will be no impunity and no retreat," he added.
Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province.
And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of Cúcuta.
The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.
Following the signing of the deal, thousands of left-wing rebel fighters laid down their arms.
However, a significant number of Farc members, who did not agree with the deal, refused to disarm and joined dissident groups instead.
While forced displacement, child recruitment and the numbers of attacks on security forces dropped in the aftermath of the deal, there has been an upsurge in recent years driven by dissident Farc factions and criminal groups fighting for control of drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion rackets.
Colombia's first left-wing president, who was in power from August 2022 to August 2026, tried to negotiate with these armed groups as part of what he called his "total peace" strategy.
However, the talks stalled and collapsed with several of the criminal groups violating ceasefires they had agreed to observe.
De la Espriella was elected on a promise to crack down on "narcoterrorism" and has been scathing about his predecessor's approach.
He has also been critical of the 2016 agreement, calling it a "false peace".
In a post on X, uploaded shortly before news of the car bomb in Villavicencio spread, he referred to the peace deal as a "mess", describing it as a "waste of public resources" and the "cause behind Colombia's ruin".
Former President Juan Manuel Santos and Rodrigo Londoño - the two men who signed the peace deal on behalf of the Colombian government and the Farc respectively - defended it in an interview with BBC Mundo ahead of the anniversary.
Santos said that De la Espriella was "totally wrong" to call it a "false peace".
"He wants to use, or has bought into that cynical and mistaken theory that the violence we see today is the result of the peace deal, when the exact opposite is the case," Santos said, arguing that the problem lies with the lack of implementation of the agreement.

The Best Espresso Machines for Home Baristas

The Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle. Espresso is forceful and finicky, and a little intimidating, and yet so essential that astronauts might take it into orbit. A home espresso machine remains the most intense and expensive device I regularly operate before my first cup of coffee.
I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don't make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup. And so my top-rated espresso machine, the Fellow Series 1, earned its place on WIRED's counter by combining ease of use with a solid build, consistent temperature, and rare control over pressure—an industry-beating mix of nerdiness and hand-holding friendliness. But I also know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup. For an entry-level device, I pretty much always recommend the straight-ahead Breville Bambino, among the lowest-cost machines with PID-controlled temperature.
Note that this guide mostly covers classic, hands-on espresso machines with portafilters. We do also include the De'Longhi Rivelia, our top pick among super-automatic espresso machines that require little more than a button press. Frequently Asked Questions
How Do I Test Espresso Machines?
Over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon. Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include Jaina Grey, Jeffrey Van Camp, Kat Merck, Tyler Shane, Pete Cottell, and Scott Gilbertson.
On each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four styles of drink, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.
I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it, and on any of my top picks I've made at least fifty drinks. Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner—and so some of our less-recommended devices are dismissed a bit earlier.
What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.
I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s possible is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.
On machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.
On any semiautomatic machine that decides the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.
I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.
How I Select Espresso Machines to Review
In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.
I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most users. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.
But I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.
This means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.
The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.
But hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.
What Beans Are Best for Espresso?
First off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.
But traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean.
Does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.
It's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. (See here for an explainer on light-roast espresso.) But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.
One thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are more likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.
Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse. For fresh beans delivered to your house, check out WIRED's guide to the best coffee subscriptions.
Espresso Accessories That Make for Great Cups
If you're spending this much on an espresso machine, you'll want to invest in a good grinder and even a scale, as well as a few other devices that make your shots better, and your life a little easier.
An espresso-capable grinder: If your espresso machine doesn't come with a grinder, you'll need one. Preground bag beans are especially difficult to use when making espresso, and will likely lead to off-flavors or channeling. But not just any grinder will do. You'll need a good grinder that can grind consistent beans finely enough for espresso. WIRED's top-pick Baratza Encore ESP is always a good choice—positioned squarely at the fulcrum where more expensive grinders begin to offer diminishing returns.
An accurate scale with a timer: Most grinders, and a goodly portion of espresso machines, do not offer a precise scale. But a precise scale is what you need to get espresso ratios right. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu loved the Acaia brew-by-weight scale ($400) that automatically connects to the La Marzocco Linea Mini and a few other devices via its companion app. But a far less sophisticated scale can still help you measure your shot size and control the dose you want on each espresso shot. If you're not precious about beauty, there's always this low-cost, little no-name scale. It's accurate to a 10th of a gram, and has a timer to boot.
The best knockbox: When you're done with that portafilter filled with coffee grounds, what do you do with it? Beat it against the side of a trashcan? Dig out those grounds into the sink? Nah. You need a good knock box. And somehow this jobby-job from Breville is the best one I've ever found. It's sturdy, the cross bar is in the right spot so that the grinds dump cleanly into the bin, and the bottom has enough grip that the box doesn't scoot around on the counter. Simplicity is competence.
Not all steaming pitchers are created equal, notes WIRED contributing reviewer (and former barista) Pete Cottell. As opposed to the sad piece of aluminum that probably came with your espresso maker, this Brewista offers thick walls for heat retention, a precision tip for expert latte pours, and a thermometer sticker on its side so you can get a rough gauge of milk temperature without hunting down an actual thermometer. It can also take a beating. This is your new frothing pitcher.
Other Machines We Like
Breville Oracle Jet for $2,000: The Breville Oracle Jet is my previous top pick for threading that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness, before getting displaced by my new top-pick Fellow device. The Oracle Jet remains a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent Baratza Encore ESP ($200). This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from an Americano to a flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini. And yet the Jet's easily accessible for anyone who can figure out an iPhone, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You'll be nose-deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. Note that manual milk steaming with the Jet's powerful wand is still better than the automatic version.
Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro for $750: Tradition is the opposite of what Ninja does. This is the company that made the soft-serve Swirl, the Slushi, and the portable air fryer. Ninja is all about the extras. And Ninja doesn't judge. And so of course Ninja jumped in with both feet on cold-foam coldspresso. In fact, the new Luxe Cafe Pro makes the best cold foam out of any espresso machine I've tried, with a whisk that whips up plant milk or cow milk into thick, creamy, dense, beautiful froth—ready for your ridiculously complicated cold caramel-vanilla latte TikTok recipe. What I didn't expect was that Ninja would also nail the fundamentals so well, on only its second entry into the espresso market. The relatively accurate by-weight dosing is nice. So is the excellent steam wand that also outpaces most contenders on automatic hot foaming, adjustable to multiple densities of foam. The Pro clears up some oversights in the previous-model Premier, including an easy tamping lever, and a hot water spout. Maintenance, whether descaling or purging, is also as easy as it gets. Just don't use this grinder with light roast beans. Medium or dark only.
Breville Oracle Dual Boiler for $3,000: This update to the previous Breville Dual Boiler espresso machine is a powerful, truly impressive machine in many regards. It combines the easy touchscreen operation and automatic dosing and tamping of WIRED's previous top-pick Oracle Jet with a welcome “manual” mode that lets you play with pre-infusion and bloom while monitoring a digital pressure gauge on the touchscreen. I kinda love this as an exercise in future-retro design—or whatever the inverse of steampunk is—but also as a means of really controlling my shot, and getting a lot more crema and body out of it. The dual boiler heats up very fast—like four minutes fast—and gives you the wonderful temperature stability and consistency you expect from a dual boiler, plus the ability to steam milk and make espresso simultaneously. The production model I received had a very tight portafilter fit, which loosened up after the first 30 shots or so but initially required some muscle. I also haven't been able to get good results with lighter-roast beans, which led to the occasional under-filled portafilter that had to be retamped manually. We'll update as we resolve those quirks, but can attest that for medium to dark beans, this Dual Boiler is an absolute beast.
Meraki Espresso Machine for $1,999: Meraki is a young Hong Kong–based company. Last year, it was still Kickstarting funds for its debut Meraki Espresso Machine. But the company started off with a bang, with a premium semiautomatic double-boiler machine offering features you don't find even in machines that cost hundreds more. This means a Timemore grinder that'll grind by weight within two-tenths of a gram precision. PID temperature control. Easy pre-infusion. A quiet rotary pump. Another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. A powerful steam wand that regulates the temperature of froth within about 3 degrees for whatever milk drinks strike your fancy. A tamper with satisfying heft, and a tamping station that feels like luxury. Frankly, despite having to overrotate the portafilter for proper fit, its wondrous aesthetics and ease made it a contender for our top picks. But service is always a worry among newer, direct-to-consumer entrants, and the wackily complicated descaling procedure makes maintenance a concern.
Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier for $600: Ninja has already released an upgraded Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro version ($750) after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the Luxe Cafe Premier, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED's mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.
De'Longhi La Specialista Opera for $900: Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It's the best De'Longhi espresso machine I've tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.
De'Longhi La Specialista Touch for $1,000: De'Longhi's new Touch, released this year, isn't merely a touchscreen version of the very analog Opera—though it is just as handsome as the Opera. Instead, it offers a very specific set of trade-offs. Like De'Longhi's Rivelia, there's a bean-assist function that you can save for each bean you like. It's also got a better steam wand, with the ability to read the temperature of the milk you're steaming, as you steam it. In fact, it's maybe more intuitive overall. But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. This should work for most people, but minus a pressure bar or a shot timer, it can also feel like a bit of a black box.
La Marzocco Linea Mini for $6,600: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu spent two weeks with La Marzocco's Linea Mini, a home version of the fancy espresso machines you'll see in coffee shops around the world. The price may be eye-searing, but Chokkattu did find the resulting elixir to be absolutely fantastic—and the same went for La Marzocco's customer service while Chokkattu was dialing in his machine. It offers a lot of room for experimentation, and sports a killer cool-touch steam wand that froths milk in seconds.
De'Longhi Stilosa for $150: The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It's still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You're not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it's a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you'll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never showed signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. In fact, we're now revisiting the Stilosa as our budget pick, after catching a few tips on how to use the Stilosa for light roast espresso.
Breville Barista Express Impress for $800: This espresso machine is the more tricked-out sibling of the Breville Barista Express. It includes more grind and dosing settings and automates some of the more complicated parts of brewing consistently good espresso, like getting just the right amount of beans ground per shot.
Breville Dual Boiler for $1,600: The previous-generation Breville Dual Boiler is an absolute tank of an espresso machine. It's huge. It's heavy. It makes amazing espresso. But while its size makes brewing espresso feel luxurious, it does eat up a lot of space and needs a little time to heat up, versus newer Brevilles like the Oracle Jet that favor thermoblock-style heaters. But a dual boiler does mean you can brew shot after shot, with steamed milk and hot water at the same time, without having to wait in between shots. The new Breville Oracle Dual Boiler ($3,000) is already on the market, but you can still pick up the previous generation for half the price.
Cuisinart EM-160 Slim for $250: The lowest-cost espresso maker from Cuisinart's new espresso line is among the slimmer espresso machines out there, less than 7 inches across. This makes it a treasure for certain kitchens. The espresso quality is about what you'd expect from a pressurized portafilter: smoother, less nuanced, but also pretty forgiving for beginners trying to dial in a bean. This'll be best for those who mix milk with their espresso. Same goes for the fast-dripped “cold espresso” option, which takes a couple minutes to complete and comes out a bit tannic, but mixes well with cold milk or a lot of ice. You'll need a grinder if you don't want sad supermarket beans.
Superkop Manual Espresso Maker for $600: This manual espresso machine is technically not a Jackie Chan movie. The Superkop is instead a quite finely engineered espresso device. It looks pretty, and unlike other manual espresso machines, you don't need a strong arm to use it. So if you want to pull espresso, but not pull it hard, the Superkop is your huckleberry. That said, $600 is a lot of money for a manual device. Buy it if you know you'll love it.
Also Tried
Gevi Espresso Machine With Grinder and Milk Frother for $350: WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell prized the pressure control and built-in grinder on this Gevi espresso machine, when you take into account the near-unfathomable low price for a machine with this functionality. Alas, a somewhat erratic steam wand makes it hard to recommend.
Cuisinart EM-640 Espresso Bar for $650: Cuisinart rolled in with some ambition on this semiautomatic espresso machine, with a built-in grinder and a non-pressurized, bottomless portafilter meant to play in the same sandbox as Breville's top devices. Alas, I really couldn't get consistency on either dosing or grinding from the device's built-in grinder—and the system for customizing the dose in particular was mostly wild guesswork. This all added up to botched shots, wild spray from the portafilter, and none of the ease one wants from a semiautomatic.
De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $675: This semiautomatic De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo comes with a built-in burr grinder makes great espresso right out of the box, and is slimmer than other espresso machines in its category, It does have quirks: It includes a little plastic adapter needed to attach the portafilter to the grinder spout, and a little stepstool for your espresso cup to keep the coffee from splashing. It's a good machine, but I'd upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.

Every time I called my cousin Arun* around 9 a.m., his voice would echo, as though he were in a bathroom. “I’m on the throne, I’ll call you in 20 minutes,” he would say. The first time I heard this, it took me a while to understand what ‘the throne’ was, and as if that was not confusing enough, what was he doing there for 20 minutes. Perplexed, I asked him why he had the phone in the bathroom when he was doing his morning business, to which he casually replied that he would sit on the throne solving Wordle, crosswords and reading the news until he ‘downloaded’. A couple of months ago he told me that he was diagnosed with early stages of haemorrhoids and was on treatment. I advised him on this matter, stressing how his morning ritual could be contributing to his condition. This ultimately led to his ‘conscious reduction of phone time in the bathroom’. His words, not mine. Recently, he proudly announced that his scheduled ‘throne time’ was now down to six minutes, every morning after breakfast.
Bathroom humour is universal. Cinema is no exception — it has found humour and dependable plotlines from this predictable ritual. Just one instance is in Lokesh Kanagaraj’s Vikram, where a character pulling the flush coincides with the house exploding. Thankfully, the consequences of spending 20 minutes on the toilet are far less dramatic.

Telangana, which boasts of high agricultural productivity especially in paddy production where it ranked among the top States in the country, has significant non-performing assets (NPA) in the agriculture sector.
The total NPAs as on September 30 stood at ₹7,304.66 crore, which is 3.65% of the total out standings of ₹2 lakh crore. Of these, short term crop loans accounted for highest number of NPAs at ₹4,213 crore of 4.87 lakh accounts, followed by agricultural term loans at ₹1,759.53 crore of 1.35 lakh accounts.
NPAs of agricultural ancillary activities amounted to ₹1,242.21 crore and those pertaining to agricultural infrastructure stood at ₹88.93 crore. According to information, 4.59% of the outstanding short term crop loans, 2.75% of agriculture term loans, 3.28% of agriculture infrastructure and 2.99% of agricultural ancillary activities are in NPA category.
Banks claimed that they allowed the benefit of interest under interest subvention through Pavala Vaddi (3% interest) and Vaddi Leni Runalu (interest free loans) to farmers who paid promptly at the time of repayment of loans and submitted claims worth ₹725.18 crore for 2014 to 2018 to the Agriculture department. As banks made provision for the outstanding claims of ₹725.18 crore, it had adversely affected their fund position.

For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
Sign up for NPR's Up First morning newsletter for the stories you need to start your day.
On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared an AI-generated image on social media.
It's based on that striking photo of the president from 2024, just after he survived an assasination attempt. Surrounded by Secret Service agents, his face bloodied, Trump hoists a defiant fist in the air.
In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Huang. An Nvidia flag flies behind him. And in his hoisted fist, he holds a red bra.
"I was absolutely flabbergasted," says Bo Young Lee, who worked as chief diversity officer at Uber for five years starting in 2018.
To Lee, it seems Trump is suggesting that the Nvidia CEO is as important to the country as he is.
"But then also the red bra is an indication that it's open hunting season for women," she says. "It stirs up all sorts of stereotypes and misogynistic perspectives about women."
To others, the image drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, as long as you're successful, anything goes.
The White House has not responded to NPR's questions about what Trump was trying to say with the image.
Spy intrigue overshadows workplace transgressions
Even as Huang's return to Nvidia has been cheered by investors, some employees and Trump, it has sparked shock and disbelief among others, including those who have long worked to improve workplace culture in Silicon Valley.
"It's actually unfathomable to me," says Lee, who now serves as an adviser to AI4ALL, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing diversity, inclusion, and responsible practices in artificial intelligence.
After The New York Times revealed that Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S government believes is a Chinese intelligence asset, Lee watched as the broader conversation was dominated by concerns about national security, corporate governance and Nvidia's stock price.
That scandal overshadowed allegations of other problematic behavior in the workplace, specifically Huang's alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, one of Huang's many direct reports.
"Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is," says Lee.
The fact that Powell is herself a senior leader who makes a lot of money shouldn't matter, Lee says. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent, "simply for the fact that there is this power differential."
Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct. By Monday morning, that didn't seem to matter.
"The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia," the board said in a statement.
Lee says that response sends a message to Nvidia employees and all of Silicon Valley that it's OK to break the rules as long as you come clean.
"'Just be transparent with us,'" she imagines the board saying.
Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about Lee's concerns.
A deepening of "tech bro" culture in Trump's second term
In Silicon Valley, there have been private conversations about Huang's alleged workplace transgressions and the power dynamics at play, but women don't appear eager to speak publicly.
NPR reached out to two dozen women who work in the tech space. Freada Kapor Klein was one of the few willing to talk. The social impact investor says conversations about workplace behavior are much quieter than they have been in other eras, such as in 2017 and 2018, when a number of venture capitalists resigned amid allegations they were sexually harassing female entrepreneurs.
In 2017, Kapor Klein and her husband, Mitch Kapor, used their positions as early investors in Uber to publicly call out the company over its toxic culture, one they said tolerated bullying and harassment. The co-founder and CEO Travis Kalanick ended up resigning. Kapor Klein hoped it'd be a teachable moment.
But now, she feels Silicon Valley has gone backwards.
"Tech bro culture is stronger now than I have seen it in decades," she says, adding that Trump's attacks on DEI have amplified that culture.
Among women and people of color in Silicon Valley, she says there's now real trepidation about the anti-DEI sentiment — the axing of programs, chief diversity officers and employee resource groups.
"All of the supports or mechanisms have been pretty much stripped away," she says.
"All that matters is money"
To be clear, Huang has not been accused of predatory behavior. Still, Kapor Klein says his swift comeback is troubling.
"It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," she says. "If you are thought of as a singular talent, you can violate corporate policy, you can possibly threaten national security, you can make up your own rules as you go, you can create toxic workplace culture — as long as you bring in the money."
By the end of last week, Nvidia's stock had fallen almost 49% from its peak in October, and about 27% from before Huang's resignation. On Monday, it rebounded significantly.
Lee says Silicon Valley has always had an unhealthy relationship with its "genius founders."
"We elevate these leaders to god-like levels, and that's been done to Mark Zuckerberg, and that's being done to Sam Altman, and that's definitely [been] done to Jensen Huang," says Lee. "You become untouchable at that point."
Kapor Klein says what's unfolded at Nvidia has made abundantly clear that AI companies need guardrails for their CEOs, not just for the tools they're creating.
"We see a board that ignored that," she says. "There are no guardrails on this CEO's behavior."
NPR's Scott Horsley contributed to this story.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows RSS members armed with swords surrounding the Jama Masjid in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, injuring several Muslims and trapping others inside. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS members attacking a mosque in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, injuring several Muslims and trapping others inside.
Fact: The video is from Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, and shows a group of Hindutva supporters brandishing swords and playing loud music outside Shahi Jama Masjid in April 2022. The Ghaziabad Police have also dismissed the claim as fake, clarifying that no such incident occurred within the Ghaziabad Commissionerate. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts from April 2022 featuring the same visuals (here, here, and here). According to these posts, the video is from Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, and shows a group of Hindutva supporters brandishing swords and playing loud music in front of a mosque.
We also found an article published by Muslim Mirror on 12 April 2022, featuring an image identical to a frame from the viral video.
The same video was posted on X by Hindutva Watch on 12 April 2022. The accompanying caption identified the location as Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
The incident was also mentioned in a VICE News article published on 22 April 2022, which reported that Hindu groups carrying weapons, including guns and swords, marched through Muslim neighbourhoods during Ramadan, playing provocative and Islamophobic music and raising inflammatory slogans. The article alleged that Hindu extremist groups were linked to some of the processions associated with the violence.
To further verify whether the footage was recorded outside Shahi Jama Masjid, Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, we checked Google Maps for Street View imagery and photographs of the location, but none were available. We then compared the surroundings visible in the video with an image of Shahi Jama Masjid in Sarangpur, published in a Dainik Bhaskar article. The mosque’s architectural features and other identifiable elements matched those visible in the video, confirming that the footage was recorded outside Shahi Jama Masjid in Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
The Ghaziabad Police also responded to the viral claim through a post on their official X account dated 19 November 2026. They dismissed the claim as false and misleading, clarifying that no such incident had occurred within the Ghaziabad Commissionerate. The police further stated that legal action was being taken against those spreading the misinformation and urged the public not to circulate misleading claims.
To sum up, a video from Madhya Pradesh is falsely shared as showing RSS members attacking a mosque in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh.

The Rotary Club of Madras (RCM) and the Tamil Nadu government have entered into a partnership to provide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination to 3.5 lakh adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
The partnership, valued at approximately ₹200 crore, is among the largest public-private initiatives for HPV vaccination in India. It was acknowledged in the presence of Darez Ahamed, Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Tamil Nadu government.
High-risk HPV infections account for more than 95% of cervical cancer cases. HPV vaccination during adolescence helps prevent infections caused by high-risk HPV types and reduces the risk of cervical cancer later in life.
Bobby Krishna, president of the Rotary Club of Madras, said the partnership was part of Rotary’s efforts to work with the government on large-scale vaccination programmes. The club also aims to vaccinate one million children as it approaches its centenary in 2028-29, building on its work under the Polio Plus programme.

Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.
Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.
Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years
Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.
For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.
Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians
India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.
In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press
Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.
In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …
The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.
Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.
In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’
Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.
What else we’re reading about
Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.
Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was said to have had a major makeover.
Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.
Your Diwali celebrations
Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.
 In India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK
 My favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany
 There used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai

Vibe check
It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.
Riswan, who’s been freestyling for eight years, is one of the two Indians to win Instagram Rings 2026 award recognising creators. The other is Chanel model Bhavitha Mandava.
Riswan’s big break came with a video filmed at Keralamkundu waterfall, where he pulled off a freestyle move before gracefully arching the ball into the water. The clip has since clocked more than 600m views. Last year, he was invited to watch his sporting idol, Lionel Messi, play in Argentina.

The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as against 13 in FY25. At the same time, a growing number of startups turned profitable or moved closer to profitability after years of cost rationalisation to adjust to the new funding realities. Despite a tough Q4 for many startups due to geopolitical uncertainties, Indian startups are expected to improve their top and bottom line numbers in FY26. Of the 112 startups in the tracker, 68, or about 60.7%, reported profits in FY26. However, the profitability picture remained uneven. Together, these 68 startups generated a net profit of ₹14,822 Cr, while the remaining 44 posted a cumulative loss of ₹34,904.4 Cr, underscoring that sustainable profitability remains a work in progress for a section of the ecosystem. Even so, the scale of India’s startup ecosystem continued to expand. The 112 companies generated ₹4.98 Lakh Cr in operating revenue in FY26, a sharp 32.5% increase from ₹3.75 Lakh Cr in FY25. To help you track the financial health of new-age tech companies, Inc42 has launched the FY26 Financial Tracker, bringing together key financial metrics in one place. The tracker will be updated periodically with the latest financial disclosures and deeper insights into the performance of India's startup ecosystem.
