'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
‘Medicare for all’ is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight over "Medicare for All."
The midterm elections resulted in victories for several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act, which despite incendiary politics made incremental reforms, barely squeaked into law in 2010 after similar disputes..
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
"It's cosplay"
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase "Medicare for All" actually means. "It's cosplay," said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. "When you say 'Medicare for All,' people think 'Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.'"
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF's public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
"I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs," she said of survey respondents' support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. "I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program."
Medicare faces headwinds
A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033.
Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump's second term began.
"Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs," Brodie said.
There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.
Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as "a socialist takeover of our healthcare system" — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.
Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It's the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.
A deeper dissatisfaction?
There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous "Harry and Louise" ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially.
KFF's September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That's a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they'd rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have.
Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it's up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page.
HealthBent, a regular feature of KFF Health News, offers insight into and analysis of policies and politics from KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner, who has covered health care for more than 40 years.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

Senate Democrats introduced such a bill in August. House Democrats introduced a similar bill in November.
In November, a claim (archived) circulated that Senate Democrats introduced a bill that would prevent U.S. President Donald Trump from issuing a pardon to himself.
For example, one social media user who shared the claim posted an image of Trump and wrote, "Senate Democrats Introduce Bill To Ban Trump From Pardoning Himself Bill Makes Clear Presidents Cannot Pardon Themselves"
The claim also circulated on Instagram and X (archived, archived).
The claim was true. Democratic senators actually introduced the bill the claim referred to, titled "Abuse of the Pardon Prevention Act of 2026," in August, before the midterm elections.
Democratic representatives introduced a bill with the same title in the House in November.
Both bills sought to, among other measures, prohibit presidents from pardoning themselves. This prohibition would apply to Trump if either of the bills became law he was president (he could, however, veto such legislation). Trump suggested during an interview on "60 Minutes" on Nov. 8 that he thought he had the power to pardon himself but that he did not expect to do so.
Both bills included a section titled "Prohibition on Presidential Self-Pardon" that read:
The President's grant of a pardon to himself or herself is void and of no effect, and shall not deprive the courts of jurisdiction, or operate to confer on the President any legal immunity from investigation or prosecution.
According to Democratic Reps. Mike Levin and Jason Crow, who introduced the House legislation, their bill was intended to crack down on a pardon system they claimed had become "a cash-for-clemency economy, fueled by pardon brokers that advertise special access in exchange for lucrative fees" under Trump.
Aside from prohibiting self-pardons, the House bill also would require the Department of Justice's Office of the Inspector General to investigate pardons with a potential conflict of interest.
In an interview with CBS News, Levin pointed to Trump's October 2025 pardon of Binance founder Chaopeng Zhao as an example of a pardon that had a potential conflict of interest. Zhao pleaded guilty to federal criminal charges of violating and causing a financial institution to violate the Bank Secrecy Act by not maintaining an effective anti-money-laundering program in 2023
Trump also has used his pardon power more broadly in the past, for example to pardon "individuals convicted of offenses related to events that occurred at or near the United States Capitol on January 6, 2021," immediately after he took office for his second term.
At the time this of this writing, the Senate had not yet voted on the bill Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada introduced in August. The equivalent House bill also hadn't faced a vote.
Speaking to CBS News, legal experts expressed concerns that the Senate bill, if enacted into law, would encroach on the president's constitutional right to issue pardons.
According to Constitution Annotated, a legal analysis of the Constitution published by the Library of Congress, rulings by the Supreme Court have established that:
… the power of the President is not subject to legislative control. Congress can neither limit the effect of his pardon, nor exclude from its exercise any class of offenders. The benign prerogative of mercy reposed in him cannot be fettered by any legislative restrictions.
As currently written, it would appear that the bill's clause to outright prohibit self-pardons would limit or affect the presidential pardon power, meaning the bill could be considered unconstitutional.
Constitution Annotated noted that legislators have successfully enacted "legislation facilitating the exercise of the pardon power" by writing laws that funded "Executive Branch positions to review clemency petitions." The Senate and House bills appeared to suggest something similar by requiring the Department of Justice's Office of Inspector General to investigate some pardons.

'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?
- Published
Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.
The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.
But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.
By that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.
A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.
The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.
United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.
"We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us," said the 21-year-old.
"There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good.
"It's all about character now."
Tough tests before the transfer window opens
United are giving little away about their plans for the January transfer window.
For now, it is being stressed, Pochettino's priority is to get the most from the players currently at his disposal.
However, there was sympathy with former boss Michael Carrick's belief he had been let down in the summer window and there was a plan to address that.
That situation remains. A striker is thought to be Pochettino's priority given United's only recognised number nine, Benjamin Sesko, is out at least until January with a shin issue that has bothered him since March.
United have a long-standing issue at left-back. First choice Luke Shaw missed his eighth successive game on Sunday and the only other orthodox left-back in senior ranks is England Under-20 international Harry Amass, who didn't even make the bench at Anfield.
However, Pochettino worked with Shaw at the start of his career at Southampton and feels the 31-year-old can be a positive influence on his group.
The reality though is United still have nine games to play before they can make any changes to their squad.
Among those fixtures are home games against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland.
Newly promoted Coventry are four points ahead of United, who are second from bottom. Forest and Sunderland are in the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford club.
A trip to Crystal Palace - the one side below United, and the other Premier League club to replace their coach during the international break - looms on 13 December.
After Wednesday's encounter with Sporting, Pochettino's side have one Champions League game before the end of the year - against RB Leipzig on 8 December.
Any solutions to be found to the current mess over the next five weeks have to come from within. If they don't, light-hearted discussions about a first relegation since 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty start to get serious.
"They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three," Ashley Young - a Premier League winner with United - told Match of the Day.
"They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat.
"It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them. I am sure he will be able to do that when he has been longer in the job."
Fixing a leaky defence
Pochettino shut down a question about United's terrible recent defensive record when he spoke to the media immediately after the game at Anfield.
"Tell me only about the circumstance today," he said. "I wasn't [here] in the past."
That is true - and may also have been a useful diversion exercise in avoiding a dissection of a defensive unit he is still getting to know.
However, Pochettino knows United have kept one clean sheet all season - against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. He will also know United have now conceded 19 goals in their past six games.
Pochettino's big decision at Liverpool was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire.
"He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," said the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss.
It was not clear when Pochettino meant.
In the 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October, De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months following major back problems that eventually required surgery, largely because Leny Yoro was suspended and Lisandro Martinez was injured. He then played for two minutes against Roma on 3 November, when he was thrown on as then manager Carrick searched desperately for a winner.
Most goals can be broken down into a number of mistakes that compound to make an eventual negative outcome.
Team positioning has been mentioned as a reason De Ligt found himself exposed under a high ball at Anfield. However, his failure to deal with it presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.
But United have been conceding bad goals all season. Numerous players have been culpable.
There is a limit to what Pochettino can do in the time available. However, he wants to maximise what he can do.
Whereas Carrick tended to let his starting players have a day off after matches, the new regime has decided a warm-down session at Carrington is the better option.
And defensive organisation was surely one of the key points his coaching team had on their list of things to work on when the players began preparations to face Sporting on Wednesday.
Will January be the answer Man Utd need?
With £70m summer arrival Carlos Baleba injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, Pochettino must find a way to protect United's goal, which might require additional support in midfield.
The strengths of Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are with the ball. Either with three in the middle of defence or a third man in midfield, a way needs to be found to stop opposition attacks running straight at the defence.
In his recent interview with Sky Sports, United chief executive Omar Berrada said the club needed to be "disciplined" in the transfer market and avoid spending huge sums on players who would not necessarily make the squad better.
But the fact former Chelsea midfielder Andrey Santos went five games between Premier League starts under Carrick from the opening-day defeat at Hull - and was only introduced for the final three minutes at Anfield - suggests there are doubts over the Brazilian, who cost £48m in the summer.
Underneath that is the knowledge United borrowed from their revolving credit facility around all their major summer purchases and did the same again earlier this month when Pochettino was hired at a cost of just over £7.5m.
In public accounts released last week, United confirmed there was another £160m available in credit - but also they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £236m of which is due within 12 months.
Neither before nor after the transfer window opens do any simple solutions to United's predicament present themselves.
Last season, fellow 'big-six' club Tottenham did not save themselves until the final day of the season.
Confidence remains high at Old Trafford the situation will not be quite so dire for them, but it could be a very bumpy ride.

Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
- Published
This judgement that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people is historic. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The Rohingyas are getting justice that is long overdue. At least 10,000 were killed when their communities were attacked by Myanmar's security forces and local militias in 2017.
In the huge camps in Bangladesh where more than one million Rohingya refugees have been living since they fled the terrible events of 2017, crowds gathered around screens to watch the President of the ICJ, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, deliver the court's verdict.
He recalled some of the evidence heard by the court since the Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It described acts of mass murder, rape, torture and the destruction of villages, sometimes with Rohingya residents burnt to death inside their homes.
- Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules 
  - Published4 hours ago
The decision by a majority of nine votes to six at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will also have a significant impact on the other genocide cases currently being heard by the court by reasserting and clarifying the standard of evidence needed to prove genocidal intent.
They include South Africa's case that Israel committed genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza in its response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Israel has repeatedly and vehemently denied the allegation.
The court's landmark decision also reinforces those who believe in the rules that were made to regulate the way that power is wielded after World War Two. The 1948 Genocide Convention was a vital part of the structure that was built around the United Nations to stop a repeat of the unfettered brutality, war and genocide in the years before the defeat of the Nazis.
The rules and conventions established after 1945 have been under unprecedented pressure in the era of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. On the day of their summit in China, the ICJ issued a reminder that international law still exists and perhaps can show that the use of force against civilians has consequences.
Lawyers will study the way in which the Gambia proved the crucial point that the state of Myanmar intended to commit genocide.
Proving intent is the biggest challenge in a genocide case at the ICJ. Showing that atrocities occurred is not in itself enough.
The key phrase from the Genocide Convention, adopted by the United Nations after the Nazi Holocaust of European Jewry, defines the crime as "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national ethnical, racial or religious group".
The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.
That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.
In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.
Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.
According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent.
"The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."
In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.
The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.
The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".
The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide.
"If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over.
"But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."
The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.
The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.
That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.
The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".
It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.
Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.
Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.
But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".
Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.
He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.
She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
But whatever the threats coming from the Trump Administration, it is clear that delivering justice to the Rohingya people will refocus attention on Israel's conduct in Gaza, South Africa's case at the ICJ and on the continuing plight of Palestinians in the ruins of Gaza, where more than 1,400 have been killed by Israel since the ceasefire just over a year ago.
It would be wrong, lawyers say, to view the Myanmar case as a dress rehearsal for the case against Israel.
"It risks distracting from the Rohingya, who should appropriately be our focus," according to Janina Dill, from Oxford University.
"Litigation on their plight is not a test case for a conflict that the world has chosen to pay more attention to."

JAKARTA – Police in Indonesia have charged a former police chief with treason after an investigation into alleged illegal wiretapping widened to activities authorities claim were aimed at undermining public trust in Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s government, a senior official said.
The charges followed accusations that officials were involved in the widespread and unauthorized wiretapping of phones belonging to Prabowo as well as government officials, activists and journalists.
Six officials have now been named as suspects, the chief of the police’s criminal investigation unit, Asep Safrudin, said late on Monday, including former Police Chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, known as a political ally of Prabowo’s predecessor Joko Widodo. He is unrelated to President Prabowo.
“The suspects allegedly agreed to, prepared for and initiated treason with the motive of maintaining the position of the police chief ... by lowering the people’s trust in the government of President Prabowo Subianto,” Asep said.
Treason charges are rare in Indonesia and carry the maximum penalty of death, Indonesian law stipulates.
Arrested earlier this month, Listyo allegedly ordered and received wiretap reports from the other suspects, Asep said.
Asep said authorities also seized 20 “One Piece” flags, symbols that have appeared at anti-government demonstrations in Indonesia.
Asep said authorities are probing whether the suspects were involved in “exploiting” the mass demonstrations.
The other suspects, all of whom Asep referred to by their initials, are alleged to have committed acts such as mobilizing the demonstrations and creating social media content that disparaged the police, Asep said.
Two of the suspects were dishonorably discharged from the police in separate ethics hearings earlier this month.
Reporters could not immediately contact the suspects. Presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The allegations against Listyo have fueled speculation about tensions between Prabowo and his predecessor Widodo.

Melbourne, Nov 24: The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.
The Digital Duty of Care Bill would require Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.
Proposed law mirrors European online rules
The legislation is similar to the European Union's Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act passed a year later.
The proposed legislation would set minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.
“We can't cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra.
Wells announced on Tuesday her centre-left Labour Party government had accepted amendments proposed by the minor Greens party to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.
Greens say bill takes power back from US corporations
Greens leader David Shoebridge confirmed his party had agreed to support the amended bill.
“Today we are taking power back from a handful of billionaire-owned, largely US corporations and giving it back to Australians who have been paying too high a price for their profits,” Shoebridge said in a statement.
The Senate will likely pass the bill on Wednesday and the House of Representatives, where the government holds a majority, would pass it into law before Parliament rises for the year on Thursday.
The Greens' amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars (USD 72 million) to 5 per cent of a tech company's global revenue.
US President Donald Trump's administration expressed “serious concerns” in a submission in September to a parliamentary committee examining the draft law. US concerns included how Australia would designate what constitutes “foreseeable harm.”
US warns bill would lead to censorship of lawful speech
US Ambassador to Australia David Brat said he had conveyed his government's objections to the amended legislation to Wells on Tuesday.
“Vaguely defined harms,' backed by penalties of up to 5 per cent of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.
“As Australia's largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors,” he added.
Wells said of their conversation: “There are points of difference and we're ironing them out.”
The conservative opposition Liberal Party shares US concerns that the bill empowers government ministers and the nation's online safety watchdog to judge what was harmful. Opposition lawmakers oppose the legislation.
“This bill undermines both the online safety of Australians and our freedom of expression,” senior opposition senator Sarah Henderson told reporters.
The Greens' amendments would also give people a legal right to sue social media companies in Australian courts for harms suffered online.
It follows Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest having to go to US courts to sue Meta over scam ads on its platforms that use his likeness without permission. The case is not yet resolved.
In October, a US judge ordered Meta to pay New Mexico USD 25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Bill would let social media users opt out of algorithms
Australia's bill would also let social media users opt out of algorithms that send them content and empower Australia's online safety watchdog to remove apps and websites that fabricate naked images from genuine images of people.
It would also require protections for children against content that promotes eating disorders, hostile ideas about women, pornography, crime or dangerous stunts, or causes serious mental health distress.
Lisa Given, an information sciences expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, described the draft legislation as “very good” and largely in line with European laws.
“It'll be very interesting to see what happens now globally,” Given said. “I've always been of the view that if countries can band together and put through similar legislation, collectively we have a better chance of actually pushing Big Tech to make real changes in terms of the design of their systems.” (AP)

A new study has found that DNA methylation, a natural process that acts like a "dimmer switch" to turn genes down or completely off, varies more than expected across different brain regions in genes linked to PTSD.
Stress and trauma can leave molecular marks in the brain that may help explain the development of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a mental health disorder in which one experiences flashbacks or nightmares of a terrifying or life-threatening event.
The study, published in the journal 'Cell Reports', also found that among people affected by PTSD, the molecular variations appeared to be driven by a number of factors, including the sex and race of the person, and whether the trauma exposure occurred in childhood or adulthood.
"The question that our research aims to address is 'What is really different about the PTSD brain?'" corresponding author Frances Champagne of the University of Texas at Austin, US, said.
"The study found greater variation in DNA methylation patterns across brain regions in people with PTSD than in people with major depressive disorder. It also revealed considerable differences among individuals with PTSD," Champagne said.
The findings could open the door to more individualised treatment options for people with PTSD in the future, the researchers said.
A detailed methylation profiling was done of postmortem brains from 302 people -- 101 with PTSD, 100 without psychiatric disorders and 101 with major depressive disorder.
Three different regions of brain were analysed in each sample: the prefrontal cortex, involved in higher level functions, including decision-making, the amygdala or the emotional centre of the brain, and the hippocampus, which manages memory.
The study uncovered specific changes in the brain linked to PTSD, including a relative reduction in oligodendrocytes -- cells that form the protective covering of neurons (myelin sheath) -- in the amygdala of people with PTSD, particularly in those exposed to trauma in adulthood.
PTSD was also associated with more pronounced DNA methylation differences in the prefrontal cortex, while major depressive disorder was associated with methylation differences in the amygdala.
The molecular patterns were associated with differences in the composition of different cell types in the brain, the researchers said.
Because they analysed postmortem brain tissue, the team was not able to confirm whether the methylation differences contributed to PTSD, resulted from PTSD, or were influenced by other factors.
The authors also noted that they lacked detailed information about symptom type and severity for each individual, which would be important for developing more personalised methods of diagnosis.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

The notice circulated online in image form. The most-shared version of the image bore traces of AI generation or editing, but another version spread simultaneously that displayed no such traces. A spokesperson for the DHS said, "This notice was not accurate and was subsequently corrected," which implies the original notice was authentic, though inaccurate. The content was the same in both versions.
An image circulated online in mid-November purportedly showing a message from the chief intelligence officer of the Chicago division of Homeland Security Investigations alerting personnel to disable Apple's "Live Listen" feature to prevent devices from capturing conversations.
The image spread on social media platforms such as Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Most of the posts featured unspecific warnings about the "Live Listen" feature, like this one from an X user (archived):
If you have an Iphone 11 or higher it is now recording audio ALL of the time it is powered on. To turn it OFF do what the green highlight says. They get you to pay for your own surveillance. https://t.co/II4KlXGeDP
— BladeoftheSun (@BladeoftheS) November 18, 2026
First, we uploaded the image to Google Lens to perform a reverse image search. The earliest instance of the image we could find came from a Nov. 15 Facebook post (archived). This post featured a slightly different version of the image with larger borders, more details at the bottom of the notice and less bolded text.
In short, though we found evidence of artificial intelligence generation in the more-popular version of the image circulating on social media, the earliest version we found didn't appear to have any AI modifications. The text read the same in both versions.
The Department of Homeland Security confirmed the notice was authentic via email. As such, we've rated the claim true — which doesn't necessarily mean the letter's contents are factual.
Unpacking the rumor
A Google Search for "HSI Chicago Live Listen" found very few prominent news organizations reporting about the notice. As of this writing, a story from the nonprofit publication The Intercept was the only one claiming to feature actual sources attesting to the notice's authenticity, though those sources remained anonymous. Media Bias/Fact Check considers The Intercept's reporting "mostly factual" but because the sources weren't named in this story, there was no way for Snopes to independently verify it.
The "recent data leak" mentioned in the notice seemed to refer to a real hack that exposed the identities of thousands of DHS workers, according to multiple trustworthy news sources.
The most-popular circulating image featured clear visual signs of being generated or altered using AI tools. The following is a comparison of an official HSI badge, from HSI Chicago's X account, against the one from the notice:
(@HSIChicago via X, Melissa Stewart Unger via Facebook, Snopes Illustration)
Images generated with AI tend to lose detail when closely analyzed. In this case, the stars that appear on the real badge have melted into an unintelligible shape under the crest, for example.
Beyond visual quirks, many AI image generators add SynthID, an invisible watermark, to the images they create. The altered image was determined to contain a SynthID watermark, according to OpenAI's AI image detector. (It's worth noting that such detectors don't always produce reliable results.)
However, the earliest version of the image we found didn't share these visual quirks and had no SynthID watermark, according to OpenAI's detector. We found no evidence AI was involved in its creation. It's possible the circulating image was the result of inputting the earliest version into an AI-upscaler, but this is not definitive proof of the notice's authenticity.
Was it right about 'Live Listen'?
The circulating notice claims the following (emphasis theirs):
The recent Apple IOS 27 update automatically enables "Live Listening" on Apple devices. This means that all the iPhones and iPads with this update, both personal and operational, are by default capturing conversations around them, transcribing them, and sending those transcriptions up to Apple for advertising purposes.
We previously clarified how the "Live Listen" feature works after claims similar to the one in the notice spread across social media. The statement about "Live Listen" in the notice is largely incorrect.
We found that a "Remote Control" feature did seem to come pre-enabled in a recent iOS update, but "Live Listen" sessions need to be started intentionally by the user and would not capture conversations around them by default. There was also no evidence to back up the claim that "Live Listen" transcriptions were sent back to Apple for "advertising purposes."
The truth?
A DHS spokesperson confirmed via email that the information in the notice was "not accurate" and explained that it was "subsequently corrected." Although the notice was not a "formal government cybersecurity advisory," the fact that the DHS corrected the notice seems to imply it did circulate internally. We reached back out for clarification, and will update the story if we receive a response.
The Chicago Enforcement and Removal Operations field office also responded to our request for comment, initially stating, "No, this is not a real memo." When we followed up to inquire about the discrepancy between its response and the DHS', the field office replied, "The information contained in the memo is not factual."
It's unclear how the notice spread from DHS staff to the general public. We reached out to the Facebook account that posted the first instance of the notice to ask how they were able to access it, and will update the story if we receive a response.

Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
The company had come under pressure from Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to reverse course and bring Huang back.
But Democrats have accused the Trump administration of selling out national security for financial gain. Huang is due to testify before Congress in early December.
His comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that had left the S&P 500 in correction territory.
Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.
But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.
Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.

With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon and Rachel Clun

Throughout U.S. President Donald Trump's second term, his administration has used social media not just to broadcast its policies and goals, but also to try to shape Trump's public image.
In November, some people on social media claimed Trump's White House posted an image of him wearing the Revolutionary War-era military uniform of the British "redcoats," against whom the American colonies fought to secure independence.
For example, one X post (archived) said, "Uhh…didn't the bad guys wear the red coats?" alongside a screenshot of the supposed White House post of the image, which bore the slogan "PATRIOTS IN CONTROL." The caption of the purported post said, "No Panicans. Patriots are still in control btw."
Users posted the same screenshot to Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and elsewhere on X (archived). Snopes readers sent us emails asking whether the White House truly posted the image of Trump wearing a British military uniform.
It did not post an image of Trump as a redcoat; the screenshot was of an altered version of a picture of Trump dressed in a suit and tie from a real White House social media post. Therefore, we've rated the screenshot fake.
The real White House post (archived), which did feature the caption "No Panicans. Patriots are still in control btw" and the slogan "PATRIOTS IN CONTROL," showed Trump wearing a black coat. The post did not make any reference to the Revolutionary War or British army.
The White House shared the same post to X (archived) and Instagram (archived).
Notably, the White House posted the image and caption on Nov. 10 on all three social media accounts, whereas the screenshot purporting to show a White House repost of Trump in a redcoat uniform appeared to begin spreading around Nov. 18, based on the posts Snopes found.
Considering the timing of the real and fake posts, it's incredibly unlikely the redcoat image was a screenshot of a real Nov. 10 post that was soon deleted, as there's no evidence that such a deleted post was noticed or discussed, or that the screenshot surfaced at any time during the intervening week.
Additionally, there is evidence the screenshot was AI-generated. Tabbing between the original White House post and the fake screenshot shows that Trump's face, not just his clothes, appears different between the two images.
In the redcoat image Trump is angled slightly more inward, toward the camera, which better shows off what he's wearing.
In the image actually posted by the White House, Trump has a rounder face and more wispy strands visible in his hair than in the redcoat image. Trump's hands are more clearly visible in the redcoat image and his legs don't appear to be moving in a way that would suggest he's walking, whereas the White House image gives the viewer a sense that Trump is walking somewhere.
"Patriots in control" is a phrase the Trump administration has sometimes used in social media posts but never before in reference to the American Revolution. The White House posted the phrase in June, the Department of Education posted it in July and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posted it in November, shortly after Election Day.
Snopes reached out to the White House by email for confirmation and will update this story when we receive a response.

An Israeli air strike has killed the head of Hamas's internal security service in Gaza.

What should it cost to insure a home in wildfire country?
As a homeowner in rural Northern California, I've lost a lot of sleep worrying about fires. It's not just that big, destructive ones are becoming more common. It's that finding affordable and reliable home insurance has become a nightmare. Without it, the most valuable asset I own could literally go up in smoke. And we've been stuck in a broken insurance market, hoping someone or something can fix it.
Which is why I was so gripped by Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi's recent two-part series on our Planet Money podcast. And it's left me thinking about the economics of making our communities safer. Insurers are spending money to figure out how to keep houses from burning down. Yet some California homeowners tell him they're investing heavily to make their homes and communities safer, and all that work has barely made a dent in their insurance bills.
In the first episode, Alexi goes to a destruction lab in South Carolina where researchers use "crash-test dummies for houses" — the type of wonderful turn of phrase that we love Alexi for — to figure out what actually works to help homes survive climate disasters. They literally light mock houses on fire and subject them to hail and hurricane-force winds to see what happens to them.
Who pays for this lab? Some of the world's biggest insurance companies. They want to know how risky homes are to insure and which building designs will limit damage and shrink the payouts they have to make if disasters strike. It's a pretty wild way to tackle an increasingly urgent question: can we make homes that can better withstand fires and other disasters?
Alexi touches on this in the pod, but insurers have been running experiments like these for more than a century. Back in the early 20th century, scientists at an insurer-funded organization called Underwriters Laboratories tested out new kinds of electrical wiring and consumer appliances to try to reduce the risk of costly fires and electrical accidents. An outfit called the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety does something similar for cars, using crash tests to push for safer auto designs.
Fighting moral hazard in fire country
The insurance industry is way more interesting than most people give it credit for. Part of the magic is obvious. It can insulate us from financial devastation. But there can also be magic in how insurers figure out how big risks really are and what it takes to reduce them. That destruction lab in South Carolina is an amazing example of that.
But Alexi's reporting has me wondering whether insurers could do more to reduce risk. It has to do with this weird thing about insurance. If someone else picks up the tab when something goes wrong, you may have less reason to do everything you can to make sure that it doesn't go wrong in the first place. Economists call this "moral hazard." It's the idea that insurance can reduce incentives to mitigate risk.
If you're a homeowner in wildfire country, that could mean being disincentivized to make upgrades to your house. Upgrades that might reduce the risk of your home burning down. Like, for example, installing a metal roof or ember-resistant vents. Those sorts of upgrades can be expensive. And if your insurer will pay for a whole brand new house in the event yours burns down, it might be harder to justify investing a ton of money to "harden" your home against fire danger. And even if you do harden it, if your neighbors don't also do it, then you still face increased risk, and it's this whole collective action problem that can make a neighborhood less safe.
One way to counter this moral-hazard problem is for insurers to offer discounts on people's insurance bills when homeowners make investments that make their homes safer. That creates incentives to harden homes and hopefully reduce a community's fire risk.
But as Alexi reports in his second episode, insurers don't seem to be giving homeowners big discounts for their efforts. Alexi travels to Paradise, Calif., where residents have been working to make their homes and the entire community safer from wildfires. Yet locals tell him the discounts being offered are tiny.
Which got me wondering… is this a market failure? If residents are doing important work that lowers the odds their homes and communities burn, shouldn't that be reflected in their insurance bills? Or do insurers have the math right? Do those small discounts actually reflect how much they expect to save on claims for wildfire damage?
Of course, even a bigger discount only helps so much if your premium is going through the roof. And here in California, as in other places across the West, it's gotten harder to find coverage at all. Insurers have been declining to renew policies in fire-prone areas, forcing families like mine onto California's insurer of last resort, the FAIR Plan.
But the problem isn't just climate change. After all, insurers have proven capable of covering all sorts of things with catastrophic risks, from skydiving businesses to rocket launches. The question is at what price, whether regulators will let them charge it, and whether homeowners can stomach those prices.
What if "fixing" the market means painfully higher prices?
As UC Berkeley economist Nancy Wallace explained when I interviewed her last year for the Planet Money newsletter, California's insurance regulations have made a bad situation worse. Proposition 103, passed by voters in 1988, required insurance companies to get state approval before raising rates. Under the regulatory system that followed, insurers had to use historical wildfire losses to set their rates, rather than forward-looking estimates from "catastrophe models." Basically, insurers were forced to look backward to price a danger that was getting worse as they looked ahead.
This system, Wallace suggested, essentially kept premiums artificially low. That may have encouraged more people to build and buy homes in fire-prone areas. And as devastating fires mounted and insurers had to make big payouts, the economics just didn't work. Insurers pulled out of the market. Wallace blamed California regulators. "They destroyed the markets," Wallace told me.
Of course, letting insurers more freely set their rates and charge more doesn't mean families will be able to afford the coverage. And that's really what's scary about this age of exploding wildfire risks. It's like the market is screaming: don't live in wooded areas! Yet millions of people already live there.
Near the end of Alexi's second episode, he asks UC San Diego economist Judson Boomhower whether some places might eventually become too risky to insure. Boomhower says that we'll find ways to keep insuring them. But the cold reality: "One sign that the market has healed will be higher prices," he tells Alexi.
As for me and my family, we recently left the California FAIR Plan for an insurer in the "non-admitted market." That market is a more free-market corner of the insurance industry, where companies have greater freedom to set prices and shape policies. Our new policy has better coverage than the FAIR Plan did. But there's a big catch: if our insurer goes belly up — say after a big fire that destroys lots of homes — we aren't protected by the state-mandated backstop that helps pay claims. Not ideal.
My family is hoping the admitted market starts working again. As Alexi reports, in late 2024, California adopted rules that allow insurers to use models that look ahead to future wildfire losses in exchange for writing more policies in high-risk areas. That will hopefully make it easier to find coverage.
With winter approaching and El Niño bringing lots of precipitation, we're hoping we can at least get a moment of reprieve from worrying about fire and home insurance. What better time to get a better understanding of the home insurance crisis than when it's keeping us up less at night?
Listen to Alexi's two-part series: Inside the insurance industry's destruction lab and Are wildfires making the future uninsurable?
Also, stay tuned for a Planet Money newsletter next fire season, when we'll report more on the explosion of California's "non-admitted market" and efforts by the state to bring its admitted market back to health.

Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho said on Monday that players who want the big salaries on offer in today’s contracts must accept the demands and risks of modern football.

Uber’s high-stakes robotaxi bet is officially ditching its human safety net. Nuro, Lucid, and Uber are starting fully driverless public road testing in the San Francisco Bay Area, with employee-only rides launching shortly after.
Uber, Nuro, and Lucid kick off fully driverless robotaxi testing
The partnership is pulling human safety drivers from its Lucid Gravity SUVs ahead of an early 2027 commercial debut.
First announced in July 2025, this three-way alliance represents Uber’s aggressive comeback in autonomous ride-hailing, after having abandoned its own troubled in-house efforts years ago. By pulling human safety operators from behind the wheel of Lucid Gravity SUVs, the companies say they are clearing a critical hurdle toward a public launch. That debut is now slated for early 2027, marking a slight slip from the partnership’s original late-2026 target. When it finally goes live, it will pit Uber directly against entrenched rivals like Waymo and Zoox on their home turf.
Driverless testing kicks off across four South Bay cities—Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale—before expanding across the broader Bay Area next year. To fuel this push, Lucid has delivered more than 100 upgraded Gravity SUVs, up from the 75 engineering vehicles on the road earlier this year.
The automaker began building pre-production models in October to clear regulatory safety approvals, and it plans to start manufacturing the actual commercial fleet in the coming weeks. Each SUV is powered by Nuro’s Level 4 “Nuro Driver” system, pairing cameras, solid-state lidar, and radar with a roof-mounted LED “halo” that flashes a rider’s initials and pickup status.
Removing the human backup comes after nearly a year of round-the-clock supervised testing in the Bay Area and Houston. Before letting the cars loose on public streets alone, Nuro put the software through grueling, high-risk edge cases on a closed track in Las Vegas to prove it could handle the unpredictable chaos of real-world driving.
The robotaxis are scheduled to hit the Uber app for Bay Area riders in the first quarter of 2027, with Houston following later that year. Looking further ahead, Uber has committed to buying at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles—including the automaker’s upcoming midsize model—over the coming years as it races to scale a global autonomous fleet.

The State government has stepped up action against illegal and unsafe cosmetics following reports of a 17-year-old girl from Areekode developing kidney disease after using a mercury-laced fairness cream.
Statewide inspections under Operation Soundarya on Sunday led to the seizure of fake cosmetic products worth more than ₹10 lakh. The Drugs Control department has also seized perfumes containing methanol and initiated action against products that violate cosmetic safety rules.
The department said inspections would continue in the coming days. Health Minister K. Muraleedharan warned of strict action against the sale of fairness creams containing excessive mercury. The government is also considering special inspection teams in all districts.
The crackdown follows the case of the higher secondary girl from Areekode, who developed membranous nephropathy, a kidney disease, after using a cream called F Tune for nearly a year. She bought the product after seeing promotions by social media influencers, particularly on Instagram. She ordered it through WhatsApp after being told that it could remove pimples, dark spots, and pigmentation.
Test results
Laboratory tests reportedly found 1.25% mercury, or 12,500 parts per million (ppm), in the cream. The permitted limit is less than 1 ppm. The girl developed swelling in her legs, fainting spells, low blood pressure and difficulty in walking. Doctors also found that she was losing excessive amounts of protein through urine. She has since recovered from the critical stage following treatment.
The girl said she first learned about the cream after seeing classmates use it. Its packaging listed ingredients such as turmeric but did not provide manufacturer or licence details. She said she would not have used it had she known it contained mercury. She has urged other users to stop using the product.
Her family has handed over the cream’s details and medical records to the police and plans to approach the consumer court. The police launched an investigation and collected details of the product for further examination. Criminal action against the manufacturers and distributors is being considered.
The cream’s Instagram page, which had been promoted by several influencers, is no longer available. The incident has also prompted complaints from others who say they experienced health problems after using similar products.
Mappilapattu singer Saleem Kodathoor said that he too developed membranous nephropathy after using a similar fairness cream. He said the illness forced him to suspend music programmes for months.
CMO’s directive
The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights has filed a case and sought reports from the Health department, police and drugs controller. The Chief Minister’s Office has directed the Health department to examine measures to prevent the sale of mercury-containing creams and strengthen inspections.
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation had earlier warned about the use of mercury and potent steroids in certain cosmetics. Mercury absorbed through the skin can damage the kidneys and nervous system. Doctors warn that prolonged exposure can cause serious health problems.
The case has raised concerns over the online promotion and sale of cosmetics, particularly products targeting teenagers, without clear information about their ingredients and manufacturers.

Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.
The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.
In that announcement the board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”
“I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.
“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.
The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO.
In the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.
Huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which said during the company’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so.
President Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a big lesson.”
Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with an Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee.
Huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The New York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies.
Alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm, and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state.
Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the company was primarily known within the gaming community. It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphics processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models.
Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first company to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.
