Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
Every time Torrie LeBlanc failed to persuade a parent to give their baby a vitamin K injection, she thought about the blood-soaked diaper.
It belonged to a newborn delivered last year, in the bustling labor and delivery unit where LeBlanc worked as a physician at the Corewell Health hospital system in Grand Rapids, Mich.
In the early hours the day after the baby girl was born, she suddenly started bleeding "from everywhere," LeBlanc recalled. Her eyes, nose, and rectum all suddenly oozed blood.
The girl's parents cried out for help from their hospital room. Nurses and doctors on the overnight shift rushed her to the neonatal intensive care unit, where they pumped fresh frozen plasma and other blood products into her small body, trying to replace what she was rapidly losing.
Her parents had declined a vitamin K injection for their baby, which is given to most newborns within six hours of birth to prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. With their baby on the verge of bleeding to death roughly 36 hours after birth, the parents agreed to let doctors administer vitamin K.
It worked. The baby survived, largely because she received treatment almost instantly, according to LeBlanc and an attending physician who helped care for the baby. Had the baby been at home when she started bleeding, they believe she would have died.
What LeBlanc witnessed has become much more common in recent years as more parents, influenced by the anti-vaccine movement and broader mistrust of the medical system, refuse to allow doctors to give their babies vitamin K shots at birth.
Nationally, the rate of newborns who do not receive intramuscular vitamin K has more than doubled, rising from 3.1% of newborns in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to research published in JAMA in November.
The spike moved LeBlanc, a pediatrician, and her colleagues to launch an initiative to reduce the rising number of vitamin K refusals at this hospital. On average, at least one family here refuses the injection for their newborn every day.
Two years in, the team won a modest victory: Vitamin K refusal rates are now flat at the hospital, even as refusals of other standard newborn medications, including the hepatitis B vaccine, continue to climb.
Still, doctors at the hospital say parents now regularly argue against everything from the once-routine vitamin shot to antibiotics for a critically ill infant.
"I honestly thought it would be easier," LeBlanc said, sitting by a sunlit window near the end of a 10-hour shift. "The more people I talk to, the more I learn about the misinformation that's online and the different reasons that people are refusing."
She paused. "It's a work in progress."
When doctors struggle to talk with parents
LeBlanc began a two-year fellowship at the children's hospital in 2024, certain she could make an impact on vitamin K refusals. After all, it's a vitamin, not a vaccine. How hard could it be to persuade parents to choose a vitamin that could save their baby's life?
Babies are born with very low levels of vitamin K, which is why the injection has been a routine part of newborn care since the 1960s. The shot is safe, with virtually no severe side effects, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And it effectively prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare condition that can involve bleeding in the brain.
Among babies who receive the shot at birth, fewer than 1 in 100,000 develop the most serious form of bleeding. But babies who don't receive it are 81 times more likely to develop the condition, according to the CDC. Of those who do, 1 in 5 die.
The shot was so effective that many doctors encountered a baby with VKDB perhaps only once in a career.
But doctors in multiple hospitals across the U.S. told KFF Health News that they now regularly see babies develop life-threatening bleeding from vitamin K deficiency. Some of those babies have died or been left with lifelong brain injuries.
Solomon Behar, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor in Los Angeles, recently treated an infant with VKDB who died.
"It just made me sad more than anything else," he said. "This was something that literally was a historical footnote up until the recent modern time, when people have decided that Mother Nature is someone that wants to work with them, rather than is trying to kill us."
Vitamin K refusals have increased dramatically in recent years alongside vaccine hesitancy.
Prominent conservative influencers suggest the vitamin K shot is tied to childhood cancer. Online parenting forums are filled with moms worried that the injection could harm their newborns, and wellness influencers on podcasts and TikTok — including some medical professionals — allege that babies have been injured by the shot or say it's unnecessary or unnatural.
When Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was asked at a congressional hearing in April to assure parents that the vitamin K injection was safe, Kennedy demurred. "I've never said anything about vitamin K," he said.
LeBlanc first saw a case of VKDB during her residency training, when a baby came into the emergency room with a nosebleed. Doctors caught it early, and the baby made a full recovery.
But she also watched as other doctors struggled with how to talk to parents who turned down the shot. "A lot of people just felt uncomfortable talking to families about it, or they didn't know what to say," she said.
Part of that was easy to fix: LeBlanc created a basic fact sheet for parents answering some of the most common questions about the vitamin K injection and explaining the risks of not getting it.
Labor and delivery nurses now use a script to offer routine newborn medications: "The standard of care for all babies born here includes vitamin K, hepatitis B vaccine, and erythromycin eye ointment," it says. "Do we have your permission to give these medications to your baby following delivery?"
The harder part is teaching doctors how to talk to parents about the fears that drive refusals.
"We can't walk into rooms where families don't know us from the doorknob and say, 'You have to do this,'" said Jaspreet Loyal, a pediatrician at Yale New Haven Hospital in Connecticut and a longtime leader in research on vitamin K refusal.
"We have to practice humility, to sit there and listen, and then come back the next day and sort of use that nudge approach."
LeBlanc helped train staffers in motivational interviewing, a technique developed for treating substance use disorders that is gaining popularity for addressing vaccine hesitancy.
It requires doctors to treat parents with a baseline of "unconditional positive regard or acceptance," one study urged. Parents' autonomy is paramount, even if their decisions conflict with medical recommendations. The minute parents feel judged, LeBlanc said, they stop listening.
The most important thing to convey, Loyal said, is "we are on the same team. You're looking out for your child. I'm looking out for your child. We may not fully agree what that looks like, but let's try."
LeBlanc gets only about 50% of parents who initially refuse the shot to change their minds. Other doctors at the hospital said their success rates are closer to 20% to 40%.
A refusal is now included in the patient's electronic medical record, so the family's regular pediatrician can bring it up at the first well-child visit. It also means that if the baby comes into the ER because of bleeding, the staff will immediately be able to see they haven't received the vitamin K shot.
And LeBlanc and Loyal, the Yale expert, argue that the rising rate of refusal means doctors need to be more open to parents who decline the vitamin K injection but want to give their baby liquid drops or crushed supplement tablets instead.
That's controversial: Taking vitamin K orally isn't as effective as the shot and requires multiple doses over several weeks or months, according to researchers. There's also no federally approved oral vitamin K supplement.
"The injection is the gold standard," LeBlanc said. "However, I would rather have them have some protection with the oral than no protection at all."
Finding compromise, with a baby's life on the line
In May, a 2-week-old baby came into Helen DeVos Children's Hospital with symptoms of meningitis, a potentially deadly infection of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
But the baby's parents had declined the vitamin K injection after the baby's birth, which meant the lumbar puncture — in which doctors insert a needle into the baby's lower back to get a sample of spinal fluid — needed to confirm meningitis was risky: What if the baby didn't stop bleeding after the puncture?
Still, as the child's condition worsened, doctors felt it was worth the risk. But then, the parents refused the lumbar puncture as well. LeBlanc recalled the mother telling her that, in her "medical opinion," she did not believe her child had meningitis.
After hours of debate, doctors offered the parents a compromise: They would treat the baby for meningitis, even without a confirmed diagnosis. That meant admitting the baby for two weeks to receive intravenous antibiotics.
Afterward, the mother wrote the medical team a thank-you note, which now hangs on a staff room wall covered with beaming photos of grateful families.
"Almost every single one of you has shown so much grace to us," the mom wrote. "Regardless of differing medical opinions, I'm so grateful for you."
On good days, LeBlanc can see that note as a win, a sign that staff are getting better at working with mistrustful families. On bad days, it feels like a symbol of a losing battle. Both families who watched their baby suffer after not receiving the vitamin K injection — the one whose child nearly died from VKDB, and the one with suspected bacterial meningitis — still declined routine vaccinations when they left the hospital.
At Yale, Loyal has learned not to take any of it personally. "At first, I used to feel like a failure every time: No, I was unable to convince somebody!" she said. Now she takes refusals in stride. "I cannot continue to spend time with someone who I cannot change their mind."
But LeBlanc worries each time she can't persuade a family to get their newborn the vitamin K injection. What if the next time she sees that baby is in the ICU? She would blame herself, she said, for not getting through to the parents.
"I couldn't convince them."
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
The contrast between the two leaders was striking.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.
There was, however, disappointment on aviation.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

When a Saudi OpenAI engineer wanted to vibe-code a better method for secretly recording meetings at the AI company, he turned to the familiar tool Codex, according to prosecutors.
Abdulrahman Alfozan used OpenAI's own popular coding product to modify a recording device that was the same kind OpenAI found tucked behind a TV in a meeting room, prosecutors said in a filing Monday, citing OpenAI records. They say he prompted OpenAI's AI coding tool, Codex, to add a voice-detection skill and used it to organize his surreptitious recordings in Dropbox.
A Monday motion by US attorneys disclosed these details, part of a back-and-forth over whether to keep Alfozan detained while he awaits trial.
The Justice Department arrested Alfozan on October 9 and charged him with using a device to intercept oral communications. He made one bid for release, about a week later. A magistrate judge deemed him a flight risk and ordered that he stay detained. He has pleaded not guilty.
Alfozan's lawyer puts pressure on the feds' investigation
On Friday, Alfozan's defense lawyer, David Rizk, asked a federal judge overseeing the case to allow him to be released on a $1 million bond. He said that prosecutors haven't yet presented evidence to support more severe charges, such as espionage or theft of trade secrets. Four of his friends, all US citizens, agreed to put up money for bond, he wrote.
Rizk also wrote that Alfozan's wife flew to Saudi Arabia with their child — evidence that a judge cited to rule he should be detained — because her student visa was set to expire.
"Mr. Alfozan's wife and child remain in Saudi Arabia because she was so deeply traumatized by the violent FBI raid that woke her last month and then the firestorm of publicity following the government's false insinuations that her husband was a spy," he wrote.
Prosecutors hope to keep Alfozan detained
In the Monday filing, prosecutors said the investigation is ongoing. There was already evidence, they wrote, that Alfozan would try to flee the country if he were released from jail.
Prosecutors said Alfozan exchanged WhatsApp messages with a member of the Saudi royal family indicating he might apply for a job at Echelon, a Riyadh-based AI company, "after the IPO" — an apparent reference to OpenAI's expected public offering next year.
They also shed light on the material they allege Alfozan gathered from OpenAI's offices. According to Monday's filing, law enforcement officials found photos on his cellphone of a document marked "CONFIDENTIAL" detailing a "strategic partnership" between OpenAI and another company. They also found audio files on his personal computer of "dozens of recordings of conversations" that took place at OpenAI throughout September of this year, including meetings that "involved discussions of what appears likely to be confidential trade secret material," the filing says.
Alfozan used his wife's account to prompt the coding tool Codex to help with the recordings, the filing says.
At a hearing last week, US Assistant Attorney Nick Parker said that the prosecutors' ongoing investigation includes the recording device, five devices taken from the couple, and both records and surveillance footage from OpenAI.
Alfozan and Rizk will square off against the prosecution over the new motion for release in a hearing on Tuesday morning before Magistrate Judge Alex Tse, who rejected the original bid for release.
Neither OpenAI nor Rizk immediately responded to Business requests for comment from Business Insider on Monday.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has de-notified and withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023) where medical colleges were liable to face penalty fines for violations of educational standards and infrastructure requirements at medical colleges.
Earlier reports in The Hindu stated NMC’s withdrawal of MSMER-2023 weakens accountability in medical education by removing provisions to fine individual faculty members and administrators up to ₹5 lakh for submitting false information. Although the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) can still penalise institutions up to ₹1 crore under separate regulations, institutional penalties may be less effective in deterring individual misconduct. Misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk.
The NMC justified the withdrawal by arguing that MSMER created overlapping assessment powers with MARB. However, scrapping the regulations entirely raises questions about the necessity of this move, particularly when non-compliance remains common and transparency in medical education is inadequate. Moreover, conflicting appeal deadlines under MARB regulations and the NMC Act could lead to legal disputes and delay enforcement. Ultimately, the NMC must clarify whether the existing regulatory mechanisms are being effectively enforced and whether their outcomes are publicly accessible without which the withdrawal of MSMER risks appearing to be a relaxation of regulatory oversight rather than a simplification of rules.
Medical experts have further warned that deterrence against practices such as ghost faculty and fabricated patient records would potentially expose students and institutions to greater malpractice and mismanagement. While some experts support the removal of regulatory duplication, they emphasise that effective oversight depends on rigorous verification, transparent reporting, consistent penalties and time-bound enforcement. The NMC must therefore demonstrate that MARB can enforce standards as effectively as the withdrawn framework; otherwise, regulatory rationalisation risks becoming a dilution of accountability.
The NMC has clarified that the MSMER introduced a parallel mechanism through which the undergraduate and postgraduate boards could assess institutions, thereby encroaching on the MARB’s mandate. While talking to The Hindu, NMC officials said the denotification is aimed at simplifying regulatory procedures and eliminating overlapping responsibilities, without compromising the quality of medical education.

Eoin Colfer, who is exec producing Disney+ animated series based on his ‘Artemis Fowl’ book series, is among the shortlisted authors for the first-ever Children’s Booker Prize. Other film and TV links evident in the selection include author and illustrator Shaun Tan, who co-directed the Oscar-winning animated short ‘The Lost Thing’.
Colfer is shortlisted for ‘War’, a graphic novel he co-wrote with Andrew Donkin and which is illustrated by Giovanni Rigano. Donkin also wrote ‘Batman: Legends of the Dark Knight’ for DC Comics. Tan, meanwhile, makes the cut with his book ‘Hometown’.
The eight-strong shortlist of titles for kids aged 8 to 12 comprises five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories.
Watch on Deadline
Stars including Adeel Akhtar (Enola Holmes), Dafne Keen (His Dark Materials) and Aidan Turner (Poldark) will read from the shortlisted titles in a series of short films showcasing the books. The films for the grown-up Booker have amassed millions of views.
The judging panel overseeing the process includes Ghosts star Lolly Adefope and bookseller Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, as well as Frank Cottrell-Boyce, a writer and screenwriter whose film credits include Paddington in Peru and Kensuke’s Kingdom. They are joined by four child judges. The inaugural Children’s Booker winner will be announced at a daytime ceremony at the Young V&A Museum in London on Feb. 2, 2027.
The main Booker Prize is regarded as the single biggest accolade in the world for a work of literary fiction. The film and TV links are evident in the scores of Booker titles that have been adapted for the screen including Hilary Mantel’s ‘Wolf Hall’ and Thomas Keneally’s ‘Schindler’s Ark’ (published as ‘Schindler’s List’ in the U.S.).
The 2025 winner David Szalay told Deadline about a film adaptation of his Booker-winning novel ‘Flesh’ from the producers of Conclave. This year’s winner, M. John Harrison, also told us about his hopes for a film adaptation of The End of Everything.
Here’s the Children’s Booker Prize shortlist in full.
‘The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen’ by Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts (Little Tiger Press)
‘Tadpole Summer’ by Catherine Bruton (Nosy Crow)
‘War’ by Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano (Hodder Children’s Books)
‘The Night I Borrowed Time’ by Iqbal Hussain (Puffin Press)
‘The Teller of Tall Tales’ by Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston (Pushkin Children’s Books)
‘The Rambler’s Curse’ by Mikey Please (HarperCollins Children’s Books)
‘Séamus Almost Famous’ by Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor (Gill Children’s)
‘Hometown’ by Shaun Tan (Walker Studio)

Moroccan federation reports incident to CAS during Senegal AFCON appeal, source says
PARIS, Nov 24 : Morocco's football federation has reported an incident to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) during proceedings on Senegal's appeal, ahead of a ruling due later on Tuesday, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
The appeal challenges the Confederation of African Football (CAF) decision to overturn Senegal's 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January's Africa Cup of Nations final.
According to the source, who declined to be named because they were not permitted to discuss the case, the Moroccan federation alleges that Senegal Football Federation (FSF) President Abdoulaye Fall spoke by phone with one of the three arbitrators on Sunday.
Reuters could not independently verify whether the call took place or establish what was discussed.
CAS said on Monday its ruling on the appeal would come on Tuesday afternoon. It was not immediately available for comment.

Why your smart TV keeps losing its Wi-Fi connection
A smart TV can drop Wi-Fi for several reasons, and most of them have little to do with the TV.
It's not uncommon for smart TVs to struggle with a Wi-Fi connection, even if it's been relatively smooth sailing for a while. Things change, furniture gets moved around, routers are upgraded, new TVs are purchased and old TVs are moved to another room. Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 tri-band routers bring faster data rates to the table, but Wi-Fi 4 (2.4GHz and 5GHz dual-band support) is still the most prevalent Wi-Fi standard in the US. For the most part, 5GHz and 2.4GHz are enough for the average household, though it's ideal for most smart TVs to use 5GHz for 4K streaming.
It's a little tougher for 5GHz Wi-Fi, however, which is faster than 2.4GHz but lacks range and struggles with passing through walls. Your router's features could be making things worse. Many routers use "band steering" when broadcasting Wi-Fi, a feature that combines bands under a single network name, switching your devices back and forth automatically. It sounds convenient. You want your device connected to the most stable band, but it can wreak havoc on your TV's Wi-Fi connection. Devices don't always get the right band, degrading your smart TV's connection stability and speed. For those with older smart TVs, the lack of compatibility could be hampering your connection as well. Older models may not support DFS channels and won't find networks using them.
How to get your TV back online for good
Isolate the problem and figure out whether it's the TV or the network by connecting a phone or a laptop to the same Wi-Fi network. If it runs fine, the issue is probably with your smart TV. If not, check your router, gateway or your internet service first.
Next, check if there's a firmware or software waiting for installation in the TV's system settings. If there's an update available but your internet connection isn't working, check the model name on the manufacturer's website to try and flash an update via USB stick instead.
Restarting could also be an easy fix. Unplug your TV for two minutes and the router for about a minute. Plug the router back in and let it reconnect before messing with the TV. If the problem persists, go into the TV's settings and clear out the saved connections. On your router settings, turn off band steering and give each available band its own name so you can choose which band the TV will use such as 36, 40, 44, or 48 instead of Auto. If the TV keeps dropping on 5GHz, set the band to a fixed channel outside the DFS range.
Most smart TV's default to a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi signal to avoid losing connection with your router. This band can interfere with special Bluetooth remote features like voice command, so try turning off the Bluetooth-reliant features on your remote. If Bluetooth is critical for accessibility reasons, switch the TV to 5GHz, bring the router closer, or go the direct route with an Ethernet cable.
Should you use 5GHz or 2.4GHz for your smart TV?
Several factors go into this, including signal strength, network congestion, router placement and the TV's capabilities. If the signal is strong, the obvious choice is 5GHz. Switch to 2.4GHz only if the TV is too far from the router to hold a steady connection with 5GHz.
Speed and crowding are typical issues in most homes because everybody has a device or ten that connects to the internet. A 4K stream needs a steady 20 Mbps (Netflix suggests 15 Mbps, but 20+ is preferable). 2.4GHz has a longer range and handles walls better, but it's slower and usually more congested because neighboring routers, microwaves and Bluetooth devices can all interfere with it. Once you've eliminated band steering and renamed your bands, try each one out. Use your TV's network status screen to make a signal strength comparison.
Consider a wired connection. A close router makes this option more feasible, so you don't have to run an Ethernet cable across ceilings and under baseboards. If there's just too much space and you can't shrink the gap between the router and TV, a mesh network is another viable alternative. Most mesh nodes have Ethernet ports, so you can place one near your TV and run an Ethernet cable from the mesh to the TV. Just make sure your mesh network has a strong connection.

- Etsy's new terms of use state that the company and its third-party partners have the right to use content posted on its platform "to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies."
- In response to backlash from vendors, Etsy said it does not and will not "use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity."

A rumor is spreading that global e-commerce marketplace Etsy updated its terms of service to allow the company to train artificial intelligence systems using artwork posted on the platform.
The allegations have caused an uproar in small business and independent artist communities, as many rely on Etsy to make sales. Artists with tens of thousands of followers have shared Instagram and X posts declaring that they had closed their Etsy shops over the company's new AI policies.
For example, one post with nearly 100,000 likes as of this writing claims that, in plain English, Etsy's terms of service allows it to "train generative AI on our artwork."
"They can package and resell that data to third parties," the post continued. "Stay on the platform, and your art is theirs to scrape. Sell. Train."
Etsy has, in fact, updated its terms of use with a new AI policy, which go into effect Dec. 16. The plain text of the updated terms of use states that any content posted on Etsy can be used "to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies."
In response to the uproar, however, Etsy's vice president of customer operations, James Ossman, said in a Nov. 16 blog post (archived) that the company does not use AI to copy artwork, nor does it claim ownership over sellers' creations (emphasis theirs):
"We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers."
However, it's unclear whether Etsy might use AI to create content in ways that artists may consider as equivalent to an AI model being trained off of their work. For example, Etsy's statement says it may use seller content to feature listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns. Etsy has not clarified whether that means the company might use generative AI to create an advertisement that uses an artist's listing photo. 
We asked Etsy for further clarification and await a response. As such, we have left this claim unrated.
The changes to Etsy's terms of use come after the e-commerce marketplace released clearer restrictions on AI use in October.
"We recognize we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted. It's changing fast, and like many of you, we're thinking seriously about what it means for Etsy, what's allowed on our marketplace, and how it impacts running a creative business," a blog post from Ossman said about those regulations.
Etsy's new terms of use, annotated
The updated language on AI is under Section 5, "Your Content," in Etsy's terms of use, which is available in full (archived) on the company's website.
Both the new terms of use and the older terms of use, which is in effect through Dec. 15, state that Etsy does not claim ownership over sellers' content, but that it has broad rights to use sellers' content for Etsy's own purposes (underlined emphasis ours): 
Content that you post using our Services is your content (so let's refer to it as "Your Content"). We don't make any claim to it, which includes anything you post using our Services (like shop names, profile pictures, listing photos, listing descriptions, reviews, comments, videos, usernames, etc.).
B. Permission to Use Your Content. By posting Your Content through our Services, you grant Etsy and third parties authorized by Etsy in its sole discretion a license to use Your content, including to operate, provide, improve, and promote the Services. We don't claim ownership of Your Content, but we have your permission to use it to help Etsy function and grow.
The "Your Content" section then goes on to explain what rights Etsy has over seller content posted on its platform. The older version of the document includes no mention of artificial intelligence. The newer version adds the sentence we underlined below:
C. Rights You Grant Etsy. (Here's the legalese version of the last section). By posting Your Content, you grant Etsy and, as authorized by Etsy in its sole discretion, third parties, a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, sub-licensable, perpetual license to use, display, edit, modify, reproduce, distribute, store, and prepare derivative works from Your Content. This allows us to provide the Services and to promote Etsy, your Etsy shop, other shops and listings, or the Services in general, in any formats and through any channels, including across any Etsy Services, our partners, or third-party website or advertising medium. […] This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy.
Etsy acknowledges in its terms of use that providing the platform with these rights "sounds like a lot" but argues that it's "necessary for us to keep Etsy going." The company's examples for reasons why it might need these rights include resizing or enhancing seller listings to optimize them for its mobile app, translating descriptions into other languages and featuring seller listings in marketing campaigns.
While the new language states that creators may have opt-out rights, a review of the company's privacy policy and supplemental U.S.-specific privacy policy found no evidence Etsy sellers can opt out of AI training entirely. It does note, however that those in the United States have the right to opt out of sales of personal data. Different states also have different data privacy laws that may be applicable.
It is also worth noting that whether or not it's legal to scrape copyrighted content is an issue that's still being hammered out in the courts, so Etsy's statement that it does not have ownership over seller content does not necessarily mean it doesn't have the right to scrape that content.
Etsy's response to backlash
Etsy's Nov. 16 post about its changes to the company's terms of use provides several examples for how the company may use content to train AI models, but it doesn't appear to be a comprehensive list (emphasis theirs):
How we use your content to train AI models: We made an update to our terms that says Etsy and our partners may use member content to develop, train, test, and improve AI and machine learning technologies. This change is meant to clarify the ways we use AI in our marketplace.
We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers.
We will continue to focus on using AI to support sellers and improve the Etsy experience, and we're committed to being transparent about how we use this technology. Here are a few examples of how we are using AI on Etsy today:
- We train models to identify potentially fraudulent accounts and related listings, helping us investigate potential issues and protect our members.
- We use AI to understand the inventory across our marketplace, so we can help buyers find your items through search and provide them with tailored recommendations.
- We build AI-powered seller tools to help you run your business more efficiently, and better understand and meet your buyers' expectations.
Etsy's post also states that its terms of use "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models."
"We use security tools designed to detect and limit unauthorized scraping, and we are continuously improving our abilities to protect your content and keep Etsy safe," the statement said.
Notably, the statement does not make it clear whether Etsy itself or authorized third parties might be able to scrape Etsy content to train AI models. In fact, Etsy's terms of use specify that users cannot scrape any Etsy page for AI training "without our express permission."

Dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
- Published
At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.

With over 1.3 billion users worldwide, LinkedIn is one of the most popular professional-networking sites.
Being active on the platform can help you build a personal brand, grow a professional network, or land a new job. However, a few common missteps can undermine your professional image.
So, Business Insider asked two etiquette experts to share the biggest LinkedIn mistakes they see — and how to avoid them. Here's what they said.
Leaving typos in posts
Stayce Wagner, founder of Spencer Crane Etiquette and a business-etiquette consultant certified through The Protocol School of Washington, told BI that LinkedIn posts should be kept typo-free.
When typing up a post, she said it's important to "take the time to put your best foot forward because you're making a first impression. People will stop reading when they see typos in posts."
Using the wrong emojis when communicating with colleagues
Elaine Swann, an etiquette expert who founded the The Swann School of Protocol, emphasized the importance of being "mindful of the emojis we use in the business arena."
For example, she said if a colleague shares a win on LinkedIn, a congratulatory comment with heart emojis could be misconstrued in the business world, even if you know the individual personally.
Only using the platform when you need a favor
Although LinkedIn can be a great tool for building career-boosting connections, Swann said it's important to regularly engage with your network and avoid using LinkedIn only when you need favors.
"Hop on every once in a while, look at what folks are doing and comment, share, or react with the 'like' button. This way, you are engaging with people, not just merely asking for something on the other end," she said.
Misusing the connecting and following options
LinkedIn offers two ways to build your professional network: follow someone to learn from their content, or, connect with someone to build deeper relationships.
Wagner said it's important to know when to use each option. Per LinkedIn's guidelines, users should only consider connecting with someone they already have a relationship with or want to stay in touch with.
If you're interested in someone's content, Wagner recommends following first and interacting with their posts. Then, if there's a real reason to send a connection request, you should do so with a personalized note.
Using AI to write without editing the content
LinkedIn is a platform for building relationships and genuine connections. So, Wagner said posting AI-written content without editing it or adding your authentic voice is a mistake that can undermine your credibility.
"In the age of AI writing everything for everyone, authenticity has taken on a new life and new importance," Wagner said.
Treating the platform like other personal social media sites
"LinkedIn is a platform geared toward business, so the content we share should not mirror what we see on other social media platforms, such as Facebook, for example," Swann told BI.
For example, romantic life updates, rants about other people (professionally or otherwise), and lifestyle posts that include excessive partying are not appropriate for LinkedIn.
Instead, Swann recommends posting content that fits the scope of business, like useful information, announcements, and industry insights.
"If you make a mistake and post something that's a little more personal, even if just a few people have commented on it or or reacted to it in some way, it's absolutely acceptable for you to delete that so it does not stay alive," Swann said.
Sending unsolicited messages
Whether you want to pitch someone an idea, offer your services, or encourage them to make a purchase, Swann said you should never do so right out of the gate.
Instead, she recommends connecting first, briefly introducing yourself and what you do, then asking if you can send additional information via email or otherwise.

Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.
But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.
Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.
Surveillance pricing versus dynamic pricing
Surveillance pricing, according to the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), is an algorithmic pricing practice that charges individuals or groups of individuals different prices “for the same goods or services.”
“The goal of surveillance pricing is to infer the highest price that the customer is willing to pay, based on consumers’ personal data and other market data,” EPIC explains.
Instacart previously practiced surveillance pricing, also called personalized pricing. In 2025, Consumer Reports found that, “based on how much Instacart says the typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year.” Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.
Dynamic pricing, or surge pricing, differs from surveillance pricing in that, instead of relying on consumer data, it uses changing market trends, like supply and demand, inventory levels, and competitor pricing, to set prices.
While dynamic pricing may charge you more for an Uber ride when it’s very busy, surveillance pricing can feel less reasonable.
For instance, Target’s app was previously accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV if they bought it while standing inside a Target store. At the time, Target said that it would match lower prices presented by customers, but many customers wouldn’t think to look for pricing discrepancies. In another instance from 2012, Orbitz was found to more prominently feature expensive hotels to people using macOS. Companies often dispute whether their practices truly qualify as surveillance pricing. But these examples all reflect companies using data about their customers to influence the prices they show them.

Gift-giving isn’t just about grabbing something solid under a determined spending limit. It’s an expression of love, a way to show someone how well you really know them. That doesn’t mean you have to do it all on your own, though. Sometimes you just need a push in the right direction to get things rolling.
The Verge’s 2026 holiday gift guide
Our latest holiday cheat sheet is jam-packed with our favorite tech, along with Play-Doh, vinyl, and plenty of analog picks.

This year, we spent hours collecting our favorites to help you get ahead of your holiday shopping. This list has everything: minimalist smart rings, Play-Doh flowers, sleek beat machines — you name it. Whatever your needs, no matter how demanding the recipient, you’ll find something exceptional below for that special someone on your list.
Cricut StickerPix Print Plus Cut

AirPods 5

Busy Bar

Equipped with a pixelated LED screen, fantastically fun buttons, and intriguing ways to play, Flipper’s open-source productivity tool breeds efficiency by, among other things, keeping coworkers from interrupting your flow with their weekend plans.
Wacaco Minipresso GR2
Espresso in the woods? Yes, please. The GR2’s magical mechanics make it possible, letting you turn 12 ounces of grounds into espresso without power. Its carrying case houses all the accessories needed to get that sweet shot of bean, making real coffee available virtually anywhere.
Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo
Digital photos changed everything, but there’s still something wonderful about the visceral touch and nostalgia of analog. Fujifilm’s Instax Mini Evo provides an intriguing hybrid that bridges these worlds, with a retro design, intuitive dials and controls, and the ability to filter like it’s 1989 (or 1889?).
TP-Link Roam 7 portable router
What if you could give the gift of stress-free Wi-Fi on the go? That’s the promise of TP-Link’s dual-band Roam 7, a portable Wi-Fi 7 router that simplifies connecting to public portals so travelers can connect everything to a single device and be done with it.
Belkin ConnectAir Wireless HDMI Display Adapter
For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.

Akai MPC Sample

Nimble SharePower Portable Charger

Ninja Crispi Microwave & Air Fryer
For those in smaller dwellings, efficient living means maximizing space. That’s where combo appliances like Ninja’s newest microwave / air fryer combo come in. The handy countertop gadget lets you zap your food, then crisp it at the end so your pizza or French fries don’t turn into a soggy mess.

Shokz OpenFit Pro

Play-Doh Blooms

Insta360 Luna Pro

Razer Kishi V3 Pro XL
Most mobile controllers have a serious size limit. Not Razer’s Kishi V3 Pro XL, which lets you throw a big ol’ tablet between the handles for a major visual upgrade. It also has high-quality joysticks, great grips, and customizable keys for USB-C tablets, along with haptics for Android models.
KPop Demon Hunters (4K Blu-ray)
So what if you’ve heard “Golden” more times than you can count? Netflix’s massive animated hit is a lot easier to gift now that it’s officially available on 4K Blu-ray disc. The story about three pop stars who band together to save humanity from a demonic boy band is an instant classic, with fantastic music and striking animation.
Blissbury Ear Pillow
If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.
Keychron K2 HE keyboard (Concrete Edition)
The Concrete Edition of Keychron’s K2 HE is not your average mechanical board. Cased in actual concrete, it offers standard keycaps to match its industrial aesthetic, both Bluetooth and 2.4GHz connectivity, and several other advanced features. This includes the ability to adjust the actuation distance of the individual Hall effect switches (hence the “HE”).
We all do it: pay a ton for a monthly streaming service for just a few series. It’s better to own the real thing, and Hacks, a hilarious drama that follows a comedian (Jean Smart) and her young writer (Hannah Einbinder) in the tumultuous “biz,” is one of HBO’s best series in years.
Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.
Knockaround Premiums sunglasses
For the person on your list whose hatred for smart glasses runs deep, Knockaround’s hip, tech-free sunglasses should hit the spot. They’re available in a variety of fun styles and offer lightweight frames and polarized lenses, with both UVA and UVB shielding for attractive eye protection.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
The first 3D Zelda game has been remade for the modern era. And if you fear it will diverge too much from the Nintendo 64 original, fear not: This carefully crafted remake delivers updated graphics and improved controls alongside the same stellar adventure we remember.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
Everyone needs a good flashlight, and perhaps your recipient’s next one should ditch the replaceable batteries. Wuben’s rechargeable G5 has a pocketable, spy-tech-inspired design, USB-C charging, and adjustable brightness. More importantly, the 400-lumen light is super compact, making it easy to stow or clip onto your bag.
If you haven’t been bombarded by the Hulken yet, it’s a rolling tote that’s blown up online. Designed to hold everything from laundry to an impromptu picnic, the durable bag is beloved for its seemingly bottomless capacity and colorful style, making it a thoughtful gift for fashionable folks on the move.
Xteink X4 Pro e-reader
If a Kindle won’t quite fit into your favorite traveler’s tight pack job, consider the Xteink X4 Pro. The tiny e-reader is easy to pop into your bag or pocket thanks to its 4.3-inch display, and the latest model offers a backlit touchscreen for a more intuitive way to explore the literary world.
Ember Mug 3 (14-ounce)
For the coffee or tea lover in your life who’s always headed to the microwave for a heat zap, Ember’s fancy-schmancy smart mug is a luxurious way to keep things toasty. With the ability to set the temperature on the mug or in the app, the Mug 3 makes it simple to keep liquids perfectly hot indefinitely.
Nalgene Narrow Mouth water bottle (16-ounce)
Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.
If your giftee is into New York City memorabilia or wants a more unique way to light up a room, this cube-shaped lamp, designed around the old MTA entrance beacons, is sure to delight. Locals will recognize the vintage symbol, which still survives in the wild, and everyone will dig the old-school vibe.
Pokémon Pokopia
Pokopia brings Pokémon to life in a cozy worldbuilding game that borrows the best from predecessors like Minecraft and Animal Crossing. The twist? The slow-burning Switch 2 title eventually rolls into an expansive adventure that lets you customize as you go.
Petkit Fresh Element Solo Automatic Feeder
When it comes to keeping your pet happy and healthy while you’re away, the details matter. Petkit’s most basic auto feeder offers peace of mind with dual-power protection, meal monitoring via the Petkit app, and a generous 12-cup capacity that should keep an adult cat fed for up to 15 days.
Fairphone 6 Plus
Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.
In many ways, the Pebble Index 01 is the gadget of our times. The stripped-back smart ring has a microphone and, with a tap of a button, records and sends your thoughts to the Pebble app over Bluetooth. You can also use it to start a timer or even add a calendar event to your phone.
Cast iced tea glass
Sure. You could put iced tea in them, but no one’s stopping you from sipping pulpy OJ or rich chocolate milk from Kinto’s stylish glassware, which was crafted with an “uninterfering design” in mind. Needless to say, a full set makes a lovely addition to any minimalist’s ensemble.
The hippest thing in audio right now is… the hippest thing from a long time ago. Enter the modded iPod Classic from Player Mods, which refreshes Apple’s media player with some 21st-century upgrades. The 5th-gen model can be customized with several color options (including a transparent case) and up to 2TB of storage.
GuliKit TT Pro controller
For those tired of experiencing Joy-Con drift with their Nintendo Switch (or stick drift on any controller), there’s the TT Pro. Loaded with the latest anti-drift tech for joysticks and customizable triggers that let picky gamers have it their way, GuliKit’s customizable wireless controllers work with PlayStation, Nintendo, PC, iOS, and Android devices.
Voicemod Key Pocket
Do you like… scary movies? That’s just one of many catchphrases that pair well with the Key Pocket, which can alter voices in real time. The tiny device sticks to the back of Apple or Android devices via magnets, granting you multiple effects for gaming, voice calls, or streaming.
OhSnap Grip Stand
Pricey yet endlessly useful, this is the kind of item you might not buy for yourself, which makes it a fantastic gift. Offering a brilliantly thin yet durable framework in a stand that also hangs, pops, and never needs to come off, it’s the ultimate phone accessory.
If someone on your list collects Game Boy, Game Boy Color, or Game Boy Advance cartridges, the GB Operator might be the perfect gift. The slick, transparent USB-C device makes it easy to play and manage classic titles on a macOS or Windows machine via emulation, with or without achievements.
Dock & Bay Picnic Blanket
Dock & Bay’s blankets are a great choice for almost everyone. They provide a soft space on which to relax or entertain, whether at the park or on your hardwood floors at home, and they’re incredibly easy to pack. Plus, they have a water-resistant bottom and come in an array of fun colors.
Sonos Beam Ultra
This radical upgrade of the middle child in Sonos’ soundbar lineup may be the best (little) soundbar you can buy. It delivers musical sound, surprisingly full and cinematic bass, and brain-tricking immersion thanks to drivers that now point every which way; it can also expand or connect with other Sonos speakers and stream almost anything.
Instruo Pocket Scion Bio-Feedback Instrument
The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.
Alienware AW3426DW QD-OLED Gaming Monitor
Your favorite gamer needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.
Lego PlayStation
Few devices evoke more sheer nostalgic joy than Sony’s OG PlayStation console from ’94. If you know a gamer, Lego’s latest replica brings it all flooding back with several brick-ified details, including a pop-up hinge, a gamepad, and a number of hidden surprises waiting to be discovered.
Fi Ultra dog tracker
Nothing can replace our furry friends, so for pets that tend to wander, only the best tracking tech will do. Enter the Fi Ultra, which uses Starlink technology via T-Mobile to track pets almost anywhere, even in cellular dead zones.
If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.
Gardyn Studio 2
If there’s someone on your list who loves plants but can’t seem to take care of them, the Gardyn Studio 2 can bring life to their living room. The smart hydroponic garden is easy to set up and features automated, AI-powered lighting, helping anyone maintain a green thumb.
Bissell ProHeat 2X Revolution Pet Pro carpet cleaner
You create a home for your pets; they create a mess for your home. It’s the circle of life (or carpet, anyway). Thankfully, Bissell’s pro-grade cleaner uses a concentrated stream of formula and 12 rows of rotating brushes to do the dirty work for you, keeping your carpets in good order.
Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.
Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro
Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for way less than Apple’s latest AirPods Pro.
Matic robot vacuum
It’s time for a smarter robovac. Thankfully, there’s the Matic, which looks less like the rambling discs that pervade the space and more like an actual robot that, well, vacuums. It doesn’t get under beds, but it also doesn’t get stuck under them, and it does a great job providing truly no-fuss cleaning thanks to its superb mapping.
OhSnap MCON controller
There’s no shortage of mobile gaming controllers, but few are as stealthy or as compact as the MCON. The sliding gamepad quickly attaches to any MagSafe- or Pixelsnap-ready phone, letting you game with a set of satisfying controls that feel more natural than most rivals.
Big Walk
It can be hard to keep in touch with friends, but Big Walk might be the game that gets the gang back together. The cooperative multiplayer title drops players into a wacky world as spherical humanoids who must solve puzzles by chatting and teaming up. You’ll want at least two copies, and sessions support up to 12 players.
The future is now, so of course we’ve got screens in sunglasses. The Viture Pro 2 are a slick pair of augmented-reality shades with speakers, micro-OLED screens, and a bonus feature: diopter-adjusting dials, which can sharpen the focus of whatever they’re mirroring from a phone or other device over a USB-C tether. Fancy!
BYOK
The BYOK (Bring Your Own Keyboard) is a distraction-free way for creatives to get their thoughts down without the allure of silly YouTube videos or notifications about their dog’s flea meds. No frills, just a low-resolution LCD screen that works with most keyboards and provides plenty of power for the long haul.
The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.
WiiM Sound smart speaker
WiiM is a popular Sonos alternative, thanks in part to excellent software that works across its multiple streaming amplifiers and other products. The WiiM Sound is the brand’s sharpest smart speaker, with accessible controls, Alexa and Google smarts, and the ability to connect to other WiiM gear in surround sound or throughout your home.
When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like the pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.
KitchenAid Artisan Plus Series 5 stand mixer
Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.
