Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.
That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where modest brick houses and tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.
But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.
It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex. The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.
South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.
The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.
Now, not only are the children getting to practice their reading, some of them have tried their hand at writing their own stories.
The newly published authors sit up front, ready to sign the pile of freshly-printed books for sale and answer questions about their process.
Thirteen-year-old Fiona Mogane, the bespectacled author of "Lindani's Modelling Journey," is one of them.
"It's about a girl who discovered a lot of challenges throughout her journey," Fiona explains. One of those challenges is that the main character Lindani's mother is an alcoholic, spending what little money the family has on drink — including government grant money meant for her daughter's welfare. She also shouts at her daughter a lot, and sometimes Lindani worries she will follow in her mother's footsteps.
Fiona writes: "Sometimes a thought intrudes on Lindani's mind, telling her that if she took some alcohol, it would make her feel better and stand up for herself …. However Lindani always pulls herself out of that thought: she knows she is stronger than that."
Phelelisa Somana, one of the coordinators of the book project, says she was impressed with the maturity of Fiona's story.
"When I read her story it had a very deep theme that I didn't expect a child to delve into in a way that she did," says Somana.
It "definitely just reminded me just how much kids are a lot smarter than they think they are," she adds. "They notice a lot more than they think they do."
Learning "Ubuntu"
Fortunately, Fiona's tale has a happy ending. Dreaming of becoming the next Miss South Africa, her character Lindani decides to try and raise the money she needs to enter a modelling contest by baking scones and selling them to her neighbors.
"She believes deep down inside that each one of her homemade scones has something special that makes them really delicious," Fiona writes.
In the end, Lindani makes enough cash to enter the contest. She comes in second place and is crowned "princess."
"She is happy because she has proved to herself that she can make a way when it initially seemed there was none," Fiona writes.
In real life, Fiona — also keen on modeling — is being raised in Alex by a single mom. Alex has high crime rates and poor government services like water and electricity. The young teenager is all too familiar with the problems, but she says there are good things about township life too..
"Alex is a crowded place, but when you're in Alex, you can learn a lot of things," she explains. "You can learn how to have Ubuntu."
Ubuntu is an African philosophy centering on community well-being and shared responsibility. As Fiona puts it: "Ubuntu is to help other people when they are in need."
Fiona, whose favorite subject at school is English, says she'd like to go to university, maybe to study medicine. And there's another dream too.
"One day, if I grow up, I want to build a big house that will be having a room with its own books," she says.
Homes without books
Fiona didn't grow up with books at home. Two-thirds of South African children don't have books at home, according to one study by UNICEF.
They won't necessarily find them at school either.
Only about 15% of public schools in South Africa have a functioning library, according to government data.
The dire state of child literacy has its roots in the home. Many children have weak early learning foundations, according to the UNICEF study, and they have no exposure to books before starting primary school.
"When I became the minister of basic education in 2024 I was confronted by the statistic of 80% of 10-year-olds who cannot read for meaning in any language," Basic Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube told NPR.
The minister says the government is trying to tackle this problem by getting more kids into early learning programs.
"We're investing ten billion rand [$58 million] over the next three years on a massive haul out of early childhood development centers," Gwarube says.
Tebogo Selekane, an English teacher at Kwa-bhekilanga secondary school, says the weekend program at Read Alex has helped some of her students a lot. Two of her students have stories in the book.
"They are doing very well in reading," says Selekane. "There's a lot of change in them... they will respond back with confidence."
A country of storytellers
At the book launch, Wandile Mathe, a 21-year-old South African writer and joint coordinator of the project, says despite South Africa's poor literacy rates, the children he coaches come from a nation of storytellers.
"I think South Africans are natural storytellers," he says. "There's always gossip going around anyway."
"In the taxi, at the line, in a shop, wherever you go, there's always someone willing to tell you a story, whether about their personal life or the things that they're seeing around," he laughs. "We're huge social commentators. Nothing will pass by and we will not comment."
The kids who contributed to the book are true to this storytelling tradition, borrowing from their lives and what they see daily in the township. As well as Fiona's story about poverty and alcoholism, there are tales about peer pressure, dangerous men on the street, losing parents and inability to pay school fees.
But it's not all doom and gloom. The heroes and heroines all find ways to overcome the obstacles, learning important lessons and making friends along the way.
For example, one of the young authors, 13-year-old Anita Maloka, wrote a story about a rural girl who moves to Johannesburg to attend school and dreams of becoming a scientist. But the school is not what she hoped.
"Sometimes two students had to squeeze together on one chair. Textbooks were scarce," she writes. The family doesn't have the money to send her anywhere better though, so the character works toward earning a scholarship at a school that "has a real science lab and an entire room just for learning to program computers and building robots."
Like her character, Anita, who dreams of becoming a marine biologist, is also working toward getting a scholarship that will take her out of the township.
But she stresses that life in Alex is "not just about struggle."
"It's about children who want to travel, to explore and dream and make their dreams come true," she says.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

Why has De Bruyne struggled at Napoli as he returns to Man City?
- Published
Kevin de Bruyne's move to Napoli in 2025 was supposed to mark a continuation of his glittering decade at Manchester City as he approaches the twilight years of his career.
Instead, the midfielder, who is widely regarded as one of the stand-out players of his generation, has seen his time in Naples threaten to turn sour amid an early injury, friction with his team-mates and rumours of a January exit.
Napoli were Serie A champions in 2024-25 - the year before De Bruyne's arrival - but are currently languishing in eighth, while they sit 27th in the Champions League after a heavy 4-1 defeat at Porto earlier this month.
Belgium international De Bruyne lifted 16 trophies in his 10 years at City and is guaranteed a generous ovation when he returns to the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday but the highs of his time in England are in contrast to the struggles he is seemingly enduring in Italy.
"Not a lot I can say for the moment," said De Bruyne when asked about his future. "I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.
"There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening."
- De Bruyne's feelings for Man City will 'never change' 
  - Published12 hours ago
- Did Man City let De Bruyne leave too soon? 
  - Published14 October 2025
- Statue, Pep's tears & a missed sitter - De Bruyne's emotional farewell 
  - Published20 May 2025
'A bad show' in quarrel with team-mate
City decided not to renew De Bruyne's contract during the 2024-25 season and the player had the choice of heading to the US with Chicago Fire or staying in one of the top-five leagues in Europe.
The 35-year-old felt he could still cut it at the highest level but his first season at Napoli was heavily disrupted by a hamstring injury which kept him out for more than four months, restricting him to 21 appearances.
Napoli finished runners up to Inter Milan to lose their Serie A title and De Bruyne reportedly said, external he was "happy" manager Antonio Conte had departed in the summer as promises were not kept regarding the style of play.
But despite making his name as a technically gifted number 10, De Bruyne's role has been remodelled into a deeper holding one under Massimiliano Allegri in an ageing squad that has struggled this season.
In Porto, the fractures were clear to see, with De Bruyne having a heated on-field confrontation, external with striker Lorenzo Lucca and his team-mates were forced to step in to diffuse the situation.
The passionate side of De Bruyne's game was shown in Manchester too.
The midfielder shouted "shut up" at manager Pep Guardiola during a Champions League game against Real Madrid in 2023, and said "let me talk" when David Silva and Fernandinho were ushering him off the pitch at half-time shortly after he was booked against Napoli in 2017.
"Speaking about the pitch, De Bruyne is the best player this year at Napoli," Naples-based journalist Vincenzo Credendino tells BBC Sport. "The point is that the whole team is having difficulties.
"We saw that there is a problem, at least between De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca. Their acting was very, very clear and I think that in that time, the two of them were wrong.
"On one hand you cannot swear at another team-mate but on the other hand, De Bruyne reproached Lucca without encouraging him, so it was a bad show."
De Bruyne 'annoyed' by wife's misinterpreted quotes
De Bruyne has played 16 times for Napoli this season - contributing four goals and two assists - but his long-term future at the club remains unclear.
In September, De Bruyne's wife reportedly, external told a Belgian publication about their desire to move back home, saying "the sooner we get there, the better" as the player leads a "very restricted life" in Naples.
Asked if the quotes had been misinterpreted, De Bruyne said: "To be honest, I am pretty annoyed because if you read the article, that none of you have read, to understand what she said.
"I was away in Belgium and a lot of noise came and a lot of bad reactions to my wife and family. I saw pictures of my house, I don't think it is OK but it is what it is and some press created this in Italy. I don't know why.
"Nobody knows my life, you will never know. People who work with me are not allowed to say anything but obviously it is something that I take away and think about. It has not been nice for my wife or for my family."
It has led to interest from the Netherlands with PSV Eindhoven making a £1.67m offer to sign him in January, but the two clubs are apart in their valuations as Napoli want up to £6.7m, according to Credendino.
"Napoli fans were not happy [with the interview]," he says. "There are many fans that say, 'OK, you can leave if you want, we are not putting chains on anybody'."
Napoli boss Allegri left the door open for a January exit by saying in his pre-match news conference the pair had "not spoken" about his future and it is "down to the players and who wants to leave" when the transfer window opens.
Maresca has fond memories of 'top guy' De Bruyne
City manager Enzo Maresca was assistant to Pep Guardiola during the 2022-23 campaign in which De Bruyne helped the club to a Treble of trophies and the Italian has fond memories of the "fantastic season" they spent together.
"No doubt, [he is] one of the best," Maresca said of De Bruyne in his pre-match news conference. "Not only personally but also for the history of this club. In the last 10 years all the trophies the club achieved Kevin was here.
"He was an important player, a top guy, polite and for me it was a pleasure to work with him."
This is not the first time De Bruyne will be facing his former club with a reunion with City in the Champions League last season.
That trip turned out to be a bitterly unhappy experience, with De Bruyne substituted after 26 minutes following Giovanni di Lorenzo's red card in the 2-0 defeat.
The midfielder will be hoping for a better result on Tuesday as he aims to park his struggles for one evening.
City and Belgium winger Jeremy Doku said: "Kevin is someone that likes football. Even at this age he loves it.
"I don't have any doubts about his quality and I am sure everything will be fine in Napoli."

Being a tech reviewer, my entire phone gallery is filled with hundreds of random screenshots. It also holds important photos of family moments, my pet, and a few other travel memories.
Because of this, my phone usually runs out of storage quickly. It also has a habit of running out at the worst possible time, showing storage-full notifications when I am about to capture something important.
I usually back up my photos to Google Drive using the Google Photos app. However, the free Cloud storage is already full.
With every Gmail account, Google offers 15 GB of free storage, which is now shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos. That storage. I wouldn’t prefer paying for more cloud storage, so I needed something that I could use to back up without paying for the cloud, and that is easy to sync between devices without manually transferring
While searching for options and thinking of building it myself, I found Syncthing, a free, open-source app that automatically transfers photos taken on your phone to your Windows PC or Mac. This is especially useful because, with a recent MacBook upgrade, I had gigabytes of unused storage.
It’s so seamless that once you take a photo on your phone, it automatically appears on your Windows PC or Mac without connecting a cable. It requires no monthly subscription and removes the friction of manually backing up files. It is also a free, open-source tool and works over Wi-Fi.
The best part is that it comes with flexible options. You can choose where photos are stored, back them up to an external hard drive, and configure it to keep copies even when you delete photos from your phone.
However, setting up Syncthing might be complex for beginners. So I created this detailed, comprehensive guide to help you set up Syncthing to automatically back up photos taken on your Android phone to either Windows or Mac.
Table of Contents
Before you begin, here are the minimum requirements for these steps to work
- You need an Android phone (I used a OnePlus 13R with Android 16)
- Ensure both are on the same Wi-Fi network for the initial setup.
- You need a Windows 10 or 11 PC, or a Mac
- Make sure your Mac or Windows PC has enough free space to back up your phone photos.
Install Syncthing-Fork on your phone
Step 1: Open the Google Play Store, search for the Syncthing-Fork app, and tap Install.
Step 2: Once the app is installed, tap Open
Step 3: The app welcomes you with an onboarding screen. Click Continue
Step 4: Next, you need to grant storage permission to the app. Tap the Grant Storage Permission button
Step 5: You will be taken to the file access settings of the Syncthing-Fork app on your phone. From there, enable the toggle that says Allow Access to Manage All Files.
Step 6: Next, you need to grant permission for battery optimization for the Syncthing-Fork app
Step 7: Next, tap Allow
Step 8: On the next screen, the app asks for location permission; you can skip it. Tap on the Continue option.
Step 9: On the next screen, the app asks for Notifications. The app uses notifications to alert you about device connections for the sharing required in the form of notifications. So you need to allow the app to send notifications. It also keeps the app running in the background.
Step 10: Tap Grant permission, then tap Allow to allow app notifications.
Step 11: That’s it; your app onboarding and setup are complete. Next, you need to download Syncthing on Windows.
Install Syncthing on Windows
Step 12: On your Windows PC, open any browser and go to the Syncthing downloads page. Scroll down and tap on the Syncthing Windows Setup option.
Step 13: Next, under the Assets section, download the installer
Step 14: Once the download is complete, click Open file
Step 15: Similar to mobile, you need to go through multiple screens to set up on Windows. There isn’t much to do; just click Next on the first five pages.
Step 16: Now, enable or disable additional tasks based on your needs. I recommend enabling automatic syncing when logging on and starting syncing after installation. Also, create a desktop shortcut to the Syncthing configuration page so that it will be easy to access in the future
Step 17: Once selected, click Next
Step 18: Finally, click Install to install it on your Windows.
Step 19: If the Windows Firewall block prompt appears, click Yes to the firewall rule
Step 20: Next, click Allow to continue installation.
Step 21: Once installed, click Finish. Make sure you enable the Syncthing configuration page.
Step 22: The configuration page opens in your default browser. The default browser security blocks access to the page. No need to worry; to bypass it, click Advanced on the warning page.
Step 23: Next, click Continue to 127.0.0.1
Step 24: Next, choose whether to send usage reports. I would suggest No.
Step 25: Next, click OK on the password notice
Install Syncthing on a Mac
If you are using a Mac, you can also set up Syncthing on your Mac to sync photos between your Android phone and your Mac. Follow the process below.
Step 26: On a Mac, open the Syncthing downloads page. Here is the link. On the downloads page, under the downloads section, click on the Syncthing-Mac OS link.
Step 27: Next, scroll down and download the .dmg file
Step 28: Click Allow to download
Step 29: Once downloaded, drag Syncthing to the Applications folder.
Step 30: Next, Open Syncthing on your Mac and allow local network access
Step 31: It opens in the default browser. Select No when the Allow Anonymous Usage reporting prompt appears. That’s it.
Connect your phone and computer
Next, connect your phone to Windows or Mac to start sharing photos. The process is similar on both macOS and Windows. For this demonstration, I am using Windows.
Step 32: Next, open the Syncthing page on your computer and click Actions at the top right.
Step 33: Click Show ID
Step 34: Syncthing shows the computer’s device ID as text and as a QR code. Scan the QR code with your phone to copy the device ID.
Step 35: Open the Syncthing-Fork app on your Phone and tap the Devices tab
Step 36: Tap the Add Device button
Step 37: Tap the QR code button, then scan the QR code shown on the desktop using your phone camera. If Android asks for camera access, tap Allow.
Note: If the QR code isn’t working, you can type the ID instead, or click Copy on the computer, send the ID to yourself in a chat or email, then paste it here.
Step 38: Next, check the device ID. Remember that it should match the ID on your computer screen.
Step 39: Give the computer a name. Tap Name and type a name you will recognize, such as Windows PC or My Mac or something that you can recognize.
Step 40: Once done, tap the check mark
Step 41: Within a minute, a yellow New Device box appears on the Syncthing page on your computer, asking you to connect your phone. It also displays a name; cross-check that the name is your phone’s model (mine is CPH2691). Then, click Add Device.
Note: If nothing appears after a few minutes, ensure both devices are on the same Wi-Fi, then reload the page. On a Mac, check that you have allowed local network access.
Step 42: Next, enter the phone name and click Save. You can enter any name that is easy to recognize, similar to how you name your desktop on your Android phone.
Step 43: Next, open the Syncthing-Fork app on your phone and check that the phone says Up to Date.
Share the Camera folder from your phone
Step 44: Next, choose the folder you want to back up. On the phone, tap the Folders tab, then tap the Add Folder button at the top right (the folder with a plus sign).
Step 45: Type the folder name. In this case, I am naming it a camera.
Step 46: Next, tap Directory to choose the folder on your phone.
Step 47: Android’s folder picker opens. If you want to back up photos from the camera, tap DCIM; this is the folder where phone cameras save photos.
Step 48: Next, tap the Camera folder.
Step 49: Finally, tap the Use this folder option
Step 50: Next, allow Syncthing to access the folder. Tap the Allow option.
Step 51: Next, under Devices, turn on the switch next to your computer’s name. This shares the folder with it.
Step 52: Next, choose the Folder Type. By default, it says Send & Receive. It means it also copies the images from your desktop to your phone. Keep it if you want to sync photos between both devices, or select Send Only in the next steps. Tap Send & Receive to open the list.
Note: Don’t skip this step. If you set up Send & Receive, deleting the backup copy on the computer also deletes the photo on your phone. So carefully choose an option.
Step 53: Open the list
Step 54: Tap Send Only
Step 55: Finally, tap Finish
Step 56: Next, tap the check mark to finish; remember that it shows as Unshared until the computer accepts it.
Accept the folder on your computer
Step 57: Now, on the computer, a yellow New Folder box appears once again. Click Add.
Step 58: Choose where to save the photos. In Folder Path, type where the backup should go. I used my Pictures folder. For instance, you can type the path: C:\Users\YourName\Pictures\Phone Backup. You can also save the photos on an external drive. You can enter the external drive path here.
Step 59: Next, click File Versioning. Make sure the photos you delete on your phone stay on the computer
Step 60:In the tab, click No File Versioning to open the list
Step 61: Here, choose the Trash Can File Versioning option. This means that when a photo is deleted on the phone, Syncthing moves the computer’s copy into a hidden .stversions folder inside your backup folder instead of deleting it.
Step 62: Next, under Clean out after option, set Keep Clean Out to 0. Zero means forever, so deleted photos are never removed from the computer.
Step 63: Next, click the Advanced tab.
Step 64:Under Folder Type, click Send & Receive to open the list
Step 65: Choose Receive Only. The computer now only receives from the phone and doesn’t transfer photos from your desktop to your phone. This is simialr to send only settings we enabled on the phone.
Step 66: Finally, click Save. Scroll down inside the window if you don’t see it, or switch back to the General tab.
Check that it works
Step 67: Next, your phone will start transferring photos to your computer. You will see an up-to-date status as a green dot next to the folder under Remote Devices. My 224 photos and videos (3.5 GB) took about two minutes over Wi-Fi. Keep both devices awake and on the same Wi-Fi until it finishes.
Step 68: You can also see the status on mobile too. On the phone, the Camera folder also says Up to Date and shows how many files it has sent.
Step 69: You can also test it by taking a photo with your camera app, then open Syncthing-Fork again. Within a few seconds, the folder shows the new photo’s name as the last file sent.
Step 70: To open the backup photos on Windows, open File Explorer and click Pictures in the left sidebar. On a Mac, open Finder and go to your Pictures folder.
Step 71: You can see a Phone Backup folder. Open it.
Step 72: You can find all backup images here.
Back up only on Wi-Fi
If you have limited data, make sure the phone backs up on Wi-Fi only, so it never uses your mobile data. Follow the steps to back up images only using the Wifi.
Step 73: In Syncthing-Fork, tap the menu button at the top left.
Step 74: Tap Settings
Step 75: Tap Run Conditions
Step 76: Keep Run on Wi-Fi on and leave Run on metered Wi-Fi off, so a large backup never runs over your phone’s hotspot
Step 77: Also, make sure Run on mobile data is off
Step 78: This is Optional: You can also enable backup only while charging, so it won’t affect your battery life; these services need to run in the background.
Automatically Back Up Your Photos Without the Cloud
This is how you can back up your photos from your phone to a Mac or Windows PC. This is especially useful if you have limited storage on your phone and don’t want to pay for cloud storage.
If you have free space on your Mac or Windows device, photos will be backed up automatically. The best part is that Syncthing also lets you back up photos to an external device connected to your computer, so all your photos are backed up without affecting your computer storage.
However, there are a few things to note. For the backup to work, make sure your phone and computer are on the same Wi-Fi, and that the Syncthing-Fork app shows a green dot at the top.
If you are using a Mac, allow local network access in System Settings (Privacy & Security > Local Network). If the backup stops after a while, the most likely reason is that Android has paused the app. To run the app again, open Settings, go to App Settings, and select the Syncthing-Fork app. In the battery settings, choose Unrestricted.
I have also noticed that sometimes the folder is out of sync on my computer. This is most likely because of the limited storage space on my Mac. To fix this, free up space and choose a folder on another drive on a Mac or Windows. If you are facing any other issues, comment below, and I will be happy to help you.

Fact Check
To determine the veracity of these claims, we ran a reverse image search on a few of the keyframes, which led us to a video uploaded by ATN Bangla, a Bangladeshi media outlet.
The video was uploaded on YouTube on May 20, 2026. The caption reads: “ঘর না ভাঙার জন্য জানালা দিয়ে আকুতি জানাচ্ছে বস্তিবাসী | Eviction Chaos | Mirpur |” (Slumdwellers plead against demolition of their homes from windows)
Comparisons between keyframes from the viral video and the ATN Bangla report shows that they are visuals from the same incident. See below:
Further, a keyword search in Bengali led us to multiple reports of an eviction drive in Mirpur around May 20. Ekattor.tv reported that slum dwellers clashed with police during an eviction drive in the Bauniabad slum area in Mirpur.
Thus, to sum up, the viral video of a demolition drive is not from Tripura, India. It is originally from Mirpur in Bangladesh and is being falsely circulated as footage of demolition of Muslim homes in India.

Srinagar, Nov 24: The cold wave tightened its grip over Kashmir as Srinagar and Pahalgam recorded the coldest night of this season so far, with night temperatures dropping sharply compared to yesterday.
An official of MeT said that Srinagar recorded a minimum temperature of minus 1.6°C, a sharp fall from minus 0.4°C recorded yesterday, which was the previous lowest of the season. The night temperature in the summer capital is now 1.3 degrees below normal.
Pahalgam, the famous tourist resort, recorded a minimum of minus 4.6°C, breaking its previous season's lowest of minus 3.8°C recorded on November 17 and again yesterday. The temperature there is 2.5 degrees below normal.
Qazigund also witnessed a further dip, recording minus 2.0°C against minus 1.6°C yesterday, while Kukernag recorded minus 0.1°C against 1.5°C yesterday.

Multiple myeloma patients have been able to utilize a surge of powerful new immunotherapies in recent years, including CAR-T therapy and bispecific antibodies like Carvykti and Tecvayli from Johnson & Johnson. But myeloma, a blood cancer, can often develop resistance against these treatments, leading to relapse.
A new biotech called Caronilex is developing a next generation CAR-T therapy that may help circumvent that resistance, and the therapy’s promising safety profile could make it a potential candidate for use against autoimmune diseases as well.
Researchers showed the therapy, called TriPRIL, was able to reduce or eliminate signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, many of whom had prior CAR-T therapy, in a small, early phase trial published last week in The Lancet.

Jammu- The life and supreme sacrifice of the 16th-century farmer-saint Baba Jitto conveyed the message that a man’s greatest strength was truth and self-respect, Jammu and Kashmir Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha said while inaugurating the 10-day annual Jhiri Mela on Tuesday.
Speaking at the mela on the outskirts of Jammu city, Sinha called for farmers’ empowerment, preservation of Dogra cultural heritage and collective efforts to build a developed, prosperous and inclusive Jammu and Kashmir.
One of the biggest farmers’ fairs in northern India, Jhiri Mela registers an annual footfall of 10 to 12 lakh devotees, mainly farmers from the Jammu region, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh and Haryana, who arrive to commemorate the sacrifice of Baba Jitto, who laid down his life resisting exploitation of a feudal landlord nearly 500 years ago.
The lieutenant governor paid tributes to Baba Jitto and his daughter Bua Kauri, describing the annual fair as a celebration of faith, devotion and love, besides a symbol of the region’s cultural heritage and collective consciousness.
He said visiting the Jhiri Mela every year had become like a sacred pilgrimage for him, offering a unique sense of belonging and spiritual experience.
Describing Baba Jitto’s life as an immortal saga of truth, courage and justice, Sinha said the legendary farmer was an ordinary man with extraordinary ideals and character.
When the zamindar demanded an unjust share from the crop he had cultivated through hard work, Baba Jitto refused to bow before injustice, making it clear that a farmer’s labour, sweat and rights must be respected, Sinha said.
“His struggle was not merely for his crop; it was a struggle for the rights of every hardworking individual and for the dignity and respect to which every farmer is entitled,” he said.
Sinha said the real tribute to the sacrifices of Baba Jitto and Bua Kauri would be to build a society where no farmer was compelled to fight alone for his rights and dignity.
“This cannot be the sole responsibility of the government or any individual official. We need a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to establish such a system,” he said.
Emphasising the importance of agriculture in India’s civilisation and cultural heritage, the lieutenant governor said farmers had for centuries fulfilled people’s food requirements and also enriched its traditions.
Referring to initiatives under the Holistic Agriculture Development Programme, Sinha said efforts were underway to transform Jammu and Kashmir’s agriculture, horticulture and dairy sectors.
Expansion of storage facilities, grading and packaging units, along with crop diversification, were among the measures aimed at enhancing farmers’ income, he said.
He said policy changes and new schemes were being implemented to move agriculture beyond traditional cultivation towards an integrated system that would enable farmers to produce better-quality crops at lower costs and secure remunerative prices for their produce.
Sinha stressed the need to equip farmers, particularly small and marginal farmers, with modern technology and scientific knowledge, enabling them to respond to changing market demands.
Agriculture and food sectors offered immense opportunities for employment generation, particularly for youth, he said, urging young people to use their talent, technical knowledge and innovation to make farming more productive and profitable.
Sinha also highlighted the importance of promoting millet cultivation, saying a campaign had been initiated in September to bring more farming families under the initiative.
With farmers facing increasing economic pressures and declining groundwater levels, he stressed the need for better water management and climate-resilient agricultural practices.
Millet crops could play an important role in this direction, he said, adding that sustainable farming practices were essential to address the challenges posed by climate change.

The Oct. 30 sell-off on Wall Street ignited doubts about whether the huge investment in artificial intelligence will earn the returns investors expect. Those concerns have persisted, with even Anthropic’s initial public offering on Nov. 19 failing to halt the broader tech sell-off.
If the AI bubble bursts (assuming it is a bubble) and takes some medical AI companies down with it, health care will face a serious problem. A health AI company’s market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things. If funding runs out because investors decide to walk away, hospitals could lose the chance to complete evaluations of potentially useful medical tools. Giving up on medical AI would be a financial decision — but it may look like a clinical one. The financial markets will decide which medical AI technologies survive before hospitals have had the opportunity to establish whether these technologies benefit patients.
If investment in medical AI technologies experiences a sharp fall, companies will lose funding, forcing them to reduce their activities or stop supporting their technologies completely. The impact of such an event could be felt across the entire health care system: Companies are developing AI tools ranging from interpreting scans to identifying patients at risk of developing medical complications due to treatments. Clearly, some of these tools will eventually prove useful in clinical settings, while others will not. The point is that neither an impressive AI tool nor a falling stock price tells us which AI tool deserves a place within the health care system.
To illustrate this point, let’s take cancer clinical trials as an example. In one study, researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Emory University examined electronic medical records using AI systems to identify patients who may meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in clinical trials. Determining eligibility involves a demanding manual screening process examining things like tumor characteristics, previous treatments, and lab results.
Interestingly, the findings revealed that using the AI system improved accuracy of assessing enrollment eligibility for the cancer clinical trials, but it didn’t reduce screening time significantly. It’s not clear whether such improvements would lead to an increase in patient enrollment. In another study, researchers in Australia from the Victorian Cancer Registry at Cancer Council Victoria and Monash Health utilized an AI system to analyze pathology reports with the goal of identifying patients eligible for enrollment in cancer clinical trials. The AI system was able to successfully identify more eligible patients when compared to standard screening procedures, but ultimately utilizing the AI system didn’t result in increased patient enrollment into the clinical trials. The study didn’t establish why, which brings to focus that screening improvements doesn’t necessarily lead to higher clinical trial participation.
Taken together, these two studies illustrate the potential utility of AI systems in health care. They also make clear that improvements are needed before such AI systems become an integral part of health care system.
Based on my experience in senior leadership in oncology drug development, I think that medical AI systems should be developed and evaluated based on the general framework that we currently apply in the research and development of new innovative cancer drugs. What I mean by that is when it comes to the AI systems promising early results are important, but it is critical not to celebrate a success too early. Ultimately the value of the AI system depends on whether it eventually benefits the patient. We need to determine whether using a particular medical AI leads to better clinical decisions, better patient identification, reduction of unnecessary work, or improved access to treatment.
If the AI bubble bursts, these success metrics could become more difficult to achieve. Companies developing medical AI systems may lose their funding, downsize, or even withdraw support for their products. Worst of all, they could close before hospitals have finished assessing their AI systems.
Clinicians could, of course, return to doing their work as they did before the introduction of the medical AI system. But that would mean the health care system loses the opportunity (and valuable data) to determine whether such medical AI tools could have offered meaningful improvements and patient impact.
The clear answer is not to try and save each struggling AI company, but to make sure that hospitals and health care system are able to complete their assessments of medical AI systems even if a given company reduces its services or even goes out of business.
Before adopting such medical AI systems, hospitals should establish clear success criteria and build systems in place to track, store, and ensure that the research data generated about the medical AI systems are available for independent evaluation even if the AI company supporting such a system no longer exists. Such plans would make sure that any financial difficulties that may affect a relevant AI company would not prevent the hospital or the health care system from determining whether a given medical AI system could benefit patients.
David Adler is chief scientific officer at the PATHORA Institute of Pathology & Tissue Medicine, with more than 15 years of experience in oncology research and drug development.

On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.
SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).
Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.
Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.
“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”
Millions allegedly harmed
Millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.
“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a press release.
States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.
Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”
“Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.
SpaceX responds
Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the company has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety said that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.
“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”
However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises users how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.
Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok users, states alleged.
Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”
In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”
“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”
Grok CSAM, NCII may trigger steep fines
It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”
As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.
“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.
Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users.
“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.
Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.
“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.
AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.
The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.
The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.
Carr: California rules “designed for a bygone era”
“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”
If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.
“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.
California says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

Quick Answer
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia is about more than personal misconduct. It raises serious questions about conflicts of interest, abuse of power, and Silicon Valley’s habit of excusing tech leaders. His departure sends a vital message: no amount of genius, wealth, or market success should place anyone above accountability.
So Jensen Huang will not be returning to Nvidia, in spite of a groundswell of support. And though it might shock some tech bros, I think it is the best thing that could have happened to tech.
The tech world witnessed one of its most dramatic unravelings this month, perhaps the most significant one in years, if not decades. All was going smoothly; AI was still the sun the tech world was revolving around, and one of the biggest planets revolving around it was Nvidia. The company was not just in on living, breathing, and thriving on AI development but at the center of bettering AI for others, as it manufactured AI chips.
When current affairs become… well, current affairs
It all came crashing down when a report was published in The New York Times, revealing news of an affair. This was not the run-of-the-mill gossip that’s seen in the scandal section in tabloids, but news that changed the trajectory of Nvidia and possibly AI.
Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, was found to be having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (unrelated, although having the same surname), a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company. Alice was suspected of being a Chinese spy by US intelligence. Megaspeed was one of the major buyers of Nvidia’s AI chips, and, as per reports, it diverted chips worth USD 2 billion to China against regulations, although both Megaspeed and Nvidia deny any wrongdoing.
Following the news, A LOT went down. Huang seemed to swing into damage control and issued an apology for the affair, promising cooperation with an investigation into it. The tech world thought the worst was over. After all, what could make this worse? Then the New York Times, on 11 November, released a report citing another extramarital affair. This time it was reported that he was in a relationship with Nvidia’s Vice President of Health Care, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to Huang. After trying to save face and his 41-year-long marriage (Jensen Huang is married to Lori Huang), Huang had to resign and leave his post as CEO at Nvidia on 12 November.
But this is not the story of a person’s personal slip-ups, or the extra-marital affair story that much of the media is making it to be. It is actually much bigger than that.
It’s not about infidelity, but about power and misconduct
While Huang has received a fair deal of criticism for his conduct, he has received a lot of support too, especially from Silicon Valley, where it seems that when there is a tech billionaire in question, the rules that apply to the rest of the world cease to apply to them. If you build an important enough product, accumulate billions of Dollars, and build some political connections, what would otherwise be a big no-no suddenly becomes negotiable, and the boundaries around right and wrong start to get hazy.
Affairs and flings are nothing new to the world of tech in particular, or the world of celebrities in general, but this case is more than just a personal lapse of judgment. Had Huang’s affair(s) been something that had happened outside of the workplace or if he had fallen for someone who had nothing to do with tech (an actress, an influencer, a trapeze artiste, et al.), this would have been an entirely different conversation. But his intimate relations with his employee and a customer – and the fact that we are being asked to overlook them – shine a light on what might be wrong with the inherent culture at not just Nvidia but in Silicon Valley.
While most concerns have revolved around Alice Huang being a Chinese spy and sensitive AI technology crossing borders, allegations which have not yet been proved, what is clear beyond doubt is that Huang misused his position as the CEO of one of the biggest companies in the world, on both the client and employee side.
In both of his affairs, Huang was the person of power, with Alice Huang and Kimberly Powell. The client in question bought billions of dollars’ worth of AI chips from Nvidia, and given her intimate relationship revelation with Huang, it would be difficult to rule out that the business deals made between the two were in no way influenced by the relationship. We are not even getting to the part of Alice Huang being a Chinese spy, and whether she managed to get sensitive information and AI chips from Jensen Huang for China, which would give China the AI leverage it needs to get ahead of the US in the AI race. Even if she was “just another client,” does it not still remain a bother that a person who has been hailed as a tech demi-god could not control his urges long enough to get through business? Similarly, his second affair with a senior employee working at Nvidia who directly reported to him, and, as per reports, was promptly promoted during her time at Nvidia, does bring up some very serious questions about preferential treatment, conflict of interest, and company power dynamics.
This is not about Huang’s infidelity, but his ability to make sound decisions. A lot of the evidence suggests that in a situation where he could misuse his position of power, he did. It was not just his moral compass that was compromised, but his professional one too. The fact that this happened, and that the former Nvidia CEO has still received a lot of support, not only raises concerns about the culture at Nvidia, but also about the overall priorities of Silicon Valley.
When the stock market decides where to draw the line
Since Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, a number of executives, tech CEOs, and even the US President himself have come out in support of him. Media channels have had extensive discussions on the matter, and many have marked the (so far) two affairs as a “personal lapse of judgment” and think Huang’s potential as a tech genius outweighs his failings. Elon Musk has compared his exit as “it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak”, while other leaders like Sam Altman, Steven Chen, Tim Sweeney and many more have pushed for his comeback. President Donald Trump has said he would “not mind” seeing Huang reinstated as CEO, and Musk has even offered to hire him.
Now, there is no doubt that Jensen Huang is a genius who has built one of the most important businesses in the world of tech. Many fear that without him, Nvidia would tank, and this would have a devastating impact on AI. However, since the reports of his affairs have come out and his resignation, Nvidia’s stock has taken a nosedive, and so have many other AI stocks. In fact, many are predicting that Huang’s exit might burst the AI bubble, which, for obvious reasons, is way worse for the tech world in general than any lapse in professional and moral code of conduct. Accountability seems to count for little as long as the stock market is doing well.
Time to take the Tech God pedestal away?
Given this groundswell of support, the easy decision for Nvidia would perhaps have been to let Jensen Huang walk back in as if nothing happened and sit back and see the share prices spike. It actually seemed likely, and Huang himself had posted on X (where he was given a free blue tick by Elon Musk), offering to make a comeback if the board considered it would be in the best interest of the company. However, on 18 November, Nvidia ruled out the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. And while this led to groans of disappointment from many of the tech bros, we actually think it was the right call to take.

While a company has responsibilities towards its shareholders, it also has to keep its employees and clients in mind. Share prices cannot be used as an automatic defense against misconduct, especially at the highest level. Unfortunately, over the past few decades, tech brilliance has been placed on a pedestal, giving a handful of people immunity from general human misconduct. Bouts of bad temper, abusive behavior, and so much more are often turned a blind eye to because a person is perceived as a “Tech God,” a person who is part of the genius crowd that is building a better, brighter future for us all. But recent times have revealed that many of these tech gods whom we have trusted, and largely exempted from strict governance or interference, cannot even follow simple, basic rules that govern mere mortals. And these handful of people, who cannot even follow the basics, are sitting in boardrooms and are now deciding the future of billions of people, even those who have not opted for an AI-laden future or are not even aware of what AI is.
Jensen Huang’s conduct – and the support he has received – now raises the question of whether the people we were told are tech geniuses are as reliable and trustworthy as the narrative around them has painted them out to be. Or are they just a bunch of power-hungry, wealth-accumulating techies who have way too much autonomy for comfort?
The Huang affair (pun intended) marks an important phase in modern tech. While we still do not know how it will all end – there are endless conspiracy theories doing the rounds – we do hope it will teach many in the tech world not to turn a blind eye to “personal and professional misconduct,” just because a person is seen as a genius and is perceived to be good for the world in general and the stock market in particular.

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

New leaks reveal the iPhone 18e will have a redesigned camera plateau
We've also got further confirmation the iPhone Air 2 will have a second camera.
Apple seems to have adopted a new strategy for the iPhone launch, splitting it into two phases. After launching the premium iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo in September, Apple is preparing new versions of the lower-priced models — and it looks like they'll look a lot more like the more expensive iPhones. CAD images of the new iPhone 18e seen by Engadget show a redesigned camera bump on the back of the phone, similar to the one on the Pro models. The images come from a source familiar with Apple's supply chain who who had previously shared accurate tips on the colors of the iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro before they were announced.
The current iPhone 17e doesn't have a camera bump — instead, the lens has a small protrusion and sits flush against the back of the phone, with the microphone and LED flash also embedded in cutouts directly in the rear glass. But according to CAD images seen by Engadget, Apple appears to be considering changing that with the iPhone 18e. The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone. It's somewhat similar to the camera module on the M5 iPad Pro (which you can see in the image below).
Interestingly, it seems that the iPhone 18e will be the only model to feature this new camera plateau. The same files include the CADs for the base iPhone 18 and the iPhone Air 2, both of which are expected to launch alongside the 18e next spring. Did Japan just experience its first baby bump in a decade?
For years, it has been the poster child for low fertility, with births falling every year since 2015. But in the first six months of 2026, there was an unexpected uptick: Births of Japanese nationals rose 0.4%, or 1,379 more than in the same period in 2025. Some supporters of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi were quick to claim this as more evidence that she’s restoring the country to its former glory; others noted that, since she took office only in October 2025, all these babies were conceived under her predecessor.
Coming in the year of the hinoe uma, the Fire Horse of the Chinese zodiac, it seems impressive. The last such year, 1966, put a massive dent in births thanks to a bygone superstition that girls born in the year of the Fire Horse made poor wives .
But it’s certainly no sea change. In fact, the blip might be over. Births in Japan are closely linked to marriages and those are down again this year after rising for the past two years in a rebound from Covid, which suppressed encounters of all kinds. The increase is also tiny next to the more than 14% jump in births next door in South Korea.
However, there is a win hiding in plain sight in Japan’s data. As the earliest industrialized country to suffer falling births, Japan remains synonymous with the problem worldwide. But in recent years almost all of the developed world has followed, including several of its neighbors, where the decline has been faster and steeper. As a result, Japan is now the surprising outlier among East Asia’s richest economies. It has the highest fertility rate of the group, at 1.14. All of its peers have fallen below 1. A rate of around 2.1 is needed to hold population levels steady.
For years, many assumed that Japan’s low figure was the floor. Now the obvious question is what kept the fertility rate from tumbling below one — and are there lessons for the world in what looks like, if not success, then at least a lesser degree of failure?
As the trend of falling births spreads beyond Asia, it’s important to find an answer. One analysis comparing only Japan and South Korea noted that Japanese women marry younger , perhaps due in part to Korea’s expensive weddings, which traditionally include a large lump-sum housing deposit. In both countries, children are overwhelmingly born in wedlock.
Another paper, published this year, found that the two countries mirrored each other for years but began to diverge in the early 2000s. That gap stems largely from a drop in births to Korean women in their late 20s, something that did not happen in Japan, and which the authors link to a larger number of young Korean men not employed. In other words, the longer young people have to scrape by, the more fertile years are lost. That is intuitively sound, though it doesn’t tell the whole story: Singapore marries at around the same age as Japan, yet the city-state’s fertility rate is just 0.87.
Takaichi supporters are jumping the gun by claiming this as a win. The prime minister herself has declared no such victory; she has described population decline as a “quietly advancing national crisis,” and is compiling a comprehensive strategy to tackle it. It’s also a very regional victory: The gain is entirely due to Tokyo, which Governor Yuriko Koike attributes to her generous support policies, but which may simply reflect that young families who once would have moved to leafier environs outside of the capital are staying put instead.
Japan should take the win nonetheless. It's policies are unlikely to stem the downward trend in births, but look at what they have done: The share of working women who stay in their jobs after a first child has risen from about 50% to almost 70%. Daycare waiting lists are largely a thing of the past. Men taking parental leave has soared from under 3% in 2015 to over 50% today. Japan has set itself a frankly unachievable fertility goal of 1.8; measured against that, any policy will fail. Compare that with other countries in the same situation, however, and things start to look a little better. Even Tokyo’s rate, which is the lowest in Japan, is 50% higher than Seoul’s.
Sixty years ago, the Fire Horse scared off a quarter of Japan’s births, yet this year it barely registered. One superstition about babies has finally died. The next should be the idea that the country is the world’s demographic basket case.

The vote was to move the draft resolution out of the Third Committee of the U.N. on Social, Humanitarian and Cultural Issues. It passed, with 175 countries voting in favor of it. Six countries abstained: the U.S., saying the mentions of “sexual and reproductive health” and "safe abortion" were "disappointing"; Russia; Argentina; Belarus; Burkina Faso and Cameroon. One country, Somalia, voted against it. The draft resolution will now go to the U.N.'s General Assembly Plenary for adoption.
In November 2026, a rumor spread that the U.S. had joined Russia in not voting for a United Nations resolution meant to protect women and girls against violence.
The claim made the rounds on social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. On X, a post shared the supposed image of the voting board showing that the U.S. and Russia were among six countries abstaining and that Somalia was the sole country to vote against it (archived):
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers searched the website seeking information on the rumor.
The claim was true. On Nov. 17, the U.S., Russia, Argentina, Belarus, Burkina Faso and Cameroon all abstained from voting to push a draft resolution that sought to protect women and girls against all types of gender-based violence out of the Third Committee of the U.N. on Social, Humanitarian and Cultural Issues. This was according to a summary of the session published on the U.S. website. Somalia was the sole country to vote against the resolution.
It is worth noting that this text was not final as of this writing. Instead, the Third Committee passed the draft resolution to the General Assembly Plenary for adoption.
Why the U.S. and Russia abstained
The specific draft resolution, on the "Intensification of efforts to prevent and eliminate all forms of violence against women and girls: gender-related killings of women and girls" (also referred to as "L.16" in the 81st session of the Third Committee, or C. 3), was the topic of debate during the committee meeting that led to the vote.
In its explanation, the U.S. cited the mentions of "sexual and reproductive health" and "safe abortion" as the reason for abstaining to vote, calling them "disappointing":
It is disappointing to see the controversial terminology of "sexual and reproductive health" and the notion of "safe abortion" in operative paragraph 4 of this resolution. The United States believes in legal protections for the unborn. There is no international "right to abortion," whether under that name or under other terms like "sexual and reproductive health." Nor is there any duty on the part of States to finance or facilitate abortion.
It is true that the revised draft resolution mentions sexual and reproductive health in the context of educating girls about it and in the context of enhancing access it to it for women and girls (pages 7 and 8 of the PDF). The text also seeks to guarantee access to "safe abortion where such services are permitted by national law" (Page 8 of the PDF). The two sections that include these mentions are in the fourth paragraph of the draft resolution.
During the debate, the representative for the U.S. said about a separate resolution that her country supports "the overall goal of the text," but that "the meaning of sexual and reproductive health must be determined by reference to national laws."
"The United States reaffirms its position that gender can only be defined by biological sex as male and female," she added.
In addition, the committee session summary said, the representative for the Russian Federation introduced a series of amendments to L.16 to "promote women and girls' role in the family and delete language that would reduce protections for them, including 'gender-based violence' and 'intimate partner violence.'"
The summary of the session also gave more details about what the resolution would do:
By the text, the Assembly would strongly condemn all forms of violence against women and girls, online and offline, particularly gender-related killings, including femicide, and urge States to take measures to eliminate such violence against women in all their diversity.
For further reading, Snopes confirmed the U.S. was the only nation to vote against the U.N. Commission on the Status of Women's agreed conclusions during the commission's 70th session in March 2026.

GTA 6 is the biggest PlayStation launch of all time
PS5 players logged 683 million hours of cumulative gameplay over its launch weekend.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest PlayStation launch in history, Sony Interactive Entertainment has revealed. It has set the record not just for the PS5, but for all five console generations released over the past three decades "across multiplayer, free-to-play and single-player titles." SIE's Tim Turi has announced that for the game's opening weekend ending on November 22, players logged 683 million hours of cumulative gameplay. Each player spent an average of 17.4 hours playing over those first four days.
Based on Sony's announcement, GTA 6 seems to have boosted PS5 sales, as the company saw the biggest number of new PS5 connections on a single day since the console was launched, outside of year-end holidays. The company said it was the first game accessed on 70 percent of all newly purchased and connected PS5 consoles over its launch weekend.
Overall, more than 39 million unique players booted up the game on the console. Sony didn't elaborate on how many of those players accessed the game over its launch weekend on a PS5 Pro. But it's worth noting that the company is experiencing a PS5 Pro shortage, and GTA 6's release was expected to make it even worse.
Rockstar Games released GTA 6 on November 19 for the PS5 and the Xbox Series X|S, 13 years after the launch of the franchise's fifth installment. It also did well and quickly became one of the most played games on the Xbox. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, announced that day one retail sales reached $3.79 billion, calling it the "biggest entertainment launch in history." Despite the game's success, its developers are still apparently worried about the possibility of being impacted by layoffs currently sweeping across studios in the industry.

Following a terrorist attack on November 11 at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district, a video went viral on social media with the claim that retired Indian Army officer and journalist Pravin Sawhney described Indian military and counter-terrorism drives in the valley as “false flag operations”.
Social media users claimed that Sawhney said that operations against the Kulgam attack, the Balakot airstrikes, and Operation Sindoor were orchestrated for political gains.
X user @RedDeFactoIND (Red Vanguard) shared the viral clip, which shows an interview conducted by The Wire. (Archive)
𝗘𝘅-𝗔𝗿𝗺𝘆 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗕𝗼𝗺𝗯𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹🚨: Pravin Sawhney in Recent Interview for Wire said, “Another false flag, just like Pulwama and Pahalgam,This is a pattern”
Indian journalists and influencers are now openly questioning the government’s narrative.
The voices from within are getting louder.
#CRPFSoldiers #CRPFCampAttack #kulgamattack #Kulgam #KulgamTerrorAttack
— Red Vanguard (@RedDeFactoIND) November 12, 2026
In the viral clip, the interviewer can first be heard saying (translated from Hindi): “Sushant, I want to know from you…the theme of your latest essay is the politicisation of army…During the false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, the way the Bharatiya Janata Party used the military for political gains. My second question is that today while there is a war-like situation in the world…is testing the Pralay missile is an indication of a new false flag operation?”
“On one side China is occupying [Indian land], on the other there are CJP protests…Rahul Gandhi…,” the interviewer goes on to say before his voice is abruptly cut off.
The interviewee then seems to respond with, “Two things are very clear. One, for false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, Operation Sindoor was launched but the Indian army failed. Second, my answers are within your questions.”
Several other users on X and Facebook also circulated the same video with identical claims. Among them were X handles @KaurUdhoke3 and @HinduReformer, along with multiple public Facebook pages focusing on South Asian geopolitics. [Archives: 1, 2]
Fact Check
A closer look at the viral video reveals noticeable lip-sync discrepancies and an unnatural, monotonous cadence in the voices of both men in the interview, which are salient features of AI-generated audio manipulation.
Further, columnist and strategic affairs expert Sushant Singh has been misidentified in the viral video as Pravin Sawhney. In the viral video itself, the interviewer refers to the interviewee as Sushant, and not Pravin. Below is an image of Sawhney, who does not appear in the viral clip.
On November 13, Singh himself took to X to debunk the clip, clarifying that the video was AI-generated, and highlighting that users had also misidentified him.
This is AI generated video of an old interview, which completely fabricates my conversation with @ashubh. This Pakistan-made AI video clip not only gets my identity wrong but creates what was never said.
The original full interview of March 2025 is here: https://t.co/Y6teNLJDfg
— Sushant Singh (@SushantSin) November 13, 2026
In his post, Singh also attached a link to the original YouTube interview from which the visuals were taken. Alt News examined the original video uploaded on The Wire’s official YouTube channel in March 2025.
Comparing the viral clip with the March 2025 interview confirms that the visual frames, including Singh’s attire, the background setting, and lighting, are identical. However, the audio track in the viral clip has been changed using AI.
In the original interview, Singh makes no mention of Kulgam, Pulwama, Balakot, or any ‘false flag operations’. Instead, he is heard discussing civil-military relations and institutional oversight.
To sum up, a manipulated video of journalist and strategic affairs analyst Sushant Singh is circulating on social media with users misidentifying him as journalist and FORCE editor Pravin Sawhney. The claim that the speaker in the video termed India’s counter-terrorism measures in Kulgam and Pulwama ‘false flag operations’ is false as well.
