“A viral video has recently come to our attention. While we cannot verify its authenticity at this moment, the remarks recorded in it feature four grave allegations: claims of widespread religious conversions, an accusation that a…principal is involved in conversion activities; an allegation regarding a person wearing a saffron sari coming to a school; and a sweeping insinuation that even though the British have left, Christian missionary school administrators continue to carry a ‘British mentality,” read a statement by the representatives.
“At a time when vigilantes and hooligans are taking the law into their own hands across various districts — vandalising and launching brutal attacks on peaceful prayer meetings under the false pretext of forced conversions and desperately trying to build a fabricated narrative — the Christian community is both shocked and deeply angered to hear such an incredible, hate-mongering and aggressive speech from a usually balanced and sagacious leader like Samik Babu,” it added.
Speaking to Alt News, Moloy D’Costa, secretary of the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools and vicar-general of the Roman Catholic archdiocese of Calcutta, said, “The comments made by Mr Bhattacharya are vague. Every school has its own dress code, and there is no universal colour code. The authorities should either provide evidence or identify specific institutions and take appropriate action against them, rather than making general statements that vilify an entire community and a network of institutions.”
D’Costa also pointed out, “Several leaders in the party attended Christian missionary institutions; have they converted to Christianity? Converting to Christianity is a lengthy process. Simply visiting a church or sprinkling water is not part of that process. Accusations of forced conversion are being made from all sides, yet not a single case has been reported where anyone has been proven guilty of such actions.”
National Christian Council (NCC) state general secretary Arpan Rana strongly condemned Bhattacharya’s remarks on Christian missionary institutions, stating that “sweeping allegations without evidence” risk fostering suspicion and hostility towards the Christian community.
Rana told Alt News that Christian institutions were primarily invested in “education, humanitarian service, moral development and nation-building, not forced religious conversion,” adding that students from diverse religious backgrounds have studied in these institutions without abandoning their faiths. “Thousands of students from Hindu, Muslim, Christian and other communities have received education from these institutions while preserving their respective religious identities,” he said.
He also termed the portrayal of Indian Christianity as a legacy of British colonialism ‘historically misleading’, noting that Christianity existed in India long before colonial rule. “We expect scholarly arguments backed by evidence, not broad political claims. If any institution is found to engage in unlawful conversion, we support impartial investigations, but the entire Christian community should not be collectively accused,” he added.
Akin to other Christian associations in the state, Rana, on behalf of the NCC, urged the state government to protect Christian institutions, churches and communities, and ensure they can celebrate Christmas peacefully.
As precautionary measures, the BCP also advised churches to inform local authorities about upcoming programmes, establish a community alert system, ring church bells thrice if suspicious groups enter church premises, immediately notify police, and install CCTV cameras at vulnerable points. It also urged members to seek legal aid from BCP, maintain discipline and peaceful conduct, refrain from retaliation, and involve neighbours of all faiths and civil society members in Christmas celebrations to foster communal harmony.
Alt News has been documenting instances of hate crimes against the Christian community in West Bengal since early this year. Instances of violence, attacks, vandalism, and intimidation have often been carried out by Right-wing groups including Bajrang Dal, Vishva Hindu Parishad, and others, against individuals practising Christianity, house churches, and small Christian communities. However, in most of the cases we have reported, police action has been sparse, with fresh instances of harassment emerging regularly.

Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis
- Published
Tyson Fury says he was diagnosed with schizophrenia soon after his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.
British heavyweight Fury, 38, says he heard voices in his head threatening to hurt him and his family.
In a documentary which will be released by Netflix on Friday, Fury and wife Paris describe how he was diagnosed after being admitted to hospital with a suspected heart attack in June 2016.
"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury says.
"It was like a living version of the pits of hell. I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.
"The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder."
Doctors said Fury had suffered an anxiety attack.
Fury recalls hearing the radio talking to him, and begging Paris to get him out of the hospital because "the Illuminati" wanted him.
In the period after his victory over Klitschko, Fury gained weight and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.
"It got that bad I was hearing voices in my mind," he says.
"I wouldn't be able to sit and have a conversation because I'd be hearing stuff in my mind.
"I didn't know where to turn and no-one knew what to do. I really needed help, or check into rehab or something.
"I never got a break from it for years. I wanted to be what I thought was normal again."
After Fury was released from hospital, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder was confirmed.
The NHS describes schizophrenia, external as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech. It says the main symptom of bipolar disorder, external is extreme changes to your mood.
Fury describes a "turning point" in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween.
"I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked," he says.
"I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on.
"I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, 'I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I'm a fat mess addicted to alcohol'."
He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training.
It resulted in another world title when he beat Deontay Wilder in 2020.
Fury is preparing for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December.
The fight will be broadcast live on Netflix.

An open jail, family detention centre: Delhi planning first detention centre for female foreign nationals
Centre is managed by Delhi government, FRRO, and CRPF to hold foreign nationals awaiting deportation for visa violations or after completing prison sentences.
Delhi will set up the national capital's first detention centre for female foreign nationals in Narela's Lampur near the Delhi-Haryana border, with a family detention centre and an open jail being planned, officials said.
Lampur Detention Centre, which currently houses male foreign nationals held under immigration and other laws, is set to expand to accommodate female foreign nationals. According to officials, the Delhi government and the prisons department are working on a broader plan to address the growing number of foreign nationals awaiting deportation.
Two jail officials told HT that the plan also includes setting up a family detention centre and an open jail in Narela. Security staff at the Lampur detention centre and Tihar jail have prepared expansion plans and shared them with the social welfare department, the home department, and the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), which is responsible for the security of the premises.
The Lampur detention
The Lampur detention centre is one of the oldest detention centres in Delhi, as its 50-year-old building is located in the Sewa Sadan complex in Lampur Village in northwest Delhi’s Narela area. The centre is managed by the Delhi government, the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO), and the CRPF to hold foreign nationals awaiting deportation for visa violations or after completing prison sentences.
Undocumented migrants, asylum seekers, and refugees are all placed at the 18.5-acre facility. As per jail officials, there are more than 280 male detainees at the centre.
At present, the female foreign nationals, who have to be detained, are put at different community halls, homeless shelters and other temporary facilities. Officials said there is also Nirmal Chhaya, but it can only house 30 occupants.
“Since repairs and major renovation works are also pending at Lampur, we have decided to also place the female detention centre there. That way, both the male and female detainees will be placed at one place. We have more than 70-80 female detainees at times and need a bigger space to accommodate them. We are now planning to expand the Lampur centre with multiple storeys and the adjacent property to be used for Delhi Prisons,” a senior jail officer from Tihar headquarters told HT.
Most of the detainees at Lampur and other centres are Bangladeshis, followed by Nigerians and a few Pakistani nationals.
Since 2025, the Delhi government has announced plans to renovate Lampur centre due to multiple complaints from inmates (in courts) and the NHRC alleging poor medical facilities, unhygienic conditions and overcrowding.
Another jail officer said they are also planning to use the adjacent property to build an open jail in Delhi or a family detention centre.
The Delhi government on Monday said they have already approached the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) to allocate an additional 27 acres of land in Narela for the new prison adjacent to the upcoming high-security jail, as part of a broader plan to decongest the overcrowded Tihar Jail complex, officials said.
The government had earlier proposed a multi-storeyed prison at Narela but later dropped the plan. An official said a jail cannot be multi-storeyed as it could pose a security risk.

“A significant milestone in our journey towards preventive healthcare. Every dose is a step towards protecting girls from cervical cancer and ensuring a healthier future for them,” Mr. Modi said in a post on X.
The Prime Minister said he commends all the stakeholders whose efforts have ensured this remarkable feat.
The nationwide HPV vaccination campaign provides free, voluntary and single-dose vaccination to 14-year-old girls at designated government health facilities with parental consent.

Defending champion East Bengal FC continued its impressive start to the Lxme Indian Women’s League season with a hard-fought 1-0 win over Kickstart FC of Karnataka at the Kalyani Stadium on Monday.
Ugandan forward Resty Nanziri proved to be the match-winner, finding the net in the second minute of the action to hand the Moshal Girls an early lead. What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
- Published
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.
The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.
Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.
“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.
Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.
Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.
Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.
“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.
The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.
“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.
The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.
The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.
In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.
The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.
The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)
Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.
“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”
For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.
“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”
Update: 11/23/2026, 2:01 PM EDT: WIRED has updated the piece to clarify that President Donald Trump said he will defer to an appeals court on whether the material will be detonated.

Two potential vaccines against the deadly Ebola strain gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo are set to enter trials in the outbreak's epicentre next week, the World Health Organisation announced earlier this week.
There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the explosive outbreak declared in May, triggering an international public health emergency.
A total of 5,568 deaths out of 11,376 cases have been confirmed in the vast central African country's worst-ever Ebola outbreak, according to the WHO.
"We expect two candidate vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo virus to begin testing as early as next week," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a press conference at the UN health agency's headquarters in Geneva.
The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC is a single framework that can test the safety, efficacy and ability to trigger an immune response of multiple vaccines. The trial uses ring vaccination: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, kicked off the Tumaini trial on October 23, at the full-scale Phase 3 level, to determine if it also offers any protection against Bundibugyo.
Different vaccine types
The trial will now also incorporate the two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which have both gone through earlier-stage, smaller-scale Phase 1 clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab developed by the University of Oxford; the other, mRNA-1469, was developed by the US-based Moderna group using the mRNA technology made famous during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Meg Doherty, head of the WHO's science for health department, said Phase 2 clinical trials with the candidate vaccines are scheduled to begin on November 26 or 27 in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province at the epicentre of the outbreak.
If the safety and immune response data from the Phase 2 trial pass the next stage of review, the candidate jabs can move forward to a full-scale Phase 3 trial.
Children paying 'terrible price'
Doherty said that more than 140 people were enrolled in the Tumaini trial, with thousands of contacts ultimately expected to sign up. The trial will also eventually expand beyond the current single site in Bunia.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
Tedros said 400 to 500 new cases were still being reported every week, with two-thirds of confirmed deaths still taking place outside Ebola treatment centres.
"Children are paying a terrible price. They account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths," he added.

The health condition of BJP MLA Rekha Patra has improved, with her slurred speech reducing considerably, but doctors have kept her in the intensive care unit (ICU) for close observation, hospital sources said on Tuesday (November 24, 2026).
The Hingalganj MLA was taken off ventilator support on Monday (November 23, 2026) and has not required it since. She is now able to speak and communicate any physical discomfort to doctors, while the slurring in her speech has also reduced significantly, BJP leader Archana Das Majumdar said.
However, the three-member medical team treating her is not willing to take any chances and has recommended that she remain in the ICU for continued monitoring.
Hospital sources said she was still receiving supplemental oxygen due to low oxygen levels in her body.
While other clinical parameters indicate a positive recovery, doctors remain concerned about possible complications arising from the poisoning.
Following the suspected poisoning, excessive saliva had accumulated in Ms. Patra's mouth. As she was not fully conscious, some saliva entered her lungs, affecting oxygen supply to the body, an earlier CT scan had found.
Doctors said the effects of impaired oxygen supply to the lungs may not become immediately apparent and could manifest after some delay.
A repeat CT scan of her chest was scheduled for Tuesday (November 24, 2026) afternoon to assess the extent of any lung damage. Her further recovery would depend, among other factors, on the findings of the scan, they said.
Meanwhile, doctors are yet to establish the exact composition of the suspected poison detected in her stomach.
According to the medical team, the substance found in her stomach was described as a herbal larvicide (herbal pesticide), but its precise ingredients remain unknown.
The container of the pesticide, details of which were provided by her family members, did not carry any information about its composition.
In the absence of clarity over the ingredients, doctors at the private hospital are continuing treatment based on the symptoms associated with poisoning.
Ms. Patra suddenly fell ill at her residence in Hingalganj around 9 p.m. on November 21. She was initially taken to a local hospital and subsequently shifted to Basirhat Super Speciality Hospital after receiving preliminary treatment.
She remained under treatment there for nearly four hours, but as her condition did not improve significantly, doctors decided to refer her to Kolkata around 3 a.m. on November 22.
Her referral card mentioned that family members had reported suspected ingestion of a poisonous ‘herbal larvicide’.
At the time of treatment in Basirhat, her blood pressure was recorded at 124/70 mmHg and pulse rate at 110 beats per minute. She required oxygen support at four litres per minute.
Doctors also noted that she was drowsy and responding minimally to verbal calls. Attempts to revive her by applying pressure on her chest did not yield much response, prompting the decision to shift her to Kolkata.
Her condition was critical when she was admitted to the hospital on the morning of November 22. Later, state Health Minister Sharadwat Mukherjee said she was showing signs of improvement.
Ms. Patra rose to prominence during the movement against Trinamool Congress leaders in Sandeshkhali. The BJP subsequently fielded her from the Basirhat Lok Sabha constituency in the 2024 elections, but she failed to win.
She later won from Hingalganj assembly constituency in the 2026 West Bengal State elections.
Recently, she had expressed resentment against a section of the BJP's district leadership, alleging that she was not invited to party programmes in the district.
Her health condition has since become a matter of concern within the State BJP.

What you can do with your old, discontinued Mac Pro
Mac Pros are becoming obsolete. Do they still have use?
Earlier this year, Apple discontinued its Mac Pro desktop workstation, marking an end to one of the company's longest-running product lines. Starting at $5,999 for the entry-level 2019 model and costing tens of thousands of dollars when fully equipped, the Mac Pro was (and still is) a serious investment for most people and companies. Thankfully, even though Apple has stopped making new Mac Pros, your discontinued workstation is hardly worthless.
Whether you decide to sell your Mac Pro to finance an upgrade to a new Mac Studio, repurpose the existing hardware with a new operating system or simply continue to use the workstation for years to come, you have plenty of options. The secondhand market for Mac Pros remains strong, while the modular nature of the Mac Pro means that running alternative operating systems to keep the device current is easier than it is with newer Mac products. Plus, if it's in working condition, there's nothing stopping you from continuing to use it as intended, even if its hardware is showing its age. Regardless of what you're looking to do, here's everything you need to know about what comes next for your discontinued Mac Pro and how to get the most value out of it.
Why is Apple discontinuing the Mac Pro?
Apple discontinued the Mac Pro in March 2026 in order to prioritize the new Mac Studio line of workstations. With the move to Apple silicon, which uses a highly integrated system-on-a-chip (SoC) design, a modular desktop workstation like the Mac Pro no longer makes sense. Drop-in cards like GPUs aren't compatible with Apple's in-house silicon due to Apple's use of a unified memory architecture for the Apple M-series chips. This architecture shares memory resources across the CPU, GPU and other system components, and there simply isn't a good way to introduce some third-party components commonly used with the 2019 Mac Pro. The 2023 Mac Pro, meanwhile, uses the Apple M2 Ultra SoC and lacks the modularity of the 2019 model, so it's essentially a Mac Studio in a Mac Pro shell.
Apple is also streamlining macOS around its SoC design, something that developers for popular professional software like Adobe Premiere Pro are also doing. Since it would be too cumbersome to develop this kind of sophisticated software for two different kinds of Apple architectures, Apple and its partners are focusing on what's new rather than trying to continue supporting an increasingly obsolete architecture. Without sufficient software support, it makes little sense to continue producing the Mac Pro.
Can you still use your discontinued Mac Pro?
While Apple isn't producing new Mac Pros, that doesn't mean you have to get rid of yours. Developers are streamlining their apps for Apple M-series Macs, but some app support for Intel-based Macs will likely continue for another couple of years, like security updates and minor fixes. This support will vary between developers, though, and Apple's latest macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn't support the Intel-based Mac Pro.
If you have the 2023 Mac Pro, you don't have anything to worry about right now. It will be supported for years to come, and that support includes macOS 27 Golden Gate. Third-party apps will also support the 2023 Mac Pro for as long as they support the Apple M2 Ultra SoC.
If you're not getting the support you need from macOS on your old Mac Pro, you can install a new OS, either with a virtual machine or through a completely new installation. A guest OS doesn't get rid of macOS, and paid apps like Parallels make installing Ubuntu Linux and Windows 11 relatively painless. There are also free VM options that can help extend your discontinued Mac Pro's life.
Attempting a full install of a new OS might also be an option, but it's a complicated process and comes with some risk of bricking your Mac Pro for good. There are online resources to walk you through the process, but you'll need some technical know-how, so if you aren't comfortable with that, do not attempt it.
Are old Mac Pros worth anything?
If you're going to get rid of your old Mac Pro, don't just recycle it — plenty of people will be willing to buy it from you. Many professional workflows, like video editing or running a network server, require a lot of memory but don't necessarily need the fastest processors. Professionals and students in those fields might jump at the chance to pick up a working Mac Pro for relatively cheap. Online marketplaces are good places to start, but a handwritten bulletin board notice at your local university can work just as well.
If you have a 2019 Mac Pro, its internal components might also be worth selling individually. Memory and large-capacity storage drives are especially in-demand right now, so even though stripping your Mac Pro for parts might feel unseemly, if you can't find a buyer for the whole system, this might be the way to go. Some money is better than nothing.
If you plan on getting rid of your Mac Pro, make sure to do a few things beforehand. Read through this support page on Apple's website and follow the instructions for backing up your files, logging out of accounts and performing a factory reset. The last thing you want is to give someone all your sensitive data after saying goodbye to your old Mac Pro for good.

Netflix has partnered with the BBC to bring a number of shows from its preschool channel CBeebies, including “Teletubbies,” “Hey Duggee” and “Numberblocks,” to the streamer.
As part of a six-month trial, 24 programs from the CBeebies library will be made available via a dedicated CBeebies-branded hub from Dec. 2 in the U.K. The titles will also be made available on Netflix globally (excluding China) in a distribution deal managed by BBC Studios. The deal marks a first between the broadcaster and streaming giant.
The partnership has echoes of several that Netflix — and streaming rival Disney+ — have been making with global broadcasters over the last year. In France, Netflix subscribers can now access TF1’s live linear channels and on-demand catalogue on the streamer, while Disney+ has a deal in which a rotating selection of ITV shows are available to its U.K. subscribers.
But, alongside the global nature, this deal appears to be the first such arrangement to focus solely on preschool programming. Netflix — which hasn’t produced much kids content in the U.K. — has also said it has committed to “funding a small number” of new CBeebies commissions, without providing any further details.
For the BBC, which hit a jackpot with the pre-school series “Bluey” (now a major contributor to BBC Studios’ coffers), the partnership gives it a chance to expand the reach of some of its other kids favorites.
“The BBC has some of the world’s most loved content and brands, and we’re always looking at how we can help more audiences discover them,” said the BBC’s chief content officer Kate Phillips. “This limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programmes available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience. It’s an opportunity to learn more about how partnerships can help us extend the reach of our content, which is already appreciated by millions across the U.K. every day, deliver greater value for audiences and champion outstanding British creativity.”
Added Netflix’s VP of U.K. content Anne Mensah: “CBeebies holds a special and unrivalled place in the hearts of U.K. families and we are delighted to bring that love to all our Netflix homes in the U.K. and beyond. This unique partnership allows us to work hand in hand with the BBC to support our brilliant British kids’ programme makers. We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love.”

Marco Penge claims maiden PGA Tour win: Englishman triumphs from four-way playoff at RSM Classic
Three-time DP World Tour winner Marco Penge was in danger of losing his PGA Tour card after a 2026 season disrupted by a viral illness; the 28-year-old Englishman secures his card in stunning fashion with his maiden triumph at year-ending RSM Classic in thrilling four-way playoff finish
Monday 23 November 2026 20:17, UK
English golfer Marco Penge claimed a stunning maiden win on the PGA Tour as he emerged victorious from a four-way playoff at the season-ending RSM Classic.
Penge, a three-time winner on the DP World Tour, had gone into the tournament at risk of losing his PGA Tour card for next year after a rookie season disrupted by a viral illness placed him outside of the top 100.
With a top-four finish required to retain his spot, the 28-year-old found form at the best possible time at the Sea Island Golf Club this week, and a final-round 65 earned him a spot alongside Haotong Li of China and Americans Michael Thorbjornsen and Max Greyserman in a playoff decider - all four locked at 16 under.

Penge's five-under 65 on the Seaside Course included six birdies, including one at the last, and a single bogey, while he birdied 18 again to clinch victory in the playoff after nailing his approach to 10 feet.
"I always seem to play my best golf when my back's up against the wall," Penge said following his stunning win.
"I've been through this before on the DP World Tour, keeping my card in the last event and dealing with adversity and coming back from health issues, all that stuff.

With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He said he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.
But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.
In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.
Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.
“We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” says Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”
These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.
“This is a carbon copy of 2020,” said Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.
The big difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.
Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.
On November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJT.”
Election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.
“I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and said the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”
Ticktin also said he would speak directly to Trump about the issues and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”
While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a new poll from UC San Diego.
Major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another plan: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.
“Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne said over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a new election in 120 days.”
But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Recently, I was out doing some window shopping with one of my friends. We checked out some of our usual places — a makeup store, a clothing store — but the place where my friend’s eyes really lit up was a toy store. There were floor-to-ceiling displays of Labubus and Funko Pops, Jellycats that looked like croissants, and just about every Hello Kitty product you could imagine.
Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
Legos, Pokémon, Jellycats — and the case for never growing up.
What really got my attention about the space was not the sheer volume of toys, but the lack of kids. It was mostly people our age, with the same excitement that I saw in my friend. This makes sense when you look at a breakdown of the current toy market: It’s an industry projected to be worth over $130 billion worldwide this year, and as of this summer, American adults with no kids bought more games and toys than households with children. There’s even a name for grownups who aren’t ready to put away the toybox: kidults.
According to Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, there’s a reason for our enduring fondness for toys. “The drive to play is actually biologically hardwired into our subcortex,” she told Vox. “Because of that subcortical location, the drive to play actually lasts across the entire lifespan, which means that we’re never too old to play. But our society deeply misunderstands that. We’ve slowly started to take play away as we grow up, and yet that drive is still there.”
So what does play actually do for our brains, and how can we add the playfulness of childhood back into our adult lives? We answer that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sundstrom, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
Adult consumers are making up the lion’s share of the toy industry now. What is happening in our adult brains when we play with toys?
Neuroplasticity means that our brains can adapt across our entire lifespan. Some of the similar benefits that children have with playing with toys, we actually still have as adults.
The primary reason is because of the hand-brain connection, which is essentially a two-way neurological highway. When we do fine motor movement while we’re playing with toys, it stimulates the brain regions that are responsible for our cognitive function, our emotion, and our focus. It activates these deep neural networks that go completely unused when we’re engaging in, say, passive screen time.
When we’re playing with a toy, we’re often doing something we’ve never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen. That is actually stimulating new neural pathways in our brain that support our long-term cognitive health.
The second big one is our amygdala, which is a key part of our emotional processing center in our brain, is relaxed in the state of play. A lot of us live in a stress response right now. Social media doesn’t really take us out of that stress response. It often leaves us feeling more stressed out or drained when we’re done.
I absolutely have experienced that.
But that’s not the case with the toys. When we engage in this play state with toys, our amygdala actually calms down. The amygdala is responsible for our stress response. So our stress, our anxiety, our emotional defensiveness are significantly reduced, and we enter that restorative state, which for a lot of us is really hard to access on the day-to-day.
Toys are a pathway to helping us access that more relaxed emotional state based on the reactivity of our amygdala.
When do we start being told that we’re too old for toys? What do we lose when we accept that?
Sadly, I think we’re being told that we’re too old for toys starting quite early. Specifically, when we hit the teenage years, a lot of play is replaced with, “If this doesn’t have an immediate purpose for my future career, it’s not worth the time.”
That free space to experiment, say, with Lego and even with collections and other things that stimulate our imagination and allow us to enter this world between imagination and reality, starts to slowly dwindle out, almost imperceptibly.
Parents think that they’re doing their children a service by replacing that free play time with structured sports or structured activities. Unfortunately, what happens is, slowly, the intrinsic motivation to do something gets replaced with extrinsic motivation, which very quickly leads to burnout.
It sounds like when we stop playing with toys, that’s when the optimization culture kicks in.
Exactly. We see playing with toys as extra, as a hobby, as something that doesn’t have an immediate purpose toward helping us achieve whatever our goals are. And yet paradoxically, it’s one of the most productive things we can do.
One of the things that I like to ask people is, “Where are you when you get your best ideas?” Now, the shower is the most common answer, but the second most common answer is when they’re playing with toys. You know how no one answers that question? “When I’m at my desk at 10 am answering emails.”
The creative mind flourishes in the space in between, and the space in between is the time that is spent playing with toys. But until people see it like that, it becomes really hard to fit into the hustle culture and the grind of the daily schedule.
How do we relearn how to play?
“Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference.”
The first step is to think back on our earliest memories of playing, because play is who we were before the world told us who we have to be. The second, which is a derivative of that, is understanding your own play style. For some people, building a Lego set is going to be totally playful. For other people it’s going to be a puzzle or it’s going to be a game night with a board game or a sports league.
And third, this is not about adding more to our plate. Nobody has time for that.
That’s so funny. My first thought is, “I need to put play on my to-do list.”
And that is totally contradictory to the purpose of play!
Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference. You can put play objects and toys in visible places around your environment so that you reach for that instead of your phone.
If you just crack the door open a little bit with those micro moments of play in your routine, your brain will automatically enjoy it and start looking for more opportunities to play. Just start really small and know that that’s enough.
What do you think the world looks like when adults embrace that playful spirit more?
The world looks more joyful. This isn’t all sunshine and rainbows, and play doesn’t take away from the hard things that it means to be human. Play is a healthy way to express those challenges and to express the full range of emotions.
Play can look mellow and play can look lower-energy, but what it looks like is humans honoring what it means to be human and feeling more connected with your authentic self. When we’re more connected with our authentic self, we’re more easily able to connect with the people around us and establish meaningful relationships. So I see this as a tool for societal flourishing, specifically in a technologically dominated world.

Pentagon takes fresh aim at Canada's military readiness, defence spending priorities
Washington accuses Ottawa of putting economic interests ahead of security
The Pentagon has fired a further salvo at Canada, saying the country isn't meeting its international obligations to either NORAD or NATO and is prioritizing "parochial economic and commercial interests" in its defence build up.
The complaints are contained in a U.S. Department of War fact sheet covering U.S.-Canada defence relations, which was posted online Monday.
Axios, a U.S.-based news website, was first to report the contents on Sunday.
The fact sheet takes aim at the readiness of different branches of the Canadian military, saying the air force only has 41.9 per cent of its fleet ready for operations in the current budget year and that directly affects the country's ability to contribute to the air defence of North America.
It also cites low army and navy readiness figures.
"Canadian political leadership continues to pursue unfocused global commitments, resulting in personnel and platform overextension, deferred modernizations for key equipment and low readiness rates," said the fact sheet.
"Ottawa’s prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer."
The fact sheet does not spell out precisely how Canada is not meeting its NATO commitments, but does point to the sorry state of the navy's submarine fleet, where only one of four boats is operational. It also mentions the ongoing review by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney about whether to proceed with the full purchase of U.S.-made F-35 fighters.
The release of the document comes just two days after a report surfaced in the Washington Post that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the United States and Canada.
A leading U.S. senator, Mike Rounds, who sits on the armed services committee, told the Halifax International Security Forum that the restrictions were largely symbolic in the sense that they don't affect day-to-day military operations, intelligence sharing and defence planning.
"It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance [U.S. Department of War] objectives," he said.
U.S. defence officials — uniform and civilian — must seek permission before attending social events or think-tank conferences.
The memo follows the suspension last fall of meetings between the countries through the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD), a decades-old organization that met infrequently to co-ordinate North American security.
No one in Defence Minister David McGuinty's office was immediately available for comment.
The fact sheet said Canada "has yet to articulate a resourced path" to reach the NATO target of defence-related spending of five per cent of gross domestic product by 2035 "and is deferring the largest increases needed to actualize NATO targets until after the 2029 federal election."
The latest federal budget, released Nov. 5, contains spending plans going up to 2030-31. But absent was any clear sense on what the precise rearmament plans are for the Canadian military — beyond equipment that is already on order.
The fact sheet contained the Pentagon's advice: "Canada can maximize its limited but growing defence funds by prioritizing missions important for its homeland defence and meeting NORAD and NATO obligations by committing to the best military platforms."
Retired Canadian major-general Scott Clancy, speaking on CBC's Power & Politics late Monday, said there's an undeniable political and strategic tension between the United States and Canada that — for the moment — hasn't affected day-to-day co-operation.
"I think we're seeing a continuous deterioration of that relationship," Clancy said. "So, at the operational level, my friends are telling me the relationship is as good, if not better than before, but there are some cracks" that are making it increasingly difficult to maintain the business-as-usual approach.

Can you fix a scratched CD? Here are your options
You can try toothpaste or wax, but do so at your own risk.
Just like vinyl records before them, CDs are back. As strange as it may seem if you grew up with them, CDs have become a nostalgic icon of the joys of physical media — but they're also a reminder of why we all went digital in the first place. The biggest drawback of CDs was always just how easy it can be to ruin one with a careless scratch, and that hasn't changed. If you're embracing CDs for the first time or taking them for a spin again because of the CD revival, a scratch may seem like the end for your favorite album, but there are a few time-tested ways to get your discs back in playing shape.
The first step to fixing a CD that's skipping or not playing is to see if it just needs to be cleaned. Oils from your hands and debris like dust can cause playback issues without actually damaging the disc and they're easy enough to wipe away. To start, grab a lint-free cloth like microfiber and use it to wipe the CD from the center to the outer edge. Don't wipe across the CD, as this can cause more damage. For really dirty discs, you can use a little 70 percent isopropyl alcohol or distilled water applied to the cloth, though this typically isn't necessary. If you use any kind of liquid, make sure it's completely dried before you try to play or store your discs.
DIY methods can work if you're careful
For deeper scratches, there are a few time-tested DIY methods you'll find recommended often, but none of them are foolproof. Keep in mind that if you're taking disc repair into your own hands, there's no guarantee that you'll actually make things better, and there's some chance you'll make the problem worse. That being said, it's entirely possible to buff out scratches and make CDs playable again, but whether it works depends on just how bad the damage is in the first place. For DIY disc repair, the goal is to use some form of abrasive to sand down the layer of the CD with a scratch, letting the player's laser reach the data stored deeper in the disc.
Toothpaste is one of the most common cleaners to use, since it's cheap, accessible and not too damaging. Make sure you have plain white toothpaste without any gels, beads or whitening agents, and squirt a bit on the disc. Spread it evenly, then use a lint-free cloth to wipe from the inside of the disc outward a few times, all around the disc. Then rinse it off with water and let it dry. You can perform the same process with a stronger abrasive like 3M rubbing compound if you prefer.
If your disc still doesn't work, you can apply a thin layer of wax (like shoe polish or Chapstick) to seal the scratches. Just apply the wax from the inside of the disc to the outside and wipe it away using the same motion after a few minutes. Remember to let any product you apply dry completely before using your disc.
You can't fix every CD at home
For scratches you can't get out yourself, disc repair services are also an option, though they're rare these days and you may not have one near you. These services use professional-grade machines that essentially buff discs the same way that home methods do, but they can be more reliable. If you're really serious about preserving your discs, you can also buy one of these high-end machines yourself, but since they can run into the thousands of dollars, it's not an option for most people. In most cases, seeking professional repair or buying a disc repair machine only makes sense if you're trying to preserve rare CDs with material you can't find elsewhere.
If you want to preserve the data on your CD and you're not precious about the disc itself, it's a good idea to invest in a CD burner. This lets you copy the data on the disc, keeping it safe even if the physical CD is damaged. Making copies is a good idea, since your CD collection won't last forever. In some cases, a burner may be able to record the data from a disc even when scratches are causing it to skip in your CD player, letting you make another copy later. Like with any repair method, the success of a CD burner depends on how damaged the disc is, but it's a non-destructive way of preserving your CD's contents when it works.

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) on Tuesday sounded the poll bugle in Punjab, announcing an alliance for the 2027 assembly elections and reviving their partnership after a six-year break. The two parties will jointly contest all 117 seats, with the Akali Dal taking the lead in the alliance."Big brother will be Akali Dal. We will contest all 117 seats. Bada bhai hi chief minister hota hai (The elder brother becomes the chief minister)," Union home minister Amit Shah said at a joint press conference attended by BJP president Nitin Nabin and SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal."Naturally, the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) will play the role of the elder brother. The Akali Dal and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) will contest together. Both parties will jointly contest all 117 seats, while the Akali Dal will be in the role of the elder brother," he added.
Shah said tackling drugs, corruption and law and order would be the alliance's key priorities in Punjab, a border state."The biggest hallmark of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) is that wherever there is an NDA government, law and order has remained sound.
Both of our parties have discussed several issues concerning Punjab, and we have a consensus on them," he said."Our topmost priority will be a drug-free Punjab, fixing law and order to provide security in this border state, and eliminating these gangs. This is our topmost priority, and it will be the foremost issue in the manifestos of both parties," he added.Shah further stated that a detailed manifesto would be finalised soon by the two parties for the elections, but eradicating the drug menace from Punjab and promoting Hindu-Sikh unity would be among the key focus areas."BJP, the Akali Dal, and the NDA will contest in Punjab, and we will announce several key points in our manifesto. The current government in the state, led by Kejriwal Ji, had come to power promising to eliminate drugs within three months. They promised to eliminate drugs, but the problem has not been eradicated; it has increased. In 2017, Rahul Gandhi Ji had promised that drugs would be eliminated within one term. He made that promise, but his party also did nothing to address the drug problem. Now, I want to reiterate a promise that I made there: by December 31, 2029, we will make Punjab completely drug-free," he added.Sukhbir Singh Badal to be CM face: SirsaDelhi minister and BJP leader Manjinder Singh Sirsa said Sukhbir Singh Badal would be the chief ministerial face of the BJP-SAD alliance in Punjab.Speaking to ANI, Sirsa said the alliance was formed with a broader vision of addressing Punjab's problems rather than merely capturing political power. He said its priorities included making the state free of drugs, gangsters and debt, besides resolving farmers' issues.He also congratulated Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Shah, Nitin Nabin and Badal on the alliance, and welcomed the SAD's return to NDA.The announcement, made on Gurpurab, comes with a symbolic connection to the events that led to the breakdown of the alliance.The alliance marks a revival of ties between the BJP and SAD, which parted ways in 2020 after the Akali Dal withdrew from the NDA over its opposition to the now-repealed farm laws.Under their previous seat-sharing arrangement, the BJP contested 23 of Punjab's 117 assembly seats, while the SAD fought the remaining constituencies.
