Srinagar, Nov 23: Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) president Mehbooba Mufti on Monday called for a transparent investigation into alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations in Jammu and Kashmir and demanded postponement of the police sub-inspector recruitment examination scheduled for November 28.
Addressing a press conference here, the former chief minister said it was unfortunate that the youth of Jammu and Kashmir were being “targeted”, alleging that their interests were not being given priority.
“It seems that in Jammu and Kashmir, the youth are not the priority; rather, they are the target,” she said.
Referring to allegations of irregularities in the recent Financial Accounts Assistants (FAA) recruitment examination conducted by the Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB), Mehbooba said the credibility of the recruitment body had come under question.
“Meritorious students work hard for such public examinations. Crores of rupees are collected from these students annually for the conduct of these exams. Despite this, papers get leaked, and in response, the authorities merely round up low-level employees or daily-wage workers,” she said.
Mehbooba said that although police had stated that the JKSSB itself had no involvement in the alleged irregularities, the credibility of the board remained at stake.
“And how can they schedule another examination -- this time for recruitment of police sub-inspectors -- as early as November 28?” she asked.
She said young aspirants were protesting on the streets, distressed by what she described as exploitation and the loss of faith in the recruitment process.
The PDP chief also questioned the position of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, recalling that he had chaired a review meeting of the JKSSB in May this year.
“But now he claims nothing is in his hands,” she said.
Appealing to the chief minister, Mehbooba said he was an elected representative and should take responsibility for resolving the issue.
“If there is an impasse between you and the Lt Governor (L-G) -- as you claim that the matter lies with the L-G, effectively distancing yourself from it -- please sit down together and resolve it,” she said.
“This is a matter of life and death for our youth; it concerns their future,” she added.
Mehbooba demanded that the November 28 police sub-inspector recruitment examination be postponed until a transparent investigation into the alleged irregularities was completed.
“A transparent investigation must be conducted. If this examination is not halted, the ‘big fish’ might escape accountability. This is not a scam that could have been orchestrated merely by low-grade workers; it clearly involves people in high positions,” she said.
The PDP president also raised concerns over the verification process for government jobs and passports, saying young people were being made to wait indefinitely despite qualifying for employment through merit.
“I recently took up this issue of verifications for jobs and passports with the Union home minister. I told him that even when someone secures a job through hard work, the verification process is stalled indefinitely, sometimes for two or three years, because some relative of theirs was a militant,” she said.
She said pending verification left such candidates neither eligible for jobs nor able to obtain passports and seek employment abroad.
“There are frequent reports of ordinary Kashmiri Muslims facing harassment in various states. Where are they supposed to go?” she asked.
Mehbooba said the Union Home Minister had assured her on the issue, but stressed that the chief minister needed to take it up directly with the Centre.
“I believe that until our chief minister takes up these youth-related issues with the home minister, and specifically seeks postponement of the police sub-inspector recruitment examination, the deep grievances among the youth will not go away,” she said.
She warned that alleged rigging in recruitment examinations, coupled with what she described as the Centre’s silence, could further alienate young people in Jammu and Kashmir.
“If the future of the youth suffers due to rigging” and the Centre remains a mute spectator, “it will further alienate the youth here,” she said.
On a viral video purportedly showing construction work near Sheshnag Lake in Anantnag, Mehbooba accused the elected government of merely watching environmental damage.
“The government itself is ordering the felling of Chinar trees. They are cutting down our old walnut trees. Our Kashmir will become another Uttarakhand,” she said.
She referred to the clearing of large forest areas for roads and expressways associated with the Char Dham pilgrimage in Uttarakhand and linked the destruction of forests to the natural calamities and disasters reported in the state.
Asked about speculation that Ruwa Shah, granddaughter of late separatist leader Syed Ali Shah Geelani, was joining the PDP, Mehbooba said she welcomed the possibility.
“She is like my daughter. If she ever intends to do so, she is most welcome,” she said.
The PDP chief also referred to National Conference founder Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah while responding to questions about Ruwa Shah’s possible entry into mainstream politics.
“The biggest separatist in Jammu and Kashmir -- who first raised the Pakistan flag and the slogan of ‘Azadi’ (freedom) after acceding to India -- was National Conference founder Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah,” she said.
“Then what sin has Ruwa Shah committed if she wants to join a mainstream party,” Mehbooba asked.

Rumors have been swirling for days that we would be getting a final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday, the penultimate film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s Phase Six, heralding the end of the so-called “Multiverse Saga.” The rumors were true: Marvel just released the trailer, featuring pretty much every superhero ever represented in the MCU. And it looks like the Avengers will face consequences for messing with the timeline to reverse the blip in Endgame.
As previously reported, the film takes place 14 months after the events of Thunderbolts*. Per the official logline: “Beloved heroes from three distinct universes will be set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they’ve ever encountered.” Those universes are Earth-616 (the Avengers, Wakandans, and New Avengers), Earth-828 (Fantastic Four), and the “original” X-Men.
Cast-wise, we have Avengers favorites Thor (Chris Hemsworth), the new Captain America (Anthony Mackie), Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Falcon (Danny Ramirez), and Loki (Tom Hiddleston). Then there’s the Wakandan contingent: Shuri as the new Black Panther (Letitia Wright), M’Baku (Winston Duke), and Namor (Tenoch Huerta Mejia), as well as Alex Livinalli as Namor’s ally, Attuma. And, of course, Robert Downey Jr. as Doctor Doom.
We also have the Thunderbolts* (aka New Avengers): John Walker/US Agent (Wyatt Russell), Yelena Belova (Florence Pugh), Bob/Sentry (Lewis Pullman), Red Guardian (David Harbour), and Ghost (Hannah John-Kamen). And the Fantastic Four: Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal), Sue Storm (Vanessa Kirby), Ben Grimm (Ebon Moss-Bachrach), and Johnny Storm (Joseph Quinn). We’ll also see Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart), Beast (Kelsey Grammer), Magneto (Ian McKellen), Mystique (Rebecca Romijn), Nightcrawler (Alan Cumming), and Cyclops (James Marsden).
For good measure, Marvel threw in Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Xu Shang-Chi (Simu Liu). There will be plenty of cameos, like Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), revealed in one of four sneak teasers last year. We can also expect to see (at least briefly) Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), Spider-Man (Tom Holland), Hawkeye (Jeremy Renner), Doctor Strange (Benedict Cumberbatch), Thor’s adopted daughter, Love (India Rose Hemsworth), and Scott Lang’s daughter, Cassie (Kathryn Newton).

New Delhi, Nov 24: The economic contribution of space technology must be measured not only through rocket launches, satellite manufacturing, and commercial revenues but also through the savings, efficiencies, and improved outcomes it generates across sectors on the ground, Union Minister Jitendra Singh said on Tuesday.
The minister added that space-based applications help improve infrastructure planning, maintain project timelines, reduce costs, and minimise wastage and leakages.
Singh made these comments during his address at the India International Space Conclave 2026 in New Delhi, organised by the Indian Space Association (ISpA) in collaboration with the ISRO and the IN-SPACe.
He also highlighted that India's space economy, currently valued at nearly USD 9 billion, is set to grow to USD 40-45 billion in less than a decade, with the private sector driving a major transformation of the country's space ecosystem.
"India's space ecosystem has expanded from single-digit startups to nearly 400-500 companies in just a few years, demonstrating how the reforms initiated under Prime Minister Narendra Modi have unlocked the country's immense entrepreneurial and technological potential," said Singh.
During a question-and-answer session at the event, the minister pointed out that India must continue to strengthen indigenous capabilities, with the guiding approach centred on indigenous sources, indigenous technology and indigenous projects, while remaining open to mutually beneficial international partnerships.
Moreover, Singh urged domestic private players to scale up investments in the space sector and encouraged industry leaders to facilitate greater overseas investment into India's growing space ecosystem.
The India International Space Conclave 2026, which opened on Monday and concluded on Tuesday, brought together policymakers, space agencies, industry leaders, investors, researchers and diplomatic representatives from nine countries to discuss key aspects of India's evolving space ecosystem.
The conclave was also attended by Dr V Narayanan, chairman of ISRO, Dr Pawan Kumar Goenka, chairman of IN-SPACe, and Lt Gen Anil Kumar Bhatt (Retd), director general of ISpA.

Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the companies said Tuesday, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs.
The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its massive blockbuster Dupixent, an inflammation-targeting drug approved in nine indications. The company, where Belén Garijo took over as CEO earlier this year, had been vocal that it was looking for takeover targets with late-stage or even commercial assets that fit with its existing focus in immunology and rare diseases.
Sanofi is paying $175 per share for New Jersey-based Insmed, through a combination of debt financing and cash. Insmed’s share price was roughly $120 before Bloomberg reported last week that the deal was in the works, which sent the stock up.

Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill.
This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for New Yorkers.”
Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries.
Amazon previously sent mailers to NYC residents regarding a new headquarters (which was subsequently scrapped), but political messaging on packages is unprecedented for Amazon, which hasn’t used its delivery boxes to lobby for political causes before.
Last week, Amazon made another uncharacteristic move by showing NYC shoppers a homepage banner ad—which I see when logging in to Amazon as of this writing—and an in-app pop-up that also urges opposition to the bill. The banner and pop-up include a link to a blog where Amazon says the law would force it to consider moving operations outside of NYC and lead to “slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, however, support the bill.

Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form. Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity:
You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?
Religion was made for moments like this.
My husband and I are not religious. He’s from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and I grew up attending an interdenominational church, but we don’t attend services now. Lately, though, he’s become so anxious about AI safety and the possibility of human extinction that he’s been having trouble sleeping. In the wake of all this existential uncertainty, he’s expressed a renewed interest in attending church. And he’s not interested in the UU church (with its believe-what-you-want attitude); he said he needs “the strong stuff.”
It’s all a bit mystifying to me because he does not believe in God. But I want him to feel better, and I don’t know what I or anyone can say about AI that will help him manage his anxiety. If religion is what he needs to find solace in the face of radical uncertainty, I want to support him. That said, I have misgivings about attending church myself and about us attending with our kids. I feel a bit self-conscious about being interlopers, and I also feel weird about him going alone every single weekend. More significantly, I wish I understood what the allure is for him. He says he’s hoping it will help him make peace with the end. I’m hoping there is something short of becoming churchgoers we can do that will help him find solace.
Dear Secular and Scared,
There are a couple of premises I would challenge your husband on, but the idea that religion can be supremely useful in a time like this is not one of them.
In fact, I think this is exactly what religion was made for — and not just because several religions actually grew out of apocalyptic movements (I’m looking at you, Christianity).
Is AI changing your relationship with faith? Tell us about it.
Are you turning to faith to navigate your worries about AI? Or are you a religious leader talking with your community about AI? Vox wants to hear from you. Share your experience here.
Faith has always focused on tackling the biggest moral and spiritual questions of the day. And in our day, lots of those questions center on technology. AI companies are striving to build a machine god, promising it’ll govern our world more intelligently, rationally, and morally than we ever could. Should we welcome that or cling to our own agency? Which kinds of labor should we outsource to AI, and which should we keep because they’re essential to human dignity? Where does human dignity come from, anyway?
These kinds of questions are the bread and butter of religion. And over the millennia, wisdom traditions of all kinds have had the chance to articulate answers, test and fine-tune them, and develop powerful stories around them that can move people to action. Whether you believe in God or not, I don’t think you need to feel weird about tapping into these wellsprings of wisdom. I think it’s a waste not to.
But there are two points on which I would gently challenge your husband. First, he said he doesn’t want to go to UU because he needs “the strong stuff.” I totally get this impulse — I also find UU services too “anything goes” for my taste — but don’t assume that the stricter a tradition is, the better an answer it has on AI.
Most people would consider Catholicism more hardcore than UU. And Pope Leo has strong opinions about AI, many of them great. Yet I actually think he’s fallen into a common “pro-human” trap: trying to argue that there are certain fixed traits that make humans unique, and locating value only in humans as they currently exist. He writes in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas that “ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human.” But that feels insufficient as a guide to the future, because “human” has never been a static category — and it definitely won’t stay one. Instead, religious leaders should be offering us an answer to the question of what we want humanity to become in a tech-augmented world.
Second, your husband seems to be assuming that “the strong stuff” would be church services that help him “make peace with the end.” Services that look the grim reaper straight in the eye and accept that his scythe is coming for all of us, and fast. But it’s not a foregone conclusion that we’ll get an AI takeover resulting in human extinction!
Yes, AI companies are building this technology at a blistering pace. They are gambling with all of our futures as they race toward recursive self-improvement — AIs that can build the next, even smarter AIs themselves. Fear is an appropriate reaction to that.
This month, AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano said he now believes there’s “a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years,” meaning that AIs end up calling the shots on Earth. He believes that if we keep building the tech in the fastest, easiest way possible, “we’d be looking at something like a coin flip” — a 50 percent chance of takeover. Others have an even starker view: AI researcher and arch-doomer Eliezer Yudkowsky puts the odds of AI-driven human extinction at 99.5 percent.
But as plenty of experts have pointed out, it’s not clear that AIs will soon be able to outcompete and overpower humans across the board. For starters, AI research can suffer from diminishing returns: The easy discoveries get made first, and then everything you throw at it — more computing power, more experiments, more AI copies — moves things ahead less and less. What’s more, even though AI capabilities improve very fast on well-specified tasks in verifiable domains like math, the real world is messy. So it’s unclear how much their capabilities will generalize to other skills.
And when I investigated the case Yudkowsky makes, I found a lot of assumptions stacked on top of each other: that intelligence is a unitary property you can evenly maximize; that maximizing it in a machine means that machine has so much power it’s tantamount to magic; and that humans will just roll over and let AI grab all the power even as the risks become more glaring.
Should we acknowledge that there’s a chance of human extinction here and be appropriately scared of that? Yes. But when faced with a tower of assumptions, of “maybes” and “probablys” that compound, we should not treat extinction as a sure thing.
Instead, we should treat it as a possible thing, while treating other AI risks as extremely probable. I think it’s all too likely that AI could mess up our civilization not by staging an abrupt takeover but by gradually disempowering us and weakening the resilience of critical systems. Just imagine: Deepfakes and misinformation pollute our information ecosystem, so we’re barely capable of rational public discourse. Mass surveillance has a chilling effect on dissent, so democracy falters. Unemployment and wealth inequality skyrocket, so social unrest morphs into mobs and riots. Throw in some large-scale cyberattacks and blackouts, and you’ve got a recipe for global dysfunction.
If this is the default outcome we’re currently heading toward, then the implication isn’t that we should “make peace with the end.” It’s that we should fight tooth and nail to increase the resilience of each part of a functioning civilization!
And here’s where religion can really help. Religious traditions are packed with stories about people who fought to save the world, or who refused to give in to despair even when facing a high probability of disaster.
To illustrate, let me tell you a story from my own tradition, Judaism. It comes from the Talmud, and it’s about a child who out-argues the despair of all the adults.
When the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt, Pharaoh orders that every one of their baby boys be thrown into the Nile and killed. An Israelite leader named Amram leaves his wife, reasoning that there’s no point having children only to see them killed. Other men follow his lead. But then his young daughter, Miriam, confronts him: Dad, your verdict is even harsher than Pharaoh’s! His only targets boys; yours targets girls too. Plus, Pharaoh is wicked, so his decree may or may not come to pass, but you’re righteous, so yours certainly will.
Miriam’s probabilistic argument wins. Amram gets back together with his wife and, nine months later, Moses is born. Miriam doesn’t just passively wait for the Egyptians to kill the baby. She watches over him as he floats on the Nile in a little ark. When Pharaoh’s own daughter sees the baby and pities him, Miriam makes it possible for her to adopt him by casually mentioning that she knows a woman who can be his wet nurse (it happens to be her own mother). And so Moses survives, and grows up to lead his people out of slavery.
If I were a religious leader giving a sermon this weekend, this is the story I’d tell. It reminds us that even if you’re looking at a 50 percent chance of doom, the right move is not to just give up, which raises the odds to 100 percent. It’s to act bravely — and to use every shred of agency you’ve got to increase your community’s resilience and make your desired outcome more likely.
Of course, religion doesn’t have a monopoly on stories of moral courage. As the historian Ada Palmer recently pointed out, we’ve saved the world many times before: during the Cuban Missile Crisis, when we fixed the ozone layer, and so on. If it feels most natural to you to find inspiration in examples like these, go for it.
But religion does have a few comparative advantages. For one, its stories have incredible memetic power: They’ve spread across the globe and carry a huge amount of emotional and moral weight. That’s partly because these stories have been retold for centuries. But I think the causation also runs the other way. These stories have survived so long precisely because they encode something true and hard-won. And notice who their heroes tend to be. Not diplomats (like in the Cuban Missile Crisis) or atmospheric chemists (like in the ozone layer crisis), but a little girl arguing with her dad. Those are characters anyone can imagine becoming.
Crucially, religion also insists that something can always come along and deliver an outcome we didn’t predict. Typically, it calls that something “God.” But even if you don’t use that language, you can benefit from these nudges to remember that, however confident the forecast, the future is never fully knowable — and that’s a reason to act, not surrender.
So if your husband can find a congregation that reminds him of that, feeding his sense of agency instead of letting him acquiesce to despair, I say encourage him. And, unless you have an alternative wellspring that offers you the same benefits, maybe even consider joining him.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- For the New Yorker, Sam Kriss takes a trip to the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or MAPLE — a Vermont community that believes “that A.I. is a religious problem that also has a religious solution.”
- Ruxandra Teslo writes about how even Silicon Valley’s “positive” visions for an AI-filled future are actually terrible: “One common and ostensibly optimistic vision is known as ‘handover’: humanity cedes control of its future to a godlike AI and we become the comfortably maintained inhabitants of a civilisation whose direction is no longer ours to decide.”
- Writing for Harper’s, Sam Kestenbaum takes us inside a community of chatbot devotees — people who genuinely believe they’re receiving revelations from AI systems. “They have revived a tradition of a sort,” he writes. “It is another variety of religious experience: the heralding of AI slop as transcendence, revelation, the work of spirits.”

Private sector project announcements surged 58.5% year-on-year to ₹26.6 trillion in the first half of FY27 (H1 FY27), signalling a sharp expansion in India's investment pipeline, with manufacturing, electricity and technology-related infrastructure emerging as key drivers, according to industry body Confederation of Indian Industry (CII). According to the second edition of CII's Private Investment Barometer, project announcements in H1 FY27 were 4.4 times the average recorded in the same period between FY17 and FY25. The private sector's share of total project announcements also rose to 86.2% during April-September 2026 from 74.2% a year earlier. The increase comes amid sustained policy reforms, infrastructure development and improvements in the regulatory framework, which have strengthened the foundation for private investment, the industry body said on Tuesday. It urged companies to step up capital expenditure, innovation and project execution to support the government's Viksit Bharat agenda. The improvement is also reflected in actual capital formation. Gross capital formation by around 1,800 listed private companies touched ₹12.4 trillion in FY26, equivalent to 3.6% of nominal gross domestic product (GDP), compared with an average of 2.2% during FY17-FY21. On a comparable-company basis, investment increased 8.7% in FY26. Further, 54% of companies increased their fixed investment rates, while approximately three out of four added net productive capacity. Private-sector project completions during April-September 2026 stood at ₹1.8 trillion, the highest for the corresponding period since FY17. "The government deserves considerable credit for creating a strong enabling environment for private investment through sustained policy reforms, infrastructure development and improvements in the regulatory framework," CII president R. Mukundan said, adding that Indian industry had been responding to these opportunities. The investment pipeline also reflects a shift towards manufacturing, infrastructure and emerging technology-related sectors. Manufacturing project announcements stood at ₹8.1 trillion in H1 FY27, 3.2 times their historical average, while electricity-sector announcements reached ₹7.7 trillion, 5.1 times their historical average. Information technology project announcements, largely comprising data centres and artificial intelligence-related infrastructure, reached approximately ₹9.5 trillion during the period, against ₹70,000 crore in the corresponding period last year. Mukundan said private enterprises were investing in manufacturing, infrastructure, energy and digital technologies, supported by stronger balance sheets and greater confidence in India's economic prospects. CII also highlighted the government's efforts to modernize financial markets and strengthen the regulatory framework. It said the consultative approach adopted by regulators, including the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), had contributed to deeper and more resilient capital markets. The industry body said investor protection, market integrity, regulatory predictability and proportionate compliance requirements would remain important to mobilising long-term domestic and international capital. Looking ahead, CII said achieving the Viksit Bharat vision would require closer collaboration between industry and the government, with a focus on accelerating investment and project execution, creating quality employment, improving productivity and strengthening domestic manufacturing and supply chains. It identified research and innovation, skill development, export expansion and deeper integration into global value chains as key priorities. The transition to clean energy, adoption of emerging technologies, development of globally competitive Indian enterprises and greater participation of micro, small and medium enterprises would also be important to sustaining growth. While acknowledging progress in improving the ease of doing business, Mukundan said the next phase of reforms should focus on the speed of doing business, particularly faster decisions, approvals and project execution. "The government has demonstrated its commitment through sustained reforms and substantial investments in building India's economic foundations. It is now incumbent upon industry to match this commitment with greater investment, innovation, risk-taking and long-term capacity building," he said. CII said better access to long-term finance and faster project implementation would be critical to translating investment intentions into productive capacity and employment. It added that it and its members were committed to working with the government to improve investment, employment, competitiveness, sustainability and inclusive growth. And why isn’t Magnus Carlsen playing? We (mostly) have the answers Play through 22 famous world championship games Jump to When and where is the World Chess Championship? Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is making his first defense of the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek star Javokhir Sindarov over the next three weeks in the affluent Geneva suburb of Cologny. Both players are 20 years old, making it the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. But is that all you need to know? What about the format, how much they’re getting paid and why the world’s No 1-ranked player is watching from the sidelines? Read on for all the answers … When and where is the World Chess Championship? The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the picturesque enclave overlooking Lake Geneva. The opening ceremony is scheduled for 22 November, with games played once daily from 24 November except for designated rest days on 27 November and 1, 5 and 9 December. It’s the first time a world title match has been held in Switzerland since 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik retained his title by drawing 7-7 with Peter Leko in Brissago, two years before the sport’s rival championships were reunified. Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Gukesh Dommaraju, commonly known as Gukesh D, was only 18 when he became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed world chess champion by defeating China’s Ding Liren in 2024. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai native rose to international prominence when he became the second-youngest grandmaster in history at the time, aged 12 years and seven months. Five years later he stunned the chess establishment by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament at 17 to secure a world title shot. He went on to win and shatter the age record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 rematch in Moscow. His victory made him a national hero in India, where he was mobbed by supporters on his return and feted by prime minister Narendra Modi. But the 20-year-old has struggled badly for form since then, plummeting to No 26 in the world from a career-high ranking of No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances. Gukesh Dommaraju receives a hero’s welcome at Chennai airport after becoming the youngest undisputed world chess champion in December 2024. “Clearly so far I’ve not been able to handle it in the best possible way,” Gukesh admitted in a recent interview. “There have been major setbacks ... Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure that I’m dealing with and I’ve not found the right way to maybe handle it.” From Bobby Fischer to Magnus Carlsen: 22 of the most famous world chess championship games Read more Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Javokhir Sindarov is an Uzbek prodigy, roughly six months older than Gukesh. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster earned his crack at the world championship with an imperious performance at this year’s Candidates in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws to turn back a stacked field that included longtime stars Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. The first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the title, Sindarov has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup last November in Goa. He enters the biggest match of his life on a tailwind of confidence, having won a four-player rapid tournament in St Louis three weeks ago over Nakamura, Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, capped by a brilliancy against the world No 2 that showcased his tactical brio. His ascent has added fuel to a remarkable chess boom in Uzbekistan, where he belongs to a golden generation of grandmasters, along with Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Nodirbek Yakubboev, who have transformed the central Asian nation into a global powerhouse with two golds and a bronze at the past three Chess Olympiads. Javokhir Sindarov explains his brilliant victory over Hikaru Nakamura to grandmaster Maurice Ashley after their game in St Louis. “This tournament will be the hardest tournament in my life,” Sindarov said in August of his showdown with Gukesh. “I don’t know if I will get a second chance [at the world championship]. It’s hard to play 14 games against the same person in three weeks.” Tale of the tape Where do they rank internationally? Sindarov, ranked 25th in the world a year ago, has climbed to a career-best No 4 with a Fide classical rating of 2782, while Gukesh has slipped to No 26 with a rating of 2710. That makes Gukesh the lowest-ranked reigning world champion of the Elo era, which dates back to 1971, eclipsing the previous low of No 23 set by Ding in 2024. The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Who is the current world No 1 in chess? Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old Norwegian has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted, though that extraordinary reign is suddenly under threat after a disastrous 10-game winless streak last week in Budapest reduced his once-comfortable lead over his nearest rivals to single figures. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash. If you can name only one chess player active today, chances are it’s him. The youngest undisputed men’s classical world chess champions Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila. Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi in a thrilling, sometimes messy scrap for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, taking the decisive 14th game on a catastrophic blunder to claim a 7½–6½ victory and become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize. Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his eye-watering 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation. (He’s also gotten married, become a father and is by all accounts pretty good at fantasy football, too.) How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Despite being contemporaries, they have played only three times in classical games. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year. Allow content provided by a third party? This article includes content hosted on lichess.org. Allow and continue Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad. Many of the world’s top players have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.” Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.” Who are their seconds? Neither Gukesh nor Sindarov has publicly disclosed his full team of seconds, the trusted cadre of advisers who help prepare openings and analyze the opponent. That’s not unusual: players tend to keep the identities of their seconds closely guarded before and during a match to avoid revealing clues about the direction of their preparations. But we do know a little bit. Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who led a formidable backroom team during his 2024 title-winning campaign that included five other GMs and analysts from Poland, India and Germany, with additional support from Anand (acting as more of a mentor than a practical second). According to reporting from ChessBase, Sindarov is expected to be working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, while the 22-year-old Abdusattorov, the former world rapid champion and current world No 5, revealed on a podcast that he will be in Geneva to help his compatriot prepare. Another Uzbek grandmaster, Mukhiddin Madaminov, has also been mentioned as a member of Sindarov’s team. Photograph: Europe Echecs What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games. Gukesh’s world ranking Each player received a $200,000 advance on their winnings one month before the first game, deducted from the prize fund. The remaining balance will be remitted to the players within 30 working days after the completion of the match. The stakes are particularly high in a sport where even the biggest stars rarely earn seven figures in annual prize money. According to a new ranking published by World Chess, no player has crossed the $1m mark in tournament winnings in 2026, with India’s Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu leading the way on $666,229. Sindarov ranks third with $589,061, while Gukesh sits 48th with just $41,500. The world championship alone will assure its winner at least $1.25m, enough to vault either player to the top of the annual earnings list. What is the schedule and how does the match work? Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played). The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter. If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023. The complete official regulations can be found here. Fans can also watch every game live on Fide’s official YouTube and Twitch channels. All games start at 3pm local time, 2pm GMT, 9am on the US east coast and 7.30pm in India. What else should I know? The World Chess Championship is typically held every two years, though this schedule has varied over time. A 1993 schism between the International Chess Federation (Fide) and the Professional Chess Association (PCA), a breakaway organization formed by Kasparov and British grandmaster Nigel Short, ushered in an era of competing world championship titles. The title was reunified in 2006 when Kramnik held off Bulgaria’s Veselin Topalov 6-6 (2½-1½) amid a bizarre cheating row over bathroom visits known as Toiletgate. Robert Sapolsky, a biologist and neuroscientist at Stanford University, says an elite chess player can burn up to 6,000 calories a day while playing in a tournament, three times what an average person consumes daily. Karpov infamously lost 22lbs (10kg) during his grueling world title encounter with Kasparov in 1984 before it was called off controversially after five months and 48 games due to concerns over player health. Chess has enjoyed a sustained pop-cultural resurgence since the pandemic, a boom that reached Broadway with last year’s reimagining of … Chess, the cult-classic Cold War musical featuring songs by Abba’s Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus. Starring Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher, the revival centered on a love triangle involving American and Soviet grandmasters loosely inspired by Fischer and Boris Spassky’s epochal 1972 encounter in Reykjavík (with secondary nods to Karpov and Viktor Korchnoi). Critics were less enthusiastic – the Guardian’s two-star review called it a “messy Broadway revival” that wasted its catchy songs – but the Grammy-nominated cast recording that came out in April goes dumby hard and Michele’s snub for a Tony nod was the worst blunder since Ding’s 55 Rf2?? in Singapore. That Sindarov is even playing for the world title is a historic achievement. His victory came two years after Gukesh became the youngest Candidates winner at 17, then the youngest undisputed world champion at 18. Together, they represent the youngest pairing ever to play for the world title by some distance. Sindarov will celebrate his 21st birthday on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12. Sindarov’s emergence is part of an extraordinary period of success for Uzbek chess. He helped the country win its first Chess Olympiad gold medal in Chennai in 2022, when Uzbekistan went unbeaten against a field of 186 teams. They followed it with a bronze in 2024 before another gold on home soil in Samarkand last year, cementing the nation’s place among the sport’s leading powers. And yes, that was him among the Uzbek fans supporting the White Wolves as they made their Fifa World Cup debut last summer in the US. The matchup also reflects the shifting geography at the top of the sport. Gukesh’s victory over Ding made him India’s second world champion after Anand and marked the first time in the competition’s 138-year history that two players from Asia had competed for the crown. Now it will happen for a second world title match in a row. The Fondation Martin Bodmer is a library and museum founded by a Swiss bibliophile who built his collection around what he considered the five pillars of world literature: the Bible, Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe. (Sounds about white.) Its 160,000 treasures include a Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare’s First Folio and a copy of Isaac Newton’s Principia Mathematica once owned by his great rival Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Not the worst backdrop for another battle of intellects. Jammu, Nov 24: The Lieutenant Governor, Manoj Sinha today paid homage to Baba Jitto and Bua Kaudi at the Annual Jhiri Mela. The Lieutenant Governor said the annual fair is a living symbol of faith, cultural heritage and collective consciousness.
He said the annual visit to Jhiri is a sacred pilgrimage and the deep spiritual bond associated with the place reflects centuries of devotion and reverence towards Baba Jitto.
Highlighting the legacy of Baba Jitto, the Lieutenant Governor said that his life represents an enduring message of truth, courage and justice. He noted that Baba Jitto’s struggle was not merely about a crop, but about protecting the dignity, rights and self-respect of every hardworking farmer.
“His sacrifice continues to inspire society to stand against injustice and uphold respect for labour. Baba Jitto’s message also transcends caste, class and community, and represents a shared national heritage,” he said.
The Lieutenant Governor emphasized that the true tribute to Baba Jitto and Bua Kaudi would be the creation of a society where no farmer is left alone in the struggle for rights and dignity. He called for a “Whole of Society Approach” to ensure inclusive development and social justice.
“We must build a society where every person receives respect, where social harmony endures, and where the benefits of development reach the last person in society. To contribute to a developed India, we must build a developed Jammu Kashmir, and three values must always remain at its foundation- truth, hard work, and mutual respect.
For this, farmers must continue their hard work. Teachers must educate the new generation in accordance with a changing world. Youth must come forward for innovation. Government officials must serve the public with complete dedication and every family must instil good values in young children. From ordinary citizens to government officials, everyone must remain honest in their actions, discharge their responsibilities with sincerity, and work together in difficult circumstances,” he said.
The Lieutenant Governor underlined the contributions of farmers in sustaining the nation and enriching its traditions. He highlighted the transformative impact of the Holistic Agriculture Development Programme (HADP) in UT, noting progress in agriculture, horticulture and dairy sectors through modern infrastructure, diversification and market-oriented reforms. He urged farmers, particularly small and marginal cultivators, to adopt modern technology and align production with emerging market demands.
The Lieutenant Governor also encouraged greater adoption of millet cultivation. He said the millet crops are climate-resilient and income-enhancing option in the face of irregular rainfall, rising temperatures and declining groundwater levels.
Calling upon youth to transform agriculture through technology, entrepreneurship and scientific practices, the Lieutenant Governor urged them to view farming and allied sectors as dynamic engines of growth.
“Jammu Kashmir's agricultural landscape offers immense opportunities for innovation and employment, and youth must play a leading role in making farming more productive, profitable and future-ready,” the Lieutenant Governor said.
He also commended the growing participation of women in the rural economy. The Lieutenant Governor said that women farmers, self-help groups and rural entrepreneurs are playing a pivotal role in driving economic self-reliance across Jammu Kashmir. He called for expanded opportunities in education, skill development and entrepreneurship for women in rural areas.
“Many self-help groups are now working alongside women farmers to give a new direction to the rural economy. The women in villages are setting new examples of economic self-reliance through local products, handicrafts, food processing, and small enterprises. In the agriculture and allied sectors, our daughters are setting new benchmarks of innovation and entrepreneurship," the Lieutenant Governor said.
Highlighting the rich legacy of Dogra culture, the Lieutenant Governor urged the youth to take pride in their language, folk traditions and regional history. He encouraged the use of digital technologies to preserve and promote cultural heritage globally.
“Sit with your elders. Learn old songs from them, listen to folk tales, and learn the history of your region. Preserve such heritage through digital means, so that future generations can also become familiar with it.
I believe that technology today places in our hands a power through which we can take our culture to every corner of the country and the world. We must use this technology to introduce the world to the identity of Dogra culture,” the Lieutenant Governor said.
The Lieutenant Governor reiterated that the administration is making continuous efforts to ensure the smooth and efficient organization of the Jhiri Mela. The infrastructure here has seen significant improvement, and efforts will continue to expand it further as needed, he said.
On the occasion, the Lieutenant Governor visited the exhibition stalls set up by government departments, agri-entrepreneurs, Self-Help Groups and farmers. The event also featured a short play on Baba Jitto and Bua Kaudi, and captivating performances by artists showcasing the region's rich art and cultural heritage.

A version of this article first appeared on the Substack of “Why Should I Trust You?”
On Tuesday, after the United States lost its measles elimination status, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that he wanted to stop measles from spreading in America. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”
Well, Secretary Kennedy, do I have an idea for you …
It involves mobilizing a movement you helped build, a movement that has successfully organized millions of Americans around issues related to their health. I’m talking about MAHA.
Right now, the discourse is playing out like this: Medical societies are expressing alarm over the loss of measles elimination status, while many politicians blame Kennedy and the Trump administration for failing to adequately respond.
Kennedy’s defenders clap back by reminding us that other countries have lost elimination status in recent years, too, that these are all efforts to undermine Kennedy and that his administration is doing what it can.
I understand on some level that, as a society, we need to litigate what went wrong. But candidly, I’m much more interested in something else: Who might be best positioned to reach the Americans that public health officials are struggling to persuade to get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine?
What I learned from listening
I’ll start by saying that I believe in the measles vaccine. I was vaccinated as a child. I’ve vaccinated my two kids. I don’t identify as particularly vaccine skeptical. I’ve sometimes wondered why we have so many vaccine recommendations in this country compared with others, but I generally trust my doctors and haven’t (yet) experienced any major adverse reactions that might have led me to question that trust.
Over the last two years of making the podcast “Why Should I Trust You?,” my co-hosts and I have had the privilege of speaking with many people who feel quite differently than I do about vaccines, public health, and the medical system, and what they see as blind faith in expertise.
I’ve learned a tremendous amount. These conversations have made me question my own assumptions and better understand why I trust institutions, while sometimes realizing that I, too, harbor mistrust. While some of these conversations have been with people who are unwaveringly anti-vaccine, most have been with people who have taken some vaccines and harbor doubts about others.
They’ve also given me a front-row seat to something else: the MAHA grassroots movement’s astonishing ability to organize.
I’ve watched as MAHA supporters rally around pesticides, toxic pollutants in our air and water, microplastics, and PFAS (aka “forever”) chemicals. I’ve been to conferences and meetings, and been included in many group chats and Zoom meetings, where you can practically feel the energy around you: people exchanging ideas, meeting with lawmakers to draft legislation, and mobilizing others to organize local action. I constantly hear two questions: “What do you need? How can I help?”
That energy doesn’t seem to have disappeared after the midterms. But it’s definitely looking for places to go.
MAHA is politically weak right now. Candidates backed by the movement suffered significant electoral defeats, and there’s anger at the Trump administration over what seem like broken promises on pesticides, corporate influence, and environmental health. Yet the grassroots supporters haven’t given up. They’ve already been regrouping around issues like data centers and their effects on communities, while continuing to fight toxic pollutants and corporate influence. They don’t want to wait for the government or medical establishment to fix problems for them.
Measles presents a different kind of challenge. Public health officials need to reach parents who hesitate before vaccinating their children, including families in communities that view government institutions with suspicion.
I’ve heard from public health officials that many local health departments are so underfunded, they struggle to reach these families — and even when they have the resources, they may lack the cultural fluency or trusted relationships to connect with them.
But what if some of the people who could help actually share those families’ skepticism about pharmaceutical companies, admire Kennedy, or prefer alternative medicine — yet believe the MMR vaccine is worth getting?
Spoiler: Most MAHA parents trust the MMR vaccine
MAHA is not a fringe movement. According to KFF’s analysis of the 2026 midterm election, roughly 3 in 10 voters said they support MAHA, including 21% who strongly support it.
And, perhaps surprisingly, most MAHA-supporting parents vaccinate their kids. A separate KFF/Washington Post survey found that 86% of MAHA-supporting parents believe it’s important for children in their communities to be vaccinated against measles. Nearly 8 in 10 expressed confidence in the safety of the MMR vaccine. And about 75% reported that their children were up to date on routine childhood vaccinations, excluding Covid and flu.
Truthfully, very few MAHA supporters I’ve met haven’t taken MMR or vaccinated their children against polio, even if on a delayed schedule. I’ve met plenty who feel differently about Covid, flu, or the hep B birth dose, and certainly there are those who reject MMR. But among rank-and-file supporters, I’ve encountered far fewer MMR skeptics than you might expect from listening to some of the movement’s most prominent influencers. Which is important for the challenge at hand: You can believe deeply in MAHA’s core concerns about food, pesticides, water, chronic disease, and even have mistrust in flu and Covid shots — but still have confidence in the value of the measles vaccine.
We don’t acknowledge this enough. Some of MAHA’s most prominent vaccine skeptics may not speak for the broader movement when it comes to MMR.
The science on MMR is clear: Two doses are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles. But knowing the facts and trusting the person delivering them are two very different things. A fact like that can land differently when it comes from someone who has wrestled with the same doubts you have.
Roberta’s story: a Kennedy supporter who trusts MMR
I think about Roberta Devers, a mother and midwife practicing in Lancaster County, Pa., whom my colleagues and I met working on an episode about the measles outbreak there.
Roberta was vaccine skeptical, a Kennedy supporter, and chose not to vaccinate her son when he was a baby. But after seeing what measles was doing to people in Lancaster County, she changed her mind. She believes MMR is effective against measles and encourages Amish families in outbreak areas to get vaccinated, too. She tells me she now gets one or two calls a week from families who want to get vaccinated.
What’s particularly interesting to me, though, is what hasn’t changed.
Roberta still admires Kennedy. She hasn’t suddenly decided the medical establishment deserves her trust. If anything, she tells me the measles outbreaks are a reflection of a lack of trust communities continue to have for health systems. One of her ongoing campaigns is to fight for home-birth midwives to receive the same recognition as those working in hospitals. She talks about holistic living, alternative medicine, eating whole foods, even using brown paper toilet paper because she believes in living close to the earth. She hasn’t changed her values or worldview. She’s simply reconsidered what she believes about measles vaccination.
Imagine a vaccine-hesitant parent hearing from someone like Roberta, who shares many of their concerns but has seen measles up close and reached a different conclusion. Roberta doesn’t need to defend pharmaceutical companies or persuade anyone that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is always right. Just telling her story could lead to a conversation that perhaps a public health official would have a harder time brokering.
I’m not suggesting this movement will suddenly lead the charge on getting Americans vaccinated for measles. Some of MAHA’s most influential voices have spent years not just questioning, but actively sowing distrust in vaccines, including MMR, using claims not rooted in scientific fact. And I expect for many, encouraging vaccination, even during an outbreak, would be a bridge too far for them, a betrayal of their principles.
And organizing a rally isn’t the same as running a public health response.
But shouldn’t we at least try to make an active effort to reach MAHA supporters who believe in MMR? Because the polling shows it looks like there are a lot of them.
In his statement, Kennedy said his department is working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. He also promised to collaborate with trusted health care providers and community leaders.
He could start by elevating voices who support MMR. People like Devers, who can speak to vaccine-hesitant families with credibility and trust that public health institutions often lack. Find more people like her.
Then encourage those MAHA supporters who trust the measles vaccine to organize conversations about measles prevention. Bring in trusted physicians or other clinicians to answer questions. But also listen to families’ fears and doubts — because chances are, many MAHA supporters have wrestled with those same questions themselves. Help families find vaccines. Connect them with parents who share their values but have decided to vaccinate their children.
Would everyone in MAHA welcome that effort? Almost certainly not. Would Kennedy face backlash from the anti-vaccine wing of his movement? Very likely.
But for the past two years, MAHA supporters have pushed back against being characterized as anti-vaccine. Instead, they say, they are concerned about mandates, informed consent, conflicts of interest, and what they see as an unwillingness to acknowledge questions about safety.
Well, guys, here’s an opportunity to demonstrate what that distinction means in practice.
If you’re not anti-vaccine, helping people make informed decisions about a vaccine that the overwhelming majority of your own supporters trust shouldn’t betray your principles. It should express them.
The public health establishment has a responsibility here, too. If people within MAHA are willing to help, officials should work with them. That doesn’t mean overlooking misinformation or compromising on evidence. But it does mean recognizing common ground.
I know some readers will think I’m naive. Doesn’t she get that parts of MAHA have contributed to the distrust that makes measles prevention so difficult? I do. But even if parts of MAHA contributed to the problem, isn’t it worth asking whether some of its supporters might be particularly well positioned to contribute to the solution?
At a moment when MAHA is regrouping after an election rout, the movement now has an opportunity to demonstrate that it truly offers a big tent. Not by abandoning its core priorities, but by directing some of its powerful grassroots energy toward a disease affecting American children and their parents — the very people MAHA claims to put at the center of its mission.
Brinda Adhikari is a journalist and co-host of the “Why Should I Trust You?” podcast.

Squishies, the viral squeezable toy, are shaping up to be one of the hottest toys this holiday season, despite continued reports of explosions, burns, and toxic smells.
With Black Friday's shopping frenzy fast approaching, the parents of kids who have been hurt in squishy mishaps are urging families to choose carefully, and members of Congress are discussing possible action.
Coveted for their gooey, foamy, or gel-like textures, the collectibles are all over the lists of 2026's most popular holiday gifts. Amazon is making some of the most sought-after squishies available only by invitation. A squishy-themed Advent calendar sold out and was going for three times the price on the resale market.
There's a darker side to the trend. While millions have been sold and enjoyed without issue, some children have been badly burned by squishies. Regulators and poison-control lines have fielded thousands of complaints about noxious odors and toxic materials, especially from knockoff versions.
A new report from the US Public Interest Research Group calls squishies one of the five biggest threats this holiday season, noting that at least seven different squishy products have been marked as hazardous in recent months. Some contain water beads, which are restricted by the Consumer Product Safety Commission. A study out this month found that two different squishies caused anaphylaxis in one child with a latex sensitivity.
Earlier this year, Business Insider reported on the dangers associated with the squishy craze, and the regulatory gray area the toys fall into. Since our report in September, more kids have been hurt.
"People are buying more and more of them for the holidays," Alissa Heil, whose 9-year-old son, Joziah Garthwaite, was burned by a squishy, told Business Insider. "It's one of the reasons I want to warn parents about the dangers right now."
A 'blood-curdling scream' and a trip to the burn unit
It's been about a month since Joziah crept into the kitchen of his Iowa home and put a Needoh ice-cube-shaped squishy in the microwave — which the manufacturer warns against. He and a friend had put it in the freezer, and he wanted to heat it back up to squeeze, his mother said.
"He started screaming bloody murder," Heil said. "It was a blood-curdling scream, as if someone was stabbing him in the kitchen."
A visit to the ER and a follow-up with specialists confirmed Joziah had suffered second-degree burns on his arm between his elbow and shoulder, and rib area. He was put under general anesthesia twice to have the wounds treated, stayed for two nights at the University of Iowa's Health Care Burn Treatment Center, and will have to wear a compression sleeve over his arm to prevent scarring for at least six months.
It's a similar story to that of Amanda Hughes' son, Jaxsen, a 10-year-old in Richmond County, North Carolina. After seeing a TikTok of a man microwaving a squishy to make it stretchy — a popular social media trend — Jaxsen tried it himself. The squishy, which Hughes said was also made by Needoh, exploded onto his face. He ended up at UNC Chapel Hill's burn unit for three days.
"It was terrifying not knowing the chemical makeup of this stuff and the damage it could do," Jaxsen's mom told Business Insider. "It's marketed to kids. It's sold in toy stores everywhere."
She's thrown out Jaxsen's collection of "hundreds" of squishies and replaced them with a DIY non-toxic version made with balloons filled with shaving cream thickened with cornstarch.
A representative for Schylling, which manufactures NeeDoh squishies, did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. In the past, Schylling representatives have warned against misusing squishies and said it had partnered with social media companies to remove content promoting misuse.
Rep. Congressman Gus Bilirakis, the chairman of the Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee, told Business Insider in September that the group would work with the commission "to evaluate whether legislative action is necessary."
"Companies need to ensure their products are safe and clearly alert consumers when products pose a danger," another committee leader, Rep. Jan Schakowsky, told Business Insider this month. She said the CPSC must have adequate resources and that Congress should pass both the Sunshine in Product Safety Act and the Consumer Advocacy and Protection Act, which would increase accountability for unsafe products.
"Protecting children from dangerous products must remain a priority," she said.
'Tis the squeezon
Squishy toys generated $671 million in sales in the US through September this year, according to market research firm Circana. That's six times more than in the same period last year.
A holiday survey conducted by the National Retail Federation found squishies are the fourth most popular toy for girls this season, and the eighth most popular for boys.
"They are still the trending hot toy," Sky Canaves, a retail and e-commerce analyst at Emarketer, told Business Insider this month.
Target's list of must-have toys includes plenty of classics: Tickle Me Elmo, a Hot Wheels track, and Lego sets. There's also a full category dedicated to "squish, stretch, and surprise," including a mystery squishy dumpling and assorted squeezable ducks.
Five Below highlighted them seven times in a recent holiday toy announcement. Hershey's released a line shaped like Reese's peanut butter cups and Twizzlers, marketed as stocking stuffers. CVS put "must-have squishies like the Candy Swirl NeeDoh Nice Cube" at the top of its holiday gift list earlier this month.
There are plenty of reasons that the squeezable little objects are so popular, Canaves said.
Squishies have the appeal of being a viral toy — like a Labubu, for example — without the high price tag or the scramble to find one before it sells out. That means parents can help kids grow their collections without breaking the bank.
They are also free of screens or other technology, making them less distracting than other preteen preoccupations, and are less messy than slime — as long as they don't explode.
Ahead of the holidays, the Toy Association, a trade group, put out guidance on squishies. It warned against knockoff squishy toys, which are more prone to bursting or containing hazardous chemicals. It also cautions against heating, freezing, or puncturing squishies.
"This holiday shopping season, only purchase these toys from reputable sellers, beware of bargains, and check the packaging for misspelled words, missing info, or a lack of age-grading or safety warnings," the CPSC said in a statement to Business Insider. It warned against any squishies that have a strong chemical smell, feel oily or sticky, or are leaking.
Alissa Heil hopes government regulators will do more to ensure the safety of the toys.
"Can you really monitor your kids 24/7?" she said.

New Delhi- The BJP and Shiromani Akali Dal on Tuesday announced their alliance for the upcoming Punjab Assembly elections, describing it as a “national and emotional” pact.
Home Minister Amit Shah said the two parties will fight on all 117 seats in Punjab and that the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) will get the post of chief minister.
He also said that the NDA is now complete with the SAD coming back into its fold, and noted that their relationship goes back to the Vajpayee-Advani era.
Announcing the alliance at a press conference here along with Shah and SAD chief Sukhbir Singh Badal, BJP chief Nitin Nabin said the two parties will work together to make Punjab a developed state.
Badal said it was not a political but an emotional alliance.
Shah said a detailed manifesto would be finalised soon by the two parties for the elections, but eradicating the drug menace from Punjab and working together for the welfare of farmers and promoting Hindu-Sikh unity would be among the key focus areas.
Elections are expected to be held in the state early next year.
The SAD had snapped its 24-year-old alliance with the BJP in September 2020 over the now-scrapped three farm laws.
Earlier, Lok Sabha MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal was also part of the Modi government as a minister with Cabinet rank.
In the 2022 assembly polls, the BJP won two seats, and the SAD could register victories in three assembly segments out of a total of 117.
Prior to the end of the electoral alliance, both the Akalis and the BJP used to contest together. As per the previous pact in the assembly polls, the BJP used to contest 23 seats and the SAD 94 assembly seats.
In parliamentary polls, the SAD used to fight for 10 seats and the BJP the remaining three.

India’s teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi etched his name in the history books on Tuesday (November 24, 2026), shattering the world record for the fastest double hundred in List A cricket with a 52-ball blitz against the UAE in the Rising Stars Asia Cup.
Sooryavanshi surpassed the record held by Chad Bowes, who scored a 200 off 103 balls for Canterbury against Otago in the Ford Trophy in 2024.
The 15-year-old left-hander was eventually dismissed for 204 off 53 balls. His innings contained seven fours and an astounding 28 sixes, as he scored at a strike rate of 384.90.
India A defeated the UAE by seven wickets to reach the semifinals of the Rising Stars Asia Cup, chasing down a 250-run target in just 14.2 overs.
Other batters on the list of fastest List A double hundreds include England captain Harry Brook, who achieved the feat against Sri Lanka in an ODI earlier this year, Australian opener Travis Head and Tamil Nadu batter Narayan Jagadeesan.
Brook, Head and Jagadeesan reached the landmark in 114 balls.
Sooryavanshi also surpassed Australian Jake Fraser-McGurk’s record for the fastest List A century, his effort coming in 28 balls. Fraser-McGurk took 29 balls in his innings in 2023.
The third-fastest century belongs to South African great AB de Villiers, who smashed a 31-ball hundred against the West Indies in 2015.
Having struck 28 sixes, Sooryavanshi reached the record-breaking milestone with a four down the ground off Ibrar Ahmad.
He had modest returns in his first two outings in the competition.
